asic.competition.takeaway: Broadcom is the de facto monopolist at the top end thanks to a unique combination: it designs both the accelerator and the networking gear for it. Marvell is a clear no. 2 but is losing share despite growing in absolute terms. The only real contender to dilute the duopoly is MediaTek, through Google. The EDA duopoly (Synopsys/Cadence) is invulnerable: every new custom chip is designed on their tools.

asic.demand.customerConcentration: Critically high: ~5–6 customers (Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic) are effectively the entire market. Losing one customer collapses the shares (example: Marvell fell ~13% in a month in July 2026 after rising +251% in a year).
asic.demand.pricing: NRE: $100–500M per programme. The full cycle for the customer: $2–5B. A custom chip saves 40–65% per workload against GPUs — which is what makes the switch irreversible.

asic.intro:
A custom AI accelerator (called an ASIC, or XPU) is a chip built for one specific customer's task rather than a general-purpose GPU. Large cloud operators order such chips because, measured against their own workload — usually inference on their own model — they come out 40–65% cheaper than buying GPUs. But the customer does not make the chip itself: design and manufacturing are spread across a long chain of contractors.

How it works. First the specification is fixed: exactly which operation the chip must perform and within what power budget. The chip's behaviour is then described in a specialised language, the logic is assembled from billions of transistors and physically laid out across the die in design software — standard blocks (processor cores, memory controllers, high-speed interfaces) are licensed rather than drawn from scratch. The finished layout is sent to the fab; that step is called tape-out. From it a set of photomasks is made: on a leading-edge node that means dozens of masks costing tens of millions of dollars. The fab then prints the dies, and at final assembly the die is placed on one substrate with HBM memory — without memory sitting close by, the accelerator will not get the bandwidth it needs. To make thousands of such chips compute one model as a single device, high-speed network switches are placed between them.

The most expensive and unrecoverable part is the act of development itself. There is no right to a mistake after tape-out: if a bug is found once it is in silicon, the chip is redesigned and the whole mask set remade — another few months and tens of millions of dollars per cycle. So the bulk of the budget goes not to manufacturing but to design and verification: the one-off development fee (NRE) for a single programme is $100–500M, and the full cycle of bringing out a custom chip costs the customer $2–5B. These costs are fixed — they barely depend on volume. Which means the saving against GPUs only appears at large scale, when the development cost is spread across hundreds of thousands of chips; a custom chip makes sense only for the few whose own demand is measured in gigawatts.

Who pays, and how much. Only five or six cloud operators order custom chips; their combined capex in 2026 is estimated at $660–690B, around 75% of it on AI infrastructure. They pay almost any price for a simple reason: at their query volumes, a 40–65% saving on every workload repays the development in under a year, and dependence on a single GPU supplier is removed. Contracts run years ahead and at gigawatt scale; the largest design contractor alone holds a $73B AI order book, of which about $53B is custom accelerators.

The custom-accelerator market is around $40B in 2026 (estimates range from $13B in 2024 to $150B by 2030). By chip count, custom parts overtake GPUs as early as 2027, but by revenue GPUs stay larger — the difference is price per unit. The design work itself is held by two contractors: one with ~60–85% of the market, the other with ~8–12%.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

A customer can change the accelerator design, but not Broadcom's networking chips (Tomahawk, Jericho): that is what its 60–85% share and ~65% margin rest on — higher than the pure design services (Alchip ~24%), which sell only engineering hours.

asic.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: the only one that designs both the accelerator and the network for it (Tomahawk/Jericho/SerDes). Hence ~60–85% of the market. It is the network, not the die, that cannot be routed around when leaving Nvidia.
asic.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: an 18–24 month joint design cycle with the customer's and the house's engineers working side by side. Changing partner means losing 2 years and starting again on a leading-edge node.
asic.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: a relationship with TSMC at 3/2 nm and priority on CoWoS packaging. Insurmountable for a newcomer: TSMC's 3 nm is at ~100% utilisation against demand three times capacity.
asic.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: thousands of engineers with 3/2 nm experience; every new node needs more people and more trial runs. That strengthens those already there, but does not make the position permanent.
asic.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: a weakening vector: Google has already added MediaTek and Intel Foundry, and Amazon designs Annapurna internally. As soon as volume justifies an in-house team, the design house loses the programme.
asic.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: Nvidia invested $2B in Marvell and opened NVLink Fusion to third-party chips, aiming to pull custom accelerators onto its network. If it works, the design house becomes a contractor rather than an independent supplier.
asic.moatBreakdown.takeaway: Broadcom's protection is real and rests on the network plus TSMC access: five of the six factors are strong. But two vectors weaken at once — hyperscaler insourcing and absorption into Nvidia's ecosystem. Marvell's protection (share falling toward ~8%) is markedly thinner than Broadcom's — these are assets of different quality under one theme.

asic.problems.items.0.gap: Building your own leading-edge fab costs $20–30B and takes years, and TSMC's 3 nm capacity and CoWoS packaging (chip and memory packaged together) are already contracted out through 2028 — a new player simply gets no allocation. To guarantee itself a place, AWS raised its packaging order by +1,300% at once (from ~5,000 to ~70,000 wafers), directly crowding out others. Until Intel Foundry is running, there is no alternative to TSMC at the leading edge.
asic.problems.items.0.problem: A custom chip can be designed, but there is nowhere to physically manufacture and assemble it. Every leading-edge accelerator is printed by TSMC on the 3 nm node, which in 2026 runs at nearly 100% utilisation against demand roughly three times capacity; then it has to be packaged together with HBM memory (ultra-fast memory next to the chip) using CoWoS (chip and memory on one substrate) — and packaging has become the scarcest link: capacity doubles from ~70K to ~140K wafers a month, while demand is around 1M wafers in 2026. The full cycle from start to first samples takes 18–24 months. Access to a leading-edge fab and to packaging, not the design, is what limits how many custom chips exist at all.
asic.problems.items.0.solution: TSMC is doubling CoWoS capacity (packaging chip and memory together) across 2026–2027 and starts the 2 nm node at the end of 2027 for the next chip generation. A second source is appearing: Google added Intel Foundry as an alternative fab for its TPUs (its own AI accelerators) from 2028 — the first real signal of diversification away from TSMC. New packaging is also developing (hybrid bonding, panel assembly), which takes part of the load off CoWoS. The solution is bringing physical capacity online, so it is stretched over years.
asic.problems.items.0.winners: TSMC captures most of the benefit: near-monopoly control of leading-edge nodes and packaging means it monetises the expansion itself. Broadcom wins second — as the largest design house (chip-design contractor, ~60–85% of the market) it has contracted wafers, HBM (ultra-fast memory) and substrates through FY2028 and gets a priority allocation. Closest to TSMC's quotas are the contractors with privileged access — GUC (affiliated with TSMC) and Alchip (AWS's partner on leading-edge nodes).
asic.problems.takeaway: Relieving this shortage entrenches today's leaders: the benefit of new capacity goes to TSMC and to Broadcom, which contracted it in advance, and the only door for a new player is Intel Foundry starting up as a second fab.

asic.roadmap.disruption.1.tech: NVLink Fusion — Nvidia pulls custom chips into its ecosystem
asic.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: The winners: GUC, Synopsys/Cadence (UCIe IP), TSMC (packaging).
asic.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: A new approach: instead of one enormous die, a set of small ones joined over the UCIe standard. GUC has already built a UCIe 64G prototype on TSMC 3 nm. This shifts value toward the developers of chiplet-interconnect IP and toward advanced packaging.
asic.roadmap.disruption.3.angle: Marvell's first CPO samples are 2027. Mass impact is 2–3 years out.
asic.roadmap.disruption.3.detail: Marvell (via the Celestial AI acquisition) and Broadcom (the Taurus 400G DSP) are preparing optics built directly into the chip. That will speed up data exchange between chips in a rack.
asic.roadmap.generations.0.note: co-designed with Broadcom; total workload cost ~44% below an Nvidia GPU

asic.roadmap.takeaway: Over the next 2 years the current programmes dominate (Ironwood, Trainium 3, Jalapeño) and Broadcom holds its position. The move to 2 nm (2027–2028) is the moment of vulnerability: that is when MediaTek and Intel Foundry could take a serious bite of share. The main question is not technical (the chips will get designed) but commercial: who captures the margin.

asic.scenarios.cases.0.note: a hyperscaler takes a large programme in house OR NVLink Fusion turns the house into a contractor; Marvell/GUC fall harder than Broadcom
asic.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
asic.scenarios.cases.1.note: the $73B order book converts, Broadcom holds share through its network, and insourcing moves more slowly than the market fears
asic.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
asic.scenarios.cases.2.note: the >$100B AI revenue target for 2027 is met, new customers arrive (after OpenAI's Jalapeño), and the multiple re-rates upward
asic.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~+12…+15%/yr (Broadcom, probability-weighted) — asymmetric to the upside on a low starting multiple
asic.scenarios.takeaway: The asymmetry here belongs to Broadcom: a ~20x starting point caps the downside (unlike Marvell/GUC at 67–88x), while the upside is order-book conversion and new customers. The bear case requires hyperscaler insourcing to actually reach training chips — and that is years away.
asic.supply.balance.0.detail: TSMC 3 nm at ~100% utilisation, demand ~3x supply; every large custom chip is made on this node
asic.supply.balance.1.detail: the move to TSMC 2 nm (TPU v8); initial volumes are limited
asic.supply.balance.2.detail: Broadcom has secured capacity through FY2028; new TSMC lines expand supply
asic.supply.capacityAdds.0.impact: the new process for the next generation of custom chips (TPU v8, the next Trainium)
asic.supply.capacityAdds.0.name: TSMC 2 nm
asic.supply.capacityAdds.1.impact: Google added Intel as a second fab for TPUs — diversification away from TSMC
asic.supply.capacityAdds.2.impact: the binding constraint: capacity doubles from ~70k to ~140k wafers/month, but demand is ~1M wafers in 2026
asic.supply.capacityAdds.2.name: Advanced CoWoS packaging
asic.supply.crowdingOut: Custom chips compete for the same TSMC and CoWoS packaging capacity as Nvidia's GPUs. AWS raised its CoWoS packaging order by +1,300% (from ~5,000 to ~70,000 wafers) — that is direct crowding out.
asic.supply.leadTime: 18–24 months from the start of design to first chip samples; on leading-edge nodes 2–3 trial runs are needed even for the same design
asic.supply.takeaway: Physical manufacturing is not the design houses' problem (Broadcom builds no fabs), but they depend on TSMC and CoWoS packaging. The move to 2 nm adds capacity, but initial volumes will be limited. Intel Foundry's entry through Google is the first real signal of diversification away from TSMC.
asic.supply.utilization: TSMC 3 nm: ~100%, with demand three times capacity
asic.thesis.bigIdea: The market argues about whose custom chip will beat Nvidia. That is the wrong question. On every custom chip — whoever ordered it — the same narrow circle earns: Broadcom, which designs them, and TSMC, which prints them. And here is the anomaly: Broadcom, the only player with a full stack, is priced like an ordinary semiconductor — not like the owner of the margin that it actually is.
asic.thesis.stream.1.t: Training and running AI models happens on Nvidia's accelerators, and Nvidia sells them at a gross margin of around 75%. For a hyperscaler spending tens of billions a year on chips, that 75% is someone else's profit stacked on top of its own costs. So the largest — Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft — began designing their own chips for their most repetitive, highest-volume workloads. A chip built for a specific workload saves the customer 40–65% of that workload's cost compared with buying GPUs.
asic.thesis.stream.10.t: Hence the industry's central argument: will custom chips kill Nvidia, or will Nvidia crush custom silicon? Companies are valued on the answer to that question.
asic.thesis.stream.11.t: The custom AI chip market by year, $B (spread of forecasts)
asic.thesis.stream.12.t: The numbers say both sides are right at once. By unit count, custom chips overtake GPUs as early as 2027 (~12.5M against ~10.9M) — they grow +45% a year against +16% for GPUs. But in money Nvidia holds ~70–75% of the accelerator market through 2030: its chips cost more per unit. The market is enormous for both.
asic.thesis.stream.13.t: But for an investor, «custom versus Nvidia» is the wrong question. Because the money does not sit in the chip itself.
asic.thesis.stream.14.t: The right question: who earns on every chip
asic.thesis.stream.15.t: Whichever chip wins — Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Meta MTIA, Microsoft Maia — the same narrow circle designs them all. Behind ~60–85% of all custom accelerators stands Broadcom. It is the only one with the full stack: the chip design itself plus the high-speed network that binds thousands of such chips into one cluster (Tomahawk/Jericho switches and SerDes links — the high-speed data lanes between chips).
asic.thesis.stream.16.items.0.label: Broadcom — the full stack (chip + network)
asic.thesis.stream.16.items.1.label: Alchip / GUC / other design services
asic.thesis.stream.16.items.1.note: they sell engineering hours, not IP
asic.thesis.stream.16.items.2.label: Marvell — design to order
asic.thesis.stream.17.t: Marvell is the number two (chips for Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia). But the key point: Broadcom gets paid on Google's chip, on Meta's chip and (reportedly) on OpenAI's chip. It does not care which hyperscaler wins the workload war — it collects its cheque from each of them.
asic.thesis.stream.18.note: There are only five customers — but each goes through the same narrow circle of design partners.
asic.thesis.stream.18.rows.0.3: Trains and runs Gemini; rents it out — Anthropic trains models on TPUs
asic.thesis.stream.18.rows.1.3: Anthropic trains on Trainium (project Rainier); Amazon invested ~$8B in Anthropic
asic.thesis.stream.18.rows.2.3: For its own services — Copilot and Azure
asic.thesis.stream.18.rows.3.3: Recommendation systems and inference on Llama models
asic.thesis.stream.18.rows.4.3: The first generation is being designed inside Broadcom
asic.thesis.stream.19.t: Why this business cannot be entered
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: precisely what the hyperscalers want to stop paying for
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: an own chip against a GPU on the same workload
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: custom chips as a share of AI-server cost, 2026
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: it was ~15% in 2024 — the share is growing fast
asic.thesis.stream.20.t: The protection rests on two things. First, networking IP. Anyone can draw a chip, but binding thousands of chips into a single cluster without losing speed is something a very narrow circle can do; Broadcom's SerDes lanes are its crown jewel. Second, money and time. One custom programme means $100–500M of unrecoverable development cost (NRE — paid before the first chip exists) and about two years, while the full cycle costs the customer $2–5B.
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.0.n: unrecoverable — paid before the first chip exists
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.1.l: the full cycle for the customer
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.1.n: repays in under a year when switching from GPUs
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: plus the queue at the fab
asic.thesis.stream.22.t: So only four or five companies on the planet can afford a custom chip — and all of them go through the same narrow circle of design houses. That concentrates the money rather than spreading it.
asic.thesis.stream.23.t: The real constraint is capacity, not ideas
asic.thesis.stream.24.t: And here is what the «whose chip is better» argument misses entirely: a chip can be designed, but there is nowhere to manufacture it. Every leading-edge accelerator is printed by TSMC on the 3 nm node (a generation of process technology), which in 2026 runs at nearly 100% utilisation against demand roughly three times its capacity. The chip then has to be packaged together with HBM memory (ultra-fast memory sitting next to the chip) using CoWoS (chip and memory on one substrate) — and packaging has become the scarcest link of all.
asic.thesis.stream.25.items.0.n: against demand roughly three times capacity
asic.thesis.stream.25.items.1.n: capacity is doubling — but demand is ~1M wafers
asic.thesis.stream.25.items.2.n: the queue cannot be sped up with money
asic.thesis.stream.26.t: How many custom chips exist at all is decided by access to the fab and to packaging, not by the design. And here Broadcom wins a second time: as the largest design house it has contracted wafers, memory and packaging years ahead. A newcomer simply cannot join the queue.
asic.thesis.stream.27.label: ONE CRACK
asic.thesis.stream.27.t: Google has added Intel Foundry as an alternative fab for its chips from 2028 — the first real signal of a move away from the TSMC monopoly. Worth watching, but the effect is years out.
asic.thesis.stream.29.t: The margin settles everything. It goes to those who own unique IP, not to those who do the work.
asic.thesis.stream.3.t: Why an in-house chip can beat Nvidia at all
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.0.label: Arm — architecture licences
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.1.label: Synopsys / Cadence — design software
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.2.label: Broadcom — the AI segment (design + network)
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.3.label: Marvell — design to order
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.4.label: Alchip — pure design service
asic.thesis.stream.30.t: Gross margin by layer of the chain
asic.thesis.stream.31.t: The pure design services (Alchip, GUC) sell engineering hours — a low margin and dependence on a couple of customers (Amazon alone is ~60% of Alchip's revenue). Broadcom sells IP — and keeps the margin.
asic.thesis.stream.32.t: What is priced in — and where the anomaly is
asic.thesis.stream.33.t: Nobody disputes the growth here: Broadcom's order book is $73B, with a target of more than $100B of AI revenue by 2027. The argument is about something else — who keeps the margin once the hyperscalers grow their own teams. And here is the anomaly: Broadcom, the only player with a full stack, trades at just ~20x earnings — like an ordinary semiconductor rather than the owner of the margin. A $1.85T mega cap priced as a middling name.
asic.thesis.stream.34.items.0.n: a $73B order book and a >$100B target by 2027 — cheap for a full stack
asic.thesis.stream.34.items.1.n: the price of flawless execution — on a falling share (down toward ~8%)
asic.thesis.stream.34.items.2.n: the most expensive in the sector — justified only by >50% growth with no stumbles
asic.thesis.stream.35.t: Our read: Broadcom is fair, closer to cheap; its network protects it from insourcing more than the price assumes. Marvell and GUC are the opposite case: their multiples leave no room for a single weak quarter (Alchip has already printed −29% in one).
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.0: A hyperscaler takes a large programme fully in house
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.1: The design house loses its richest contract — insourcing is real
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.0: Nvidia's NVLink Fusion connects third-party chips to its network
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.1: Broadcom's core IP (the network) is devalued — it becomes a plain contractor
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.0: TSMC and packaging capacity catch demand sharply
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.1: The shortage ends and pricing power falls across the whole chain
asic.thesis.stream.38.t: None of the signals is lit yet: insourcing is moving more slowly than the market fears, and the network remains the thing that cannot be reproduced quickly.
asic.thesis.stream.39.t: Where the sector is going — and where the money is going
asic.thesis.stream.4.t: To understand the bet you have to understand the engineering. Nvidia's GPU is a generalist: it can execute any task, but it pays for that generality in silicon and energy — part of the chip always sits idle on any given workload. A custom chip works from the opposite direction: it hard-wires ONE task (running a specific AI model) and throws away everything that task does not need. For a stable, repetitive workload that yields more computation per watt and per dollar.
asic.thesis.stream.40.t: Technically the sector is moving from a single chip to a whole system. The hyperscalers now design not just the accelerator but the network, the memory and the entire rack around it — vertical integration for control of the whole machine. The next battlefield is not the chip but the chip-to-chip network: whoever binds thousands of accelerators without losing speed holds the cluster's performance. Nvidia understands this and released NVLink Fusion, a technology that lets third-party custom chips connect to its network so it does not lose control of the interconnect. That is exactly where Broadcom's core strength lies (networking IP) — and exactly where its main risk lies too.
asic.thesis.stream.41.t: Where the money is going: hyperscaler capex (~$850B a year) is increasingly flowing into their own silicon. But they are not only paying for chips — they are paying to stake out an ecosystem. Amazon invested ~$8B in Anthropic so it would train models on Trainium. Nvidia invested $2B in Marvell. OpenAI is designing its chip inside Broadcom. Strategic stakes are a way of contracting demand for your own chip in advance.
asic.thesis.stream.42.items.0.n: a growing part flows out of Nvidia purchases and into their own silicon
asic.thesis.stream.42.items.1.n: an investment that locks in demand for the Trainium chip
asic.thesis.stream.42.items.2.n: even Nvidia invests in those who design custom silicon
asic.thesis.stream.43.t: What the hyperscalers are betting on: their own silicon, to escape Nvidia's margin and control their own roadmap — but they still go through Broadcom and TSMC. What the investor should bet on: not guessing whose chip wins, but buying the companies everyone passes through — plus the riskier pure design houses (Alchip, GUC) as leverage on the same trend.
asic.thesis.stream.44.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
asic.thesis.stream.45.t: Custom chips are not a passing fashion but a structural shift: custom silicon's share of an AI server keeps growing, and the hyperscalers will not stop running from Nvidia's margin. But what earns on that shift is not whoever's chip «wins» — it is whoever they all pass through.
asic.thesis.stream.46.t: Compressed into one thought: bet not on the chip but on the toll gate it passes through. Broadcom is the main bet (a full stack, a ~20x starting point that caps the downside, asymmetry to the upside). Marvell and GUC are the same theme but dearer and without a margin of safety. Alchip is, in effect, a bet on one Amazon contract.
asic.thesis.stream.5.t: Take Google's TPU. At its core is a systolic array: a grid of thousands of multipliers through which data flows straight through, rather than running back to memory each time. A neural network is essentially one large matrix multiplication, and here it runs as a continuous stream. A general-purpose GPU computes the same thing but keeps going back to memory — and spends more energy on the same result.
asic.thesis.stream.6.t: But the key is the split between tasks. Training a model is experimental and changeable: there Nvidia's flexibility wins. Inference — running an already-finished model billions of times in response to queries — is a stable, uniform task. That is what pays to hard-wire. And inference is becoming an ever larger share of all AI computation: a model is trained once and answers constantly.
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: a custom chip against a GPU on the same workload — by dropping the unnecessary silicon
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.1.n: in a data centre energy is a hard ceiling; the winner is not the fastest chip but the most efficient per watt
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.2.l: a growing share of all AI computation
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.2.n: a stable repetitive workload — the ideal candidate for hard-wiring
asic.thesis.stream.8.t: The flip side is fragility. A hard-wired chip does exactly what it was designed for superbly; if model architectures change noticeably, it has to be redesigned — while Nvidia simply adapts in software. So custom silicon takes not the whole market but its stable, high-volume core — precisely the part where the volume is created. That is what makes the shift structural rather than one-off: the more inference there is, the more hard-wiring there is.
asic.thesis.stream.9.t: The argument the whole market is having
asic.tldr.0: Custom AI chips (ASICs — bespoke chips for a specific task) are the fastest-growing threat to Nvidia's monopoly: their shipments grow ~45% a year against ~16% for ordinary GPUs (TrendForce, January 2026).
asic.tldr.1: Broadcom dominates (~60–85% of the market), with a confirmed $73B order book and a target of >$100B of AI-chip revenue in 2027. Six largest customers: Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and two others.
asic.tldr.2: Two main risks: concentration in 4–6 customers (losing one collapses the shares) and the threat that customers start designing chips in house.
asic.tldr.3: The most reliable positions are with the companies that get paid on every chip produced regardless of who ordered it: Broadcom (P/E ~20x, unique networking IP), and the chip-design software duopoly of Synopsys + Cadence — they earn on any custom chip, whoever ordered it.
asic.unitEconomics.costCurve: The design houses' main cost line is engineering talent, not equipment. Design cost rises with every new node: 2 nm needs more engineers and more trial runs. That raises the entry barrier and strengthens those already working at the leading edge.
asic.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Broadcom AI: ~50–65% (estimate); Marvell: ~52–59%; Alchip: ~24%; Faraday: ~47%. EDA/IP: Synopsys/Cadence ~85–90%, Arm ~95%.
asic.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: NRE per programme: $100–500M; the full cycle for the customer: $2–5B. A custom chip saves the customer 40–65% of a workload's cost against GPUs.
asic.unitEconomics.takeaway: The economics are simple: Broadcom and the EDA duopoly capture most of the margin because they own unique IP. The design services (Alchip, GUC) earn less — they sell engineering hours, not IP. For the customer a custom chip is a $2–5B investment that repays in under a year when switching from GPUs.
asic.unitEconomics.yields.0.note: a mature process, in volume production
asic.unitEconomics.yields.1.note: starts 2027; the first runs will carry a high scrap rate
asic.update.bottomLine: The growth is real and confirmed by contracts rather than forecasts. But the shares already reflect it. The entry point is not «buy now at the highs» but «build a position in Broadcom + EDA on a 15–30% correction» (such corrections are normal for this sector), holding MediaTek/Socionext as satellites.
asic.update.headline: Broadcom confirmed a $73B order book and a >$100B target for 2027 — but the valuations already embed it
asic.update.stories.0.detail: A 10 GW programme, deploying 2026–2029. OpenAI designs the architecture; Broadcom implements the chip and supplies the Ethernet network.
asic.update.stories.0.title: OpenAI unveiled Jalapeño — its first custom chip (jointly with Broadcom)
asic.update.stories.0.verdict: Another hyperscaler has chosen the custom route over dependence on Nvidia. That expands Broadcom's order book, but adds one more large customer to an already concentrated base.
asic.update.stories.1.detail: Six XPU customers: Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI + two unnamed. A $73B AI order book, of which ~$53B is custom accelerators. Q3 guidance: AI revenue $16B (+200%+ y/y). Anthropic turned out to be a ~$21B customer.
asic.update.stories.1.title: Broadcom Q2 FY2026: AI revenue $10.8B (+143%), a $73B order book
asic.update.stories.1.verdict: The leading design house confirms demand is not slowing. But the shares fell ~13% — the market found its pretext in the software segment.
asic.update.stories.2.detail: 18+ active custom programmes. Q2 guidance: $2.70B. Target AI revenue ~$11B in 2026. Counterpoint forecasts Marvell's share falling to ~8% by 2027 despite revenue doubling.
asic.update.stories.2.title: Marvell Q1 FY2027: revenue $2.42B (+28%), 76% from data centres
asic.update.stories.2.verdict: The second design house is growing in absolute terms but losing market share to Broadcom.
asic.update.stories.3.detail: Designs the inference versions of Google's TPU (v7e, v8i). It has asked TSMC for a 7x increase in CoWoS packaging volume by 2027.
asic.update.stories.3.title: MediaTek: a $10B ASIC business targeted by 2027 (CEO Rick Tsai)
asic.update.stories.3.verdict: The main contender to dilute the duopoly. If it holds Google it becomes a third force. But margins on the first programmes are thin, and the prototype slipped.
asic.update.stories.4.detail: Investors: Atreides, Nvidia, Apollo, T. Rowe Price. The CEO: «this is the last private round before an IPO». RISC-V for servers and AI.
asic.update.stories.4.title: SiFive raised $400M (Series G) at a $3.65B valuation
asic.update.stories.4.verdict: The alternative to Arm on the RISC-V architecture — no royalties, but a less mature software ecosystem.
asic.update.stories.5.detail: NVLink Fusion lets custom accelerators connect to Nvidia's network — convenient for the customer, but it makes the design house dependent on Nvidia rather than on its own networking. Joint reference designs: Marvell XPU + Nvidia CPU/NVLink.
asic.update.stories.5.title: Nvidia invested $2B in Marvell and opened NVLink Fusion to custom chips
asic.update.stories.5.verdict: A double signal: confirmation of custom chips' value, but at the same time Nvidia's attempt to keep them inside its own ecosystem.
asic.update.summary: The custom AI chip sector is at maximum acceleration: Broadcom reported +143% AI revenue growth, OpenAI unveiled its first in-house chip Jalapeño, and Marvell doubled its number of active programmes. But the shares have already played the story — Marvell rose 251% in a year, then fell 13% in July. The market no longer argues about growth (that is obvious) but about whether the design houses keep their share once the hyperscalers reach the scale that justifies their own teams.
asic.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: If the hyperscalers start designing in house, the binding constraint shifts to the development tools (Synopsys/Cadence — they cannot be replaced) and IP licences (Arm).
asic.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Broadcom: the only design house able to design an accelerator and supply the high-speed network for it at the same time (its own Tomahawk/Jericho switches + SerDes data-transmission technology). Hence ~60–85% of the market.
asic.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Medium for the design houses (their main cost is engineers, not fabs), but the customer pays for the fab: one programme costs $100–500M of NRE plus $2–5B for the full silicon development cycle.
asic.valueCapture.margins.2.source: Alchip ~24%, Faraday ~47% — depends on the NRE share
asic.valueCapture.takeaway: The durable margin belongs to those who own unique IP (Broadcom's networking) and tools (the EDA duopoly) — not to those who simply execute the order. The design services (Alchip, GUC) earn less and depend on a few large customers.
asic.verdict.bear.0: The hyperscalers (the big cloud owners) could take design in house: Google has already added MediaTek and Intel Foundry as alternatives to Broadcom, and Annapurna (Amazon) designs internally.
asic.verdict.bear.1: Nvidia is trying to keep custom chips inside its ecosystem: it invested $2B in Marvell and opened NVLink Fusion (the ultra-fast link between accelerators) to third-party chips — turning the design houses (the chip-design contractors) into dependent suppliers.
asic.verdict.bear.2: Share prices already embed years of flawless growth: Marvell ~67x forward earnings, GUC ~88x. At those multiples even a single lumpy quarter (as at Alchip: −29%) is a collapse.
asic.verdict.bull.0: The growth is confirmed by contracts: Broadcom's $73B order book, of which $53B is custom accelerators (bespoke AI chips), six customers, and a target of >$100B in 2027.
asic.verdict.bull.1: Custom chips are already 40–65% cheaper than GPUs per workload. Midjourney moved to Google's chips and cut its inference bill (the cost of serving queries to the model) from $2.1M to under $700K a month — a 3x saving. That is a decision with no way back.
asic.verdict.bull.2: The companies that earn on every chip win whatever the outcome: Synopsys/Cadence get paid for every project ($8–11B order book), and Arm for every chip produced (royalties +21% a year).
asic.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — the structural growth of custom AI chips: every new hyperscaler ASIC programme extends the demand.
asic.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the hyperscalers keep ordering custom chips from Broadcom and Marvell — or hire their own teams once the volumes justify it?
asic.verdict.sizing: The custom AI chip market: $12–13B (2024) → $30–70B (2026–2027) → >$100B (2030). The range is enormous because analysts count differently — from a narrow «the die only» to a broad «the whole system».
asic.verdict.summary: The growth is among the best in the whole chain, and the protection from competitors is the strongest, thanks to Broadcom and the EDA duopoly (the two makers of chip-design software). But the share prices already embed years of flawless execution: Marvell trades at ~67x forward earnings, GUC at ~88x. Cyclicality is medium — revenue depends on hyperscaler capex (what the big cloud owners spend on hardware) and is lumpy (NRE projects — the one-off chip development fee — start and end unpredictably: Alchip lost 29% of revenue in a quarter). The central question: will the hyperscalers keep outsourcing design — or hire their own teams and do without the middlemen?
asic.whatIsIt: A chip designed for one single task belonging to one specific customer — usually running their own AI model — rather than a general-purpose processor that can do everything. Large cloud owners order such chips because, at their enormous volumes, the computation works out markedly cheaper than buying general-purpose accelerators. The customer does not manufacture the chip itself: a long chain of contractors works on it, from design through to printing at the fab.
dram.competition.concentration: three players hold more than 90% of the market, but the product is standard
dram.competition.entryBarrier.verdict: Yes, and it is already happening
dram.competition.entryBarrier.why: Unlike HBM, a new player genuinely does enter here: the three leaders are deliberately ceding the cheap segment and the older generations to free up area for HBM — and CXMT is becoming the world's main source of new supply. The only things holding it back are its technological lag (1.5–2 generations) and the US ban on supplying EUV tools. This is the weakest protective link in the whole chain.
dram.competition.players.0.note: It regained first place in Q4 2025 — before that it had ceded to SK Hynix for the first time since 1992. Its average selling price rose 146% against the 2025 average.
dram.competition.players.0.tech: Moving to a new process (1c), catching up in HBM
dram.competition.players.1.note: Its share in ordinary memory is lower because of its HBM focus. For full-year 2025 it overtook Samsung on operating profit. Its chief calls 2027 «the worst year for supply in the industry's history».
dram.competition.players.2.note: The only American play. A record 84.9% margin, with ~$100B of future revenue contracted through 2030.
dram.competition.players.2.tech: The most advanced process (1-gamma with EUV lithography)
dram.competition.players.3.name: CXMT (China)
dram.competition.players.3.note: The main structural threat: its share rose from ~4% to ~8% in a year, with quarterly revenue +719%. Fab utilisation is 96%, with a plan to go from 320K to 420K wafers a month by 2027. Analysts expect ~11% share by 2028.
dram.competition.players.3.tech: 1.5–2 generations behind, with no access to EUV tools
dram.competition.players.4.name: Nanya, Winbond (Taiwan)
dram.competition.players.4.note: The main beneficiaries of the older-memory shortage: the three leaders are discontinuing it while demand remains. Cisco and Solidigm have even taken equity stakes in Nanya to lock in supply for themselves.
dram.competition.players.4.tech: Older memory generations (DDR4) and specialty types
dram.competition.switchingCost: This is the weak point of the whole story: memory is standard, near-identical across suppliers, and a customer can switch far more easily than in HBM. Servers still require qualification (a few months); computers and phones almost none. So when a surplus appears, prices fall fast.
dram.competition.takeaway: Formally this is a three-way oligopoly, but the product is standard, the customer can leave easily, and a new Chinese player has already entered and is doubling its share. Hence protection scores a 6 here rather than the 8 in HBM: the discipline holds exactly until someone breaks it.
dram.demand.backlog: The makers' inventories are nearly at zero — the exact opposite of early 2023, when 31 weeks of product sat in the warehouses. Even the largest computer makers with dedicated allocations are watching their stocks drain.
dram.demand.contractStructure: For the first time in ordinary memory's history, long contracts have appeared as in HBM: about half of world output is already under them, and analysts expect up to 70%. Micron has 16 agreements for 2026–2030 with ~$100B of contracted revenue; roughly 40% of them fix or cap the price, and a price floor guarantees a margin above the peak of any previous cycle. This is a fundamentally new thing for a commodity market.
dram.demand.customerConcentration: Demand has shifted to AI servers: Micron's data-centre revenue passed $25B in a quarter. Computers and phones are contracting instead. The whole cycle rests on the giants' data-centre spending (~$851B in 2026 and ~$1.15T in 2027 on BofA's estimate).
dram.demand.pricing: Next comes an expected +45% in Q3 and +30–40% in Q4 2026, and +40–45% across 2027 (Jefferies). Separately, TrendForce guides a more restrained +15–18% for Q3 — the divergence in forecasts is itself a signal that the consensus on the cycle top is coming apart.
dram.demand.soldOut.1.note: about half the industry is under long contracts
dram.demand.takeaway: Revenue visibility is unprecedented for a commodity market: half the industry is under contract, warehouses are empty, and the agreements specify a price floor. That genuinely softens the coming fall. But the flip side is that all the demand now hangs on the giants' AI spending: it was fear of a pause in that spending that knocked the shares down in July.
dram.dependencies.correlation: This market used to follow computer and phone sales. In the current cycle that link is broken: devices sell worse while memory gets dearer, because the price is set by a lack of supply. The practical conclusion: watch the giants' data-centre spending and memory spot prices, not computer sales.
dram.dependencies.downstream: Buyers have split. Only AI servers are growing (the giants' spending is ~$851B in 2026, ~$1.15T in 2027). Computers and phones are suffering: at HP, memory and storage jumped from ~15% to ~35% of a computer's cost in a single quarter, and Dell, HP and Lenovo raised prices 15–20%. Excellent news for the memory makers; a blow to demand for the device makers.
dram.dependencies.takeaway: The most reliable lower-risk way into the theme is ASML (NASDAQ: ASML): a monopoly on EUV tools, paid regardless of which maker wins share, and a far softer fall in a downturn than the memory makers themselves.
dram.dependencies.upstream.0.item: EUV tools — they print the finest layers
dram.dependencies.upstream.0.note: An absolute monopoly: 100% of the market. A growing dependency, because volume growth now comes through the move to finer nodes. SK Hynix ordered around 24 machines for $7B+, Samsung around 20. For the first time in its history ASML earned more from memory than from processors.
dram.dependencies.upstream.1.note: Three players split the market. Direct beneficiaries of the process transition and, in future, of vertical memory.
dram.dependencies.upstream.2.note: The finer the process, the more it matters to find defects. A steady business, less cyclical than the memory makers.
dram.dependencies.upstream.3.note: The raw material for memory itself. A narrow set of suppliers; demand rises from memory and HBM at the same time.
dram.dependencies.upstream.4.note: Manufacturing consumables: usage grows with output, and quality is critical.
dram.expectations.impliedGrowth: A forward P/E of 4–8 (Micron ~6, SK Hynix ~4.4, Samsung ~4.9) on a record 80%+ gross margin embeds falling profits outright: the market expects margins to return to the mid-cycle 35–45%. This is peak pricing, not cheapness.
dram.expectations.marketBelieves: The market thinks the top is already in view: the shares fell >20% from their June highs on record results, and Michael Burry opened a position against Micron. Memory has historically turned 1–2 quarters before the profits deteriorate.
dram.expectations.metrics.0.history: memory trades at 8–15x through the cycle
dram.expectations.metrics.0.note: a low P/E on a record margin means the market expects profits to fall; the classic cycle trap, not a signal to buy

dram.expectations.takeaway: A low P/E here is not a signal to buy but a warning: the market is valuing the peak profit of a commodity cycle and pricing its fall in advance. The one novelty is floor-priced contracts, which could make the trough higher than past ones. The bet is not on cheapness but on the duration of the shortage.
dram.expectations.verdict: optically cheap, but fair once the cycle turn is allowed for
dram.expectations.weThink: The shortage is physically irreducible before 2027 — the new fabs cannot arrive in time, and floor-priced contracts make the trough higher than in past cycles for the first time. But this is the most commoditised part of memory, and the market is broadly right to price a turn — the argument is not about direction but about the date: H2 2027 against 2028.
dram.intro:
DRAM (DDR5 in servers and computers) is working memory — what the processor is operating on right now. A single bit is held in a cell made of one transistor and one capacitor: the capacitor holds an electrical charge (charge present is a one, absent is a zero) and the transistor opens access to it. The charge leaks away within milliseconds, so the cell has to be recharged constantly — hence «dynamic» memory, and hence the fact that it forgets everything without power. These are the same dies that go into HBM, but laid out in a single layer rather than assembled into a stack. The product is standard and interchangeable: all three makers' versions are almost identical.

How capacity is increased, and why it comes down to money. To get more memory from one wafer, the cell is shrunk from generation to generation — that is the move to a finer node (1α → 1β → 1γ). But shrinking a cell is harder in DRAM than in logic: the capacitor has to hold enough charge for the bit to read reliably, and as the cell shrinks there is less and less room for it. So the capacitor is built not flat but as a deep, narrow «well» with an enormous height-to-width ratio, and at leading-edge nodes drawing structures that fine requires EUV lithography — expensive machines made by the world's only supplier. Every node step demands a new set of equipment, and it is the cost of that step, not a physical limit, that determines how fast bit output grows.

Why bit growth comes down to capital. Memory can be added two ways: build new fabs, or shrink the cell in existing ones. Construction has all but stopped — industry investment rose only 14% in a year (to $61B) against 30–50% in previous expansion phases, and it goes not into new ordinary-memory lines but into HBM and the move to a finer node. Meanwhile every wafer switched to HBM consumes the area of roughly three ordinary-memory wafers. The result: bit output grows only ~16% in 2026 against a historical norm of 20–30%. That is the essence of this link: supply is governed not by demand but by the makers' decision about how much to invest in capacity — and it is that restraint that creates the shortage.

Who pays, and why they pay in advance. Hence a paradox worth understanding before buying: PC and phone sales fall 10–15% in 2026, while the price of memory rises by nearly 100% in a quarter — the price is set by a lack of supply, not by a desire to buy. It has reached the point where the older DDR4 generation costs more than the new one in places, because it is being discontinued. For the first time in the commodity memory market, long contracts have appeared, as in HBM: about half of world output is already under them (analysts expect up to 70%), Micron has 16 agreements for 2026–2030 with ~$100B of contracted revenue, and some of them specify a guaranteed price floor. Buyers accept prepayment and such contracts because the makers' inventories are nearly at zero and all the demand now hangs on the giants' spending on AI data centres (~$851B in 2026 on BofA's estimate).

The key difference from HBM: there are no long customer qualifications here and no technological advantage that cannot be copied. This is the most commoditised and most cyclical part of memory, and every previous shortage ended in a collapse — the shares fell 50–60%. The market: three players hold more than 90% (Samsung ~38%, SK Hynix ~29%, Micron ~22%), plus China's CXMT at ~8% and rising; the price per bit added +93–98% in Q1 2026.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.
dram.marketSizing.bomShare.note: of a computer's cost now goes to memory and storage — it was ~15% only a quarter ago (HP data). That is why Dell, HP and Lenovo raised computer prices 15–20%: the memory increase has reached the end buyer.

dram.marketSizing.takeaway: The growth is almost entirely price rather than volume — the most fragile kind: it turns first, the moment supply catches demand. The slowdown from +95% to +45% a quarter has already begun. The direct beneficiaries so far: Micron (NASDAQ: MU), SK Hynix (KRX: 000660), Samsung (KRX: 005930).
dram.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.mix: Demand rests on AI servers alone (+20%+ in 2026). Computers and phones are actually falling 10–15% in units, precisely because memory got more expensive and devices got dearer. The cycle has one support: the giants' spending on data centres.
dram.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.price: Prices have passed peak rate of growth: +20% in Q4 2025, +95% in Q1 2026 (an all-time record), +60% in Q2, with +45% expected in Q3. The growth is still enormous, but slowing — the first sign that the cycle is passing its top.
dram.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.volume: Volumes are barely growing — that is the key nuance. Micron's memory sales rose 211% over nine months, but shipped volume only ~30%; all the rest came from price. Taiwan's Nanya actually saw volume FALL while revenue rose more than 70%. That is the signature of a market squeezed by a lack of supply, not by rising demand.

dram.mentalModel.drivers.1.note: every gigabyte of HBM takes three times the silicon — that is the cause of the shortage, not demand. But from Q1 2026 ordinary memory became more profitable than HBM per wafer, weakening the incentive to convert area to HBM — a balance worth watching.
dram.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: its share rose from ~4% to ~8% in a year, with quarterly revenue +719%; an $8.55B IPO funds a tripling of output. It targets the cheap segment the three leaders are ceding — the trigger that breaks the discipline and the price.
dram.mentalModel.framework: A standardised commodity: all three makers' product is near-identical, so the price is set entirely by the balance of supply and demand. Right now it is held up by a wafer shortage caused by capacity being switched to HBM, not by rising demand. Costs are almost fixed, so a price rise falls straight to profit — and disappears just as fast on a turn: every previous shortage ended with the shares falling 50–60%.
dram.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = bits shipped (growing weakly, ~16%) × price per bit (set by the shortage: +93% in a quarter at the peak)
dram.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: a new memory fab costs $30–50B and takes 18–36 months; that capital threshold is still high for a newcomer and keeps the market at three players plus one.
dram.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: the US ban on supplying EUV tools holds China back — but that is policy, not a property of the business: restrictions have been imposed and lifted within weeks, and CXMT covers China's domestic market without EUV anyway.
dram.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: Micron and SK Hynix produce at the lowest cost; CXMT is 1.5–2 generations behind with no EUV access, a large die and heavy scrap. But that is a lag, not brand protection — and it is narrowing.
dram.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: for the first time in commodity memory, long contracts have appeared: ~half the industry is under them (analysts expect up to 70%), with Micron at ~$100B through 2030 including a price floor. It will soften the downturn — but it is a novelty, untested by a turn.
dram.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: three players hold >90%, but the product is standard: discipline is a decision, not a property of the market, and it holds exactly until someone breaks it. CXMT has already entered and is doubling its share.
dram.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the weakest link: memory is standard and near-identical across suppliers, and for computers and phones there is barely any qualification. Customers leave easily → when a surplus appears, prices fall fast.
dram.moatBreakdown.takeaway: There is almost no protection here in the classic sense — the product is a commodity and switching is easy. It all rests on the capital threshold, export controls against CXMT, and the three makers' voluntary discipline. The novelty is the floor-priced contracts: they will soften the trough but will not abolish the cycle. Discipline breaks first when China scales output — hence an honest six rather than the eight in HBM.

dram.picksTakeaway: The pure play is Micron (DRAM + HBM on a US exchange): upside if the shortage is structural rather than cyclical. SK hynix and Samsung are the same theme, more diversified and cheaper on the multiple. Equipment (Lam Research, Applied Materials) is the calmer way to play the new fab construction. The main risk for all of them is China's CXMT: keep the position small and watch its cheap-DDR5 output.
dram.problems.items.0.gap: The main contender, China's CXMT, is 1.5–2 generations behind and cut off from EUV tools by the US ban — and without them a finer node and more bits per wafer are unreachable. Its share rose from ~4% to ~8% in a year, but it runs straight into the equipment. Any new memory fab takes 18–36 months from decision to product, so there is nothing left to relieve the 2026–2027 shortage with, and CXMT's capacity (from 320K to 420K wafers a month) only reaches the market by 2027–2028.
dram.problems.items.0.note: one caveat here: the product is standard and a customer can change supplier more easily than in HBM — so the same restraint that creates the shortage turns into a price collapse at the first sign of surplus.
dram.problems.items.0.problem: Growth in ordinary memory is constrained by a shortage of silicon wafers, and there is physically nothing with which to relieve it quickly. Almost no new fabs are being built: industry investment rose only 14% in a year (to $61B) and goes not to volume but to HBM (the stacked memory used in AI accelerators) and the move to a new process. Meanwhile every wafer switched to HBM consumes the area of three ordinary-memory wafers. The result: bit output grows only ~16% in 2026 against a historical norm of 20–30%, while data-centre demand is several times higher and the price per bit added +93–98% in a single quarter.
dram.problems.items.0.solution: With no new fabs, the only way to add bits is moving to a finer process (the 1α → 1β → 1γ nodes — successive generations of ever-smaller memory cell): the finer the cell, the more bits per wafer. At leading-edge nodes that requires EUV lithography (printing ultra-fine structures on the wafer; the machines come from the world's only supplier), made only by ASML (AMS: ASML). Micron was first to run the 1-gamma node on EUV, with SK Hynix and Samsung catching up. So the industry expands by shrinking the cell rather than by building — and the next scarce link shifts to the supply of EUV machines.
dram.problems.items.0.winners: Micron (NASDAQ: MU) — the most advanced process (the 1-gamma node on EUV lithography) and a record 84.9% gross margin; more bits per wafer on the same equipment. SK Hynix (KRX: 000660) — the cost leader, which overtook Samsung on operating profit for full-year 2025. Both win because, with the wafer count fixed, the winner is whoever squeezes more bits out of each one more cheaply. ASML takes its share: without its machines the move to a finer node is impossible.
dram.problems.takeaway: Relieving it strengthens the same three: the winner is whoever moves output to a finer node first (Micron, SK Hynix), while entry for China is closed by the EUV ban. But the protection is weaker than in HBM: the product is a commodity, so the leadership holds exactly until the first surplus.
dram.risks.0.note: The defining risk. The pattern has always repeated: a 4–7 quarter upswing, then a 4–8 quarter downturn, revenue falling 25–40%, margins from 50%+ to the low 20s or negative, and the shares losing 50–60% and falling 1–2 quarters ahead of the results. Examples: Micron −56% in 2018–19, −50% in 2022–23, −77% in the 2008 crisis.
dram.risks.1.note: The largest structural threat. It targets the cheap segment the three leaders are ceding themselves. For now it is held back by its technological lag and the US ban on lithography tools, but after 2028 this is a real variable. Even Apple has reportedly been looking at buying from CXMT.
dram.risks.2.note: The classic «shortage → surplus» pattern. Warehouses are empty now (a plus), but if AI spending pauses the turn will be sharp because of the extreme operating leverage.
dram.risks.2.risk: The cycle turns and inventories build
dram.risks.3.note: Computers and phones are falling, so all the demand rests on data centres. It was precisely that fear that knocked the shares down in July 2026. Michael Burry opened a short position against Micron on 1 July.
dram.risks.3.risk: The whole bet hangs on the giants' AI spending
dram.risks.4.note: A double effect. The US ban on supplying advanced equipment to China holds CXMT back — a plus for the three leaders. The minus: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron face price-fixing suits amid record prices.
dram.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: The most realistic architectural change, but the net effect is close to zero. The controllers for it are made by Astera Labs (NASDAQ: ALAB) and Rambus (NASDAQ: RMBS).
dram.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: The technology lets several servers' memory be gathered into a shared pool and used more efficiently. In theory that reduces the need for new memory, but it simultaneously creates demand for separate expansion modules.
dram.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: It does not abolish the market but extends its growth. The main beneficiaries are the equipment suppliers: ASML (NASDAQ: ASML), Applied Materials (NASDAQ: AMAT), Lam (NASDAQ: LRCX).
dram.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Memory dies will start being grown vertically, as flash memory already has been. That allows density to keep rising once ordinary transistor shrinking hits its limit. Timing: 2027–2030 and beyond.
dram.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: No effect within the decision horizon. There is no replacement for ordinary memory in 2026–2028.
dram.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: Alternative storage principles that have been discussed for decades. None has come close to ordinary memory's economics on cost per gigabyte.
dram.roadmap.generations.0.note: The three leaders are discontinuing it, and by end-2026 volume could fall to 20–25% of the 2024 level. Hence the shortage and prices that in places exceed the newer generation — Nanya and Winbond win.
dram.roadmap.generations.1.note: It stays the main standard for several more years. The main source of volume growth is not new fabs but the move to a finer process.
dram.roadmap.generations.2.note: A new direction: compact modules for AI servers (SOCAMM) — a third the size of the usual kind and a third more efficient. Micron ships first.
dram.roadmap.generations.3.note: The next architectural revolution — by analogy with how flash memory went 3D. It will need new equipment: ASML, Applied Materials and Lam win.
dram.roadmap.generations.3.spec: a move to 8–9 nm, dies stacked on dies
dram.roadmap.generations.4.note: Far beyond the decision horizon. It does not affect the current investment.
dram.roadmap.takeaway: There is no technological threat to the product itself — nothing can replace ordinary memory. The risk here is different: the technology is itself the source of volume growth (the move to finer nodes), which means a glut can arrive without a single new fab, simply because the same area starts yielding more memory.
