dram.scenarios.cases.0.note: spot turns, CXMT dumps, inventories build — the precedents are Micron −56% (2018–19) and −50% (2022–23)
dram.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
dram.scenarios.cases.1.note: the shortage holds through 2027 and floor-priced contracts prop up the trough, but peak rate of price growth has already passed
dram.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
dram.scenarios.cases.2.note: SK Hynix's chief is right — the shortage runs past 2030, CXMT stalls without EUV, and the giants' AI demand does not slow
dram.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~0…+5%/yr (Micron, probability-weighted) — the asymmetry is skewed downward
dram.scenarios.takeaway: The asymmetry here is dangerous: the downside is a genuine halving (the precedents are Micron −56%, −50% and −77% in 2008), while the upside is capped because the entry is late and peak rate of price growth has already passed. This is a trade on the duration of the shortage with a hand on the exit, not a buy-and-hold position.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: Almost no new ordinary-memory fabs are being built: investment rose only 14% and goes to HBM and the process transition rather than to volume.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: The Idaho fab will not run before 2027, with meaningful volume only from mid-2027.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: The new M15X building will not add meaningful volume before mid-2027 either.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.3.detail: The P5 fab only arrives in 2028.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.4.detail: The world's main source of new supply: from 320K to 420K wafers a month by 2027, doubling by 2030 and tripling by 2035 — on IPO money.
dram.supply.crowdingOut: The older memory generation (DDR4) is a separate story. The three leaders are discontinuing it and a shortage has appeared: in places the price has passed the newer DDR5, lead times have reached 30–40 weeks, and individual parts have risen several-fold. That is a distinct source of profit for Nanya and Winbond.
dram.supply.leadTime: A new memory fab takes 18–36 months from decision to product. So everything being laid down now will only affect the market by 2028: there is nothing left to relieve the 2026–2027 shortage with.
dram.supply.takeaway: The shortage is guaranteed through 2027 — there is physically nothing to relieve it with, and that is the most reliable part of the thesis. The argument is about 2028: some expect a shortage past 2030, others (Bloomberg Intelligence) think the worst has already passed in the first half of 2026 and that 2028 brings a surplus. The exit signal is spot prices turning and CXMT's output rising.
dram.supply.utilization: The fabs are fully loaded, with no spare space in the industry. Volume growth comes almost entirely from moving to a finer process: on IDC's estimate, bit output grows only ~16% in 2026 against a historical norm of 20–30%.
dram.thesis.bigIdea: DRAM looks like an ordinary memory cycle about to collapse — and the market prices the makers cheaply (a forward P/E of 4–8). But this time the cycle is broken the other way: [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] for AI is eating the wafers (the same cell takes three times the area in HBM), and the big three — Samsung, SK hynix and Micron — have shifted ~93% of output to HBM. Ordinary DDR5 quadrupled in price over autumn 2025 and rose another +90% in a single quarter of 2026, and there will be no new fabs until mid-2027. The conclusion: the shortage is structural rather than cyclical; the pure play is Micron, and the main risk is China's CXMT.
dram.thesis.stream.0.t: What it is, and why the price took off
dram.thesis.stream.1.t: DRAM is working memory (DDR5 in servers and PCs), what the processor is operating on right now. In 2026 its price took off not from ordinary demand but because [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] for AI is taking its wafers: the same capacity occupies three times the silicon area in HBM, and the big three have shifted around 93% of their combined output to HBM. As a result ordinary DDR5 went from $6.84 to $27.20 a gigabyte over autumn 2025 and rose another +90% in the first quarter of 2026.
dram.thesis.stream.10.items.0.n: like a commodity ahead of a collapse
dram.thesis.stream.10.items.1.n: but the market gives no credit for it
dram.thesis.stream.10.items.2.n: the leading candidate to break the price
dram.thesis.stream.11.t: Where we differ from the market
dram.thesis.stream.12.t: The market is right that DRAM is a commodity cycle, but it underrates how long this shortage lasts. While HBM takes the wafers and there are no new fabs until 2027–2028, ordinary memory stays structurally starved — prices and margins hold longer than the familiar cyclical model assumes. The bear side is real too: the product is standard, the customer has no reason to stay with a supplier, and China's CXMT is scaling output and could flood the market with cheap memory — at which point the cycle turns sharply.
dram.thesis.stream.14.t: DRAM's cheapness is the price of the fear of a collapse. At a P/E of 4–8 the market embeds an imminent turn. If the structural shortage holds (HBM eats the wafers, the fabs run late), the makers are cheap; if CXMT floods the market or AI demand weakens, the collapse arrives as usual. The bet comes down to one question: is this shortage structural, or just another cycle peak?
dram.thesis.stream.15.t: Where it is going, and what would break the thesis
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.0.1: a commodity collapse comes closer — bearish for the three
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.1.0: HBM keeps taking wafers and DDR5 stays short
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.2.0: The new fabs (M15X, Micron, Samsung P5) arrive on schedule
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.3.1: HBM and all memory fall together — the cycle turns
dram.thesis.stream.18.t: DRAM offers the highest growth in the chain with the worst resilience to the cycle. This time the shortage is structural: HBM has taken ~93% of output, DDR5 has risen several-fold, and the fabs run late to 2027–2028. But the product remains a commodity, and the turn will be sharp.
dram.thesis.stream.19.t: The pure play is Micron (the only large DRAM and HBM maker on a US exchange). SK hynix and Samsung are the same theme but more diversified. Equipment (Lam Research, Applied Materials) is a calmer way to play the new fab construction. The main risk for all of them is China's CXMT: keep the position small and watch its output.
dram.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: of the big three's output goes to HBM
dram.thesis.stream.3.t: Why this is not an ordinary cycle
dram.thesis.stream.4.t: Memory usually lives by a brutal commodity cycle: boom → fab build-out → glut → price collapse. This time the constraint is different — structural. HBM gives a maker 5–10x the margin (an HBM module is $60–100 against $5–10 for comparable DDR5), so with wafers short it is rational to push HBM and keep ordinary memory starved. There is no new capacity until mid-2027: SK hynix's M15X fab and Micron's first wafers arrive mid-2027, Samsung's P5 in late 2028. SK hynix warns the shortage could run past 2030.
dram.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: M15X and Micron in 2027, Samsung's P5 in 2028
dram.thesis.stream.5.items.2.l: how far out SK hynix sees the shortage
dram.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: this is no longer a typical short cycle
dram.thesis.stream.7.t: The market is a tight three: Samsung, SK hynix and Micron split almost all DRAM output. They are the same three that make [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]], so the decision «this wafer to HBM or to DDR5» is taken by the same hands. Among the listed names, Micron offers the pure play on a US exchange; SK hynix and Samsung trade in Korea and are more diversified.
dram.thesis.stream.9.t: The market prices DRAM makers cheaply — a forward P/E of 4–8, like a commodity business ahead of a collapse. The logic is familiar: prices are at a peak, so a downturn and falling profits lie ahead. That is why the multiples stay low even on record revenue — the market refuses to pay for profit it considers temporary.
dram.tldr.0: The sharpest upswing in memory's history: contract prices +93–98% in a single quarter (a record), with record margins (Micron's gross margin at 84.9%, SK Hynix's operating margin at 72%). The cause is not demand but wafers being diverted to HBM (the stacked memory used in AI accelerators).
dram.tldr.1: The pivotal fact: in Q1 2026 ordinary DDR5 memory (the current working-memory standard) overtook HBM on profit per wafer. The most profitable product in a fab is now ordinary memory, not HBM.
dram.tldr.2: Prices are set by a lack of supply rather than by demand: the fabs are switching wafers from ordinary memory to HBM, and every gigabyte of HBM consumes three times the silicon. Almost no new fabs are being built (capex +14% in a year).
dram.unitEconomics.costCurve: The cheapest producers are Micron (the 1-gamma process with EUV lithography) and SK Hynix. The most expensive, with the most scrap, is CXMT: it has a large die and no access to EUV. That is the only thing currently restraining Chinese price pressure.
dram.unitEconomics.grossMargin: The cycle's key turning point: in Q1 2026 ordinary DDR5 memory (a 64 GB module) overtook HBM on both revenue and profit per wafer. HBM used to be four times more valuable. The consequence is twofold: it stopped paying for fabs to keep converting area to HBM, and the makers gained an argument for raising HBM prices sharply in 2027 — otherwise ordinary memory is the better product to make.
dram.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: Micron's average memory price has reached a 10-year high — roughly three times the early-2024 trough. Concretely: a 32 GB memory kit cost less than $80 in mid-2025, and by June 2026 nothing below $375 will buy one. Spot prices rose roughly 700% in a year.
dram.unitEconomics.takeaway: The key fact for the decision: ordinary memory is now more profitable than HBM per wafer — it is no longer the poor relation but a fab's most valuable product. But the operating leverage cuts both ways: when prices turn, the profit will fold as fast as it grew.
dram.unitEconomics.yields.0.label: Operating leverage
dram.unitEconomics.yields.0.value: At its limit: Micron's unit cost rose 10% while revenue rose 346% — nearly the whole price increase fell to profit. It works just as harshly in reverse.
dram.unitEconomics.yields.1.label: Where the industry's profit sits now
dram.unitEconomics.yields.1.value: Ordinary memory has become the main source of profit for all three: Samsung's memory division delivered ~94% of the company's entire Q1 2026 profit.
dram.unitEconomics.yields.2.label: Where margins will return to
dram.unitEconomics.yields.2.value: The historical mid-cycle norm is 35–45% gross, around 20% and below at the trough. Today's 80%+ is not a new reality but a peak.
dram.universe.0.exposure: memory is ~77–79% of revenue, mostly ordinary
dram.universe.0.note: The purest American play. A record 84.9% margin, with ~$100B contracted through 2030. Maximum leverage to a cycle turn — in both directions. Reports 22 September 2026.
dram.universe.1.note: The HBM leader, so its share in ordinary memory is smaller. Its chief is the loudest optimist on the shortage («and past 2030»).
dram.universe.2.exposure: memory is one part of the conglomerate
dram.universe.2.note: No. 1 by share in ordinary memory, but the exposure is diluted by phones and contract chipmaking. Memory delivered ~94% of Q1 2026 profit.
dram.universe.3.note: The purest bet on ordinary memory specifically, based on the older generations. Maximum leverage but maximum risk too, plus low liquidity. Cisco and Solidigm took equity stakes for supply.
dram.universe.4.note: A direct beneficiary of the older-generation memory shortage. Up nearly 9x in a year.
dram.universe.5.note: The lower-risk way to play the theme: paid regardless of which maker wins share, and it falls markedly less in a downturn. For the first time it earned more from memory than from processors.
dram.universe.6.exposure: equipment, memory is part of the business
dram.universe.6.note: It wins from the move to finer nodes and, in future, from vertical memory. The exposure is diluted, but the cyclicality is milder.
dram.universe.7.note: The highest memory exposure among the large equipment makers.
dram.universe.8.note: Less an idea to buy than the main risk to everyone else. Asia's largest IPO of 2026, with the retail tranche 244 times oversubscribed.
dram.universe.9.exposure: a basket: Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron ~73%
dram.universe.9.note: A simple way to take the whole theme as a basket without picking an individual name. The first pure memory fund, launched in April 2026.
dram.update.bottomLine: The bottom line: the shortage is real and physically irreducible before 2027 — the new fabs cannot arrive in time. But this is the most cyclical and most commoditised part of memory, where every previous upswing ended with the shares falling 50–60%, and the market has already begun pricing a top. The sensible decision is to take this as a 12–18 month bet on the cycle rather than a long-term position: size it to survive a halving, and set the exit conditions in advance. The main exit signal is spot prices turning and CXMT's output rising sharply.
dram.update.headline: Record prices — and a 20% fall in the shares: the market is pricing a cycle top
dram.update.stories.0.detail: Asia's largest IPO of 2026: 57.9B yuan (~$8.55B), with the retail tranche 244 times oversubscribed and a debut on 27 July. The money goes toward tripling production by 2035. CXMT's share has already risen from ~4% to ~8% in a year, with quarterly revenue up 719%. It targets exactly the cheap segment the three leaders are vacating for HBM.
dram.update.stories.0.title: China's CXMT lists with $8.55B
dram.update.stories.1.detail: On 1 July Michael Burry opened a position against Micron. Three weeks later Morgan Stanley called the same sell-off «an attractive entry point». SK Hynix's chief said (10 July) that 2027 will be «the worst year for supply in the industry's history» and that demand will exceed supply even past 2030. Meanwhile Bloomberg Intelligence thinks the worst of the shortage has already passed and that a glut is possible by 2028.
dram.update.stories.1.title: The professionals disagree
dram.update.stories.1.verdict: there is no consensus on the top
dram.update.stories.2.detail: From their late-June highs, Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix and the memory fund have lost more than 20% (Micron 28–40% in places). The cause is not the current numbers but the fear that the peak is already in view: a forward P/E of 4–8 says outright that the market expects profits to fall. The historical pattern is on their side — memory shares turn 1–2 quarters before the results do.
dram.update.stories.2.title: The shares fell more than 20% on record results
dram.update.stories.2.verdict: the market is pricing not the profit but its duration
dram.update.stories.3.detail: Contract prices added 93–98% in Q1 2026 — the largest single-quarter rise on record. But then: +58–63% in Q2, with +40–50% expected in Q3. The growth is still enormous, but it is slowing, and that is the classic sign of a cycle passing its top. Analyst forecasts have started to diverge: for Q3, Jefferies guides +40–50% while TrendForce guides just +15–18%.
dram.update.stories.3.title: Prices rose at a record rate, but the growth is slowing
dram.update.stories.4.detail: TrendForce (2 June 2026) confirmed it: in Q1 2026 ordinary DDR5 memory (a 64 GB module) overtook HBM on both revenue and profit per wafer. A year ago HBM was four times more valuable. The consequences matter: it stopped paying for fabs to keep converting area to HBM, and the makers gained an argument for raising HBM prices sharply in 2027.
dram.update.stories.4.title: Ordinary memory overtook HBM on profitability
dram.update.summary: July 2026 produced a rare picture: the best results in memory's history alongside falling shares. Here is what sits behind that, and what it means for the decision.
dram.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Next the constraint becomes the move to a finer process — currently the main source of volume growth in place of new fabs. That requires EUV lithography tools, made only by ASML: the binding constraint shifts to it.
dram.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: The binding constraint is the silicon wafers themselves: they are short because the fabs are giving ever more area over to HBM. Almost no new fabs are being built, so there is physically nothing with which to expand output quickly.
dram.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Industry investment rose only 14% in a year (to $61B) — against 30–50% in previous expansion phases. And it is directed not at new ordinary-memory fabs but at HBM and the move to a new process. It is precisely that restraint that creates the shortage.
dram.valueCapture.margins.3.margin: 35–45% gross, around 20% and below at the trough
dram.valueCapture.takeaway: Right now the makers take almost everything: at Micron, ~98 cents of every additional revenue dollar falls to gross profit. But this is the peak — the historical mid-cycle norm is three times lower (35–45%), and that is where profits will return to. Equipment (ASML) earns less at the peak but earns it steadily.
dram.verdict.bear.0: China (CXMT — a new Chinese memory maker) is flooding the market with cheap memory: its share rose from ~4% to ~8% in a year, an $8.55B IPO funds a tripling of production, and it is aiming precisely at the cheap segment the three leaders are ceding.
dram.verdict.bear.1: The cycle turns — as it always does: every previous shortage ended in a glut, with revenue falling 25–40% and the shares 50–60%. The current price spike is three times stronger than the 2017–18 upswing, so the fall could be deeper too.
dram.verdict.bear.2: The market has already priced the peak: the shares fell more than 20% from their late-June highs on record results, and a forward P/E of 4–8 says outright that the market expects profits to fall.
dram.verdict.bull.0: The shortage is structural rather than an ordinary demand cycle: wafers keep being diverted to HBM (stacked memory), SK Hynix's chief says demand will exceed supply beyond 2030, and half the industry is already under long contracts (potentially reaching 70%).
dram.verdict.bull.1: The makers are keeping discipline and not overbuilding: investment rose only 14% against 30–50% in previous expansion phases, and new fabs deliver no volume until mid-2027 or 2028.
dram.verdict.bull.2: Ordinary memory has become more profitable than HBM per wafer: confirmed by TrendForce for Q1 2026, and Micron's long contracts specify a price floor guaranteeing a margin above the peak of any previous cycle.
dram.verdict.horizon: 12–18 months — the shortage holds through 2027, but then CXMT's ramp and new fabs turn the cycle down.
dram.verdict.keyQuestion: When does the DRAM cycle turn — and will China's CXMT flood the market with cheap memory before AI demand weakens?
dram.verdict.sizing: DRAM market revenue: ~$404B (2026, +144% in a year). Server DRAM is the fastest-growing segment: DDR5 +95% QoQ in Q1'26.
dram.verdict.summary: This is a combination that needs reading carefully: the growth is the highest of any link in the chain, the share price looks cheap (a forward P/E of 4–8), but the resilience to the cycle is the worst in the whole chain. The product is standard and substitutable, the customer has no reason to stay with a supplier, and the history is unambiguous: every previous shortage ended in the shares falling 50–60%. A low P/E here is not a sign of cheapness but the classic cycle trap: the market has already concluded profits will fall. Hence a 6, on a nine for growth.
dram.whatIsIt: Working memory — what the compute chip is operating on right now, holding the current task's data close at hand. It is fast, but it forgets everything when the power goes off, so it has to be constantly refreshed with current. An AI server needs a great deal of it: the larger the model, the more data has to be held ready beside the chip.
hbm.competition.entryBarrier.why: The only contender — China's CXMT — is three generations behind (~6–8 years), cut off from key equipment by US export controls, and realistically will not reach volume before 2028 — and then mostly for China's domestic market.
hbm.competition.players.0.note: Its share only falls because the market is growing: in money terms the business doubled in a year. ~90% of sales go to Nvidia: a strength and a risk at once.
hbm.competition.players.0.tech: First to every generation; ~70% of HBM4 memory earmarked for Vera Rubin (Nvidia's new accelerators, replacing Blackwell)
hbm.competition.players.1.note: Grew from ~2% to ~21% in three years — the cycle's biggest surprise. The only way to buy HBM on a US exchange.
hbm.competition.players.1.tech: HBM4 has passed qualification; the bottom logic die is made by TSMC
hbm.competition.players.2.note: Missed an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell, 2024). Coming back: lead supplier to AMD and >60% of the memory for Google's chips.
hbm.competition.players.2.tech: Spent eighteen months failing Nvidia qualification
hbm.competition.switchingCost: To change memory supplier, a customer must pass qualification again — anywhere from several months to eighteen. Until it is passed, no amount of announced capacity earns a dollar. That is why shares move slowly and predictably.
hbm.competition.takeaway: Three split the market, no one can enter, and customers cannot leave quickly — that set-up is what holds prices up. Only one thing to watch: how Nvidia divides its orders among the three at each new generation.
hbm.demand.backlog: SK Hynix holds more orders than it can produce in three years. Micron has ~$100B of contracted future revenue — several years of its revenue.
hbm.demand.contractStructure: Micron: 16 strategic agreements, ~$100B of contracted future revenue, many at a fixed price or with a floor. ~$22B of customer prepayments. Cloud giants sign multi-year contracts with a guaranteed minimum price. A letter of intent with OpenAI (Oct 2025). This is the main evidence that HBM has partly decoupled from the classic memory cycle.
hbm.demand.customerConcentration: Nvidia is ~90% of SK Hynix's sales and the industry's largest buyer. Google is scaling fastest; Amazon and Meta are more cautious. A single Nvidia allocation decision moves all three makers' shares.
hbm.demand.pricing: 2026: HBM3E up ~20% on 2025. For 2027 the makers assume a several-fold price increase. The turning point: in Q1'26 ordinary server memory (DDR5) became more profitable per wafer than HBM — a strong argument for raising HBM prices further.
hbm.demand.soldOut.0.note: all three; Micron covers ~60% of demand
hbm.demand.takeaway: Memory has never had this kind of revenue visibility: years ahead are contracted and prepaid. While the contracts hold, profits are more reliable than the market's habit from past cycles assumes — which is exactly why drawdowns like July's offer an entry point.
hbm.dependencies.correlation: HBM demand tracks hyperscaler budget announcements with a 2–3 quarter lag — their quarterly results work as a free leading indicator.
hbm.dependencies.downstream: Buyers: Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Their 2026 data-centre budgets run $600–725B (+60–77% year on year). Microsoft named more expensive memory outright as the reason its costs rose ~$25B — HBM prices already sit inside the giants' budgets.
hbm.dependencies.takeaway: The whole chain rests on 3–4 irreplaceable suppliers: Namics (private), Hanmi, TSMC, Ibiden. Two implications: this key constraint can be bought directly (Hanmi, Besi, Ibiden) — and a failure at any one of them stops all three makers.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.0.item: The special adhesive for memory assembly
hbm.dependencies.upstream.0.note: The sole supplier to SK Hynix. The shares cannot be bought, but that exclusivity is exactly why competitors cannot replicate the industry's best assembly method.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.1.item: The machines that bond the memory layers
hbm.dependencies.upstream.1.note: ~71% of the world market. The cleanest listed way to buy this key memory-assembly constraint.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.2.item: Solderless bonding machines (the assembly of the future)
hbm.dependencies.upstream.2.note: Needed once chips go above 16 layers (~2029). Already selected by Micron.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.3.item: The substrate board under the chip
hbm.dependencies.upstream.3.note: ~35% of the market. Every new multi-layer chip needs more substrate layers — demand grows faster than the chip market itself.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.4.note: Nearly 100% of AI-class assembly of this kind. Without a slot in its queue a finished accelerator cannot be produced — a mandatory link.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.5.item: The machines that drill the channels through the chip
hbm.dependencies.upstream.5.note: A duopoly. But memory is a small part of their vast business, so the exposure is diluted.
hbm.expectations.impliedGrowth: SK Hynix trades at ~5–8x forward earnings, Micron at ~12x — on record margins (SK Hynix's operating margin is 72%). That combination says outright: the market is pricing a profit fall, not growth. This is classic cycle-peak pricing, not the valuation of a growing business.
hbm.expectations.marketBelieves: The market treats 2026–2027 as peak profit and compresses the multiple in advance — in July 2026 the shares fell >20% on record results. Everyone knows memory is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first.
hbm.expectations.metrics.0.history: memory at peak profit usually trades at 8–12x
hbm.expectations.metrics.0.note: a low P/E on a record margin is not cheapness but the market betting on an imminent profit fall
hbm.expectations.metrics.1.note: the cheapest way in and the only one on a US exchange, but three quarters of the business is ordinary memory, not HBM
hbm.expectations.metrics.2.label: Operating margin · SK Hynix
hbm.expectations.metrics.2.note: at a peak; it returns to normal on a turn — which is exactly what the low multiple embeds
hbm.expectations.metrics.3.label: Memory's share of an AI chip's cost
hbm.expectations.metrics.3.note: a structural shift of value out of the compute die (~13%) and into memory — part of the premium is justified
hbm.expectations.takeaway: HBM is priced as a peak cyclical asset: a low forward P/E is a warning, not an invitation. The anomaly is that contracts and Nvidia qualification could, for the first time, stretch the peak beyond past cycles. If so, the market is wrong on the downside; if not, the low multiple honestly reflects a near turn in 2028.
hbm.expectations.verdict: SK Hynix is cheap if the shortage holds through 2027; otherwise fair
hbm.expectations.weThink: HBM has partly decoupled from the commodity cycle for the first time — floor-priced contracts, ~$22B of prepayments and the Nvidia qualification barrier stretch the peak out. If SK Hynix's chief is right that the shortage runs past 2030, then ~5–8x forward is far too cheap. The disagreement is not about direction but duration: the market looks at a quarter, we look at two contract cycles.
hbm.intro:
HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin DRAM dies and mounted on a shared substrate right up against the processor. The binding constraint on a large AI model is not arithmetic speed but the rate at which data arrives: ordinary memory hangs off a narrow bus, centimetres of board traces away, and the processor idles waiting. HBM removes that constraint — data travels over thousands of parallel lines across millimetres, and a single stack delivers more than a terabyte per second. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without HBM.

How it works. Ordinary DRAM dies are first thinned for this: the wafer is ground from the back from roughly 780 down to 30–50 microns, or a tall stack will not fit the package height and will shed heat badly. Thousands of micro-holes are then etched all the way through each thinned die and filled with copper — these are the through-silicon vias (TSVs), vertical wires connecting every layer at once. Then 8, 12 or 16 dies are stacked and bonded: either through micro solder bumps between layers (thermocompression), or, from 16-layer HBM4 onward, copper directly to copper with no gap (hybrid bonding). The stack sits on top of a bottom logic die (the base die), which runs the whole memory and talks to the processor. The finished stack is mounted on a silicon interposer beside the processor, putting memory and processor in one package.

The hard, expensive part here is not the memory cells but assembling the stack without defects and getting the heat out. At 12–16 layers with thousands of connections, one bad die or one unbonded joint kills the entire stack, taking every good layer beneath it with it. The taller the stack, the more tightly hot dies are packed and the harder it is to pull heat out of the middle, so thinning and the bonding method decide directly how many stacks come out good. The spread in stack yield is the main hidden profit lever: Samsung's HBM4 memory yielded only around 50% in early 2026 (nearly every second die scrapped), whereas the leader's proven bonding process loses markedly less. Whoever assembles with fewer defects takes the margin.

Who pays, and how much. HBM is the most expensive part of an accelerator: a single chip carries 6–8 stacks, and memory accounts for roughly 63% of the cost of a finished AI chip, against only ~13% for the compute die itself (Epoch AI). One HBM4 stack costs ~$500–550, meaning $3–4K of memory in every accelerator; each generation costs more — from ~$200 (HBM3) to $300 (HBM3E) and $500+ (HBM4). Buyers pay without haggling, because without HBM the accelerator simply does not work and the delivery queue is booked years out: cloud giants and accelerator makers prepay to reserve capacity — Micron alone holds ~$22B of customer prepayments and ~$100B of contracted future revenue. The makers, in turn, are putting tens of billions into expansion: SK Hynix has up to $75B of capex through 2028, roughly 80% of it in HBM.

Three makers hold the market: SK Hynix ~56%, Samsung and Micron at roughly ~21% each. The segment itself grows from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028) on Micron's estimate — faster than any other part of memory; demand added +130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.
hbm.marketSizing.bomShare.note: of an AI chip's cost is memory (two years ago it was 52%); the compute die itself is only ~13%. Buying «Nvidia's suppliers», an investor is in fact buying memory suppliers.
hbm.marketSizing.takeaway: The market triples by 2028 (~$35B → ~$100B), and it is paid for by the data centres of giants who have the money. The direct beneficiaries are the three makers: SK Hynix (KRX: 000660), Micron (NASDAQ: MU), Samsung (KRX: 005930).
hbm.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.mix: From 2027 growth rests more on price than on volume. Excellent for profit, but price is the most fragile support: it breaks first when supply catches demand.
hbm.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.price: 2026 contracts were signed ~20% higher; for 2027 the makers assume a several-fold price increase. Price-led growth is the most profitable kind: it falls almost entirely to the margins of SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron.
hbm.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.volume: Demand grew 130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026. The fastest growth is in the giants' custom chips (Google, Amazon): they need 80% more HBM in 2026 against +23% for ordinary GPUs — demand no longer rests on Nvidia alone.
hbm.mentalModel.chain.0: a GPU spends most of its time waiting for data, not computing
hbm.mentalModel.chain.1: memory beside the processor fixes that — it is already 63% of an AI chip's cost
hbm.mentalModel.chain.2: every HBM wafer yields a third as many gigabytes → shortage, and only three companies make it
hbm.mentalModel.chain.3: a customer spends months passing Nvidia qualification and cannot leave quickly
hbm.mentalModel.chain.4: the price rises each generation ($200 → $300 → $500+), and margins reach 72%
hbm.mentalModel.drivers.0.note: demand grew +130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026; a single accelerator carries 6–8 HBM chips — $3–4K of memory alone. Google's and Amazon's custom chips need +80% more HBM against +23% for ordinary GPUs — demand no longer rests on Nvidia alone.
hbm.mentalModel.drivers.1.note: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4). Each generation is harder and dearer, and the price increment falls almost entirely to the three makers' margins. 2026 contracts were signed ~20% higher; 2027 assumes a several-fold rise.
hbm.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: a single Nvidia allocation decision moves all three makers' shares: SK Hynix holds ~70% of HBM4 for Vera Rubin, but failing qualification on a new generation cost Samsung the whole Blackwell cycle.
hbm.mentalModel.framework: The companies called «Nvidia's suppliers» earn primarily on memory: HBM is up to 63% of an AI chip's cost, and only three makers can assemble it. Until new capacity arrives (expected by 2028), demand exceeds supply and gross margins reach ~72%. Profits hold while the shortage holds; once capacity catches demand, the cycle turns — that is memory's industry pattern.
hbm.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = number of Nvidia/AMD accelerators × HBM per accelerator (6–8 chips) × price per chip (rising each generation) × market share
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: changing supplier or generation means re-qualifying at the customer, anywhere from several months to eighteen; until that is done, announced capacity earns nothing. Missing qualification on HBM3E cost Samsung an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell).
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: SK Hynix bonds layers with ~20% less scrap and better heat removal, thanks to its proprietary method using Namics' exclusive adhesive. Whoever assembles with less scrap takes the margin; the taller the stack, the more that gap matters.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: SK Hynix 56%, Samsung ~21%, Micron ~21%; entry is closed — CXMT is 3 generations (6–8 years) behind and cut off from equipment. But with HBM4 all three passed qualification for the first time — that is competition inside a generation, not an SK Hynix monopoly.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: $75B of investment at SK Hynix alone through 2028 (~80% in HBM), plus an $89B new campus. That capital threshold shuts newcomers out, but it also becomes a risk for the makers themselves if demand wobbles.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Micron holds ~$100B of contracted future revenue and ~$22B of prepayments, many contracts with a price floor. For the first time memory is partly decoupling from the commodity cycle — but 2028 coverage is still only ~40%.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: this is still memory: the product standardises from generation to generation, and in 2027–2028 new fabs from all three plus CXMT arrive at once. In July 2026 the sector already fell >20% on the fear of a turn alone.
hbm.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is real, but this is not subscription software — it is memory. It rests on a combination: Nvidia qualification + defect-free bonding technology + the capital threshold. The one unassailable part is the difficulty of assembling without scrap, where SK Hynix leads. All of it weakens as generations standardise and new capacity arrives by 2028 — hence an honest three for commoditisation.

hbm.problems.items.0.gap: To enter, a supplier must pass Nvidia's qualification from scratch — anywhere from several months to eighteen; Samsung failed it on HBM3E (the previous stacked-memory generation) and lost an entire chip generation (Blackwell, 2024). The only new contender, China's CXMT, is three generations behind (~6–8 years), cut off from key equipment by US export controls, and will realistically not reach volume before 2028 — mostly for its domestic market. A new memory fab takes 18–36 months, with output no earlier than 2028.
hbm.problems.items.0.problem: HBM output is capped not by the memory wafers themselves but by two final-assembly steps, and both are sold out. First, building a stack of 12–16 dies with thousands of vertical connections through the silicon (TSVs — vertical channels through silicon) at a low scrap rate. Second, mounting the finished stack on a silicon substrate right against the processor (CoWoS packaging — chip and memory on one substrate; only TSMC does it). From the HBM4 generation, the bottom logic die of the chip also goes to TSMC. A single accelerator carries 6–8 stacks worth $3–4K, HBM already takes 22–30% of the whole industry's wafers, 2026 memory is fully sold out and ~90% of 2027 is contracted.
hbm.problems.items.0.solution: This can only be relieved through higher stack yield and assembly throughput, not through new wafer fabs. SK Hynix is first to perfect the layer-bonding process for each generation (for 16-layer HBM4 the industry moves to hybrid bonding — welding dies copper to copper with no gap). TSMC is expanding CoWoS packaging capacity (chip and memory on one substrate) and taking on the HBM4 base die. In parallel, the scarcest link of all is the queue for assembly machines: they are made by Hanmi (KRX: 042700) and Besi (AMS: BESI), and they are needed however the shares split among the three.
hbm.problems.items.0.winners: SK Hynix (KRX: 000660) — 56.4% of the market, first to pass qualification each generation, with ~70% of HBM4 memory reserved for Nvidia's new Vera Rubin accelerators; it wins on the best stack yield. TSMC (NYSE: TSM) — holds CoWoS packaging and, from HBM4, makes the logic die, so the next scarce link moves directly to it. Plus Hanmi and Besi: all three makers buy their assembly machines.
hbm.problems.takeaway: Relieving this constraint strengthens the current leaders: what is scarce is precisely SK Hynix's stack yield and TSMC's CoWoS packaging — the things a newcomer cannot replicate. It does not open the door to a new player.
hbm.risks.0.note: Memory is close to an exchange-traded commodity: the three makers' product is similar and they expand fabs in the same years, so supply regularly overshoots demand and prices collapse. Past collapses: 2018–19 (Micron −56%), 2022–23 (−50%, SK Hynix loss-making). HBM is partly protected by multi-year contracts, but not fully — the sector already fell >20% in July 2026.
hbm.risks.1.note: The US ban (Dec 2024) on shipping HBM and equipment to China. Short-term it supports prices; the long-term risk is China building its own (CXMT).
hbm.risks.2.note: Practically ruled out: a memory fab is $30–50B and 7–10 years. Custom HBM versions only deepen customer dependence.
hbm.risks.3.note: The risk window is 2027–2028, when all three plus CXMT add capacity at the same time.
hbm.risks.4.note: SK Hynix depends on Nvidia for ~90%; any shift to multi-sourcing redistributes shares sharply.
hbm.risks.5.note: Failing qualification on a new generation is a real risk: Samsung's miss on HBM3E cost it an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell).
hbm.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: Not a threat but a new market: it is being developed by the HBM leader itself (SK Hynix) together with SanDisk. It hits ordinary SSDs, not HBM. The way to play it is SanDisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) and SK Hynix (KRX: 000660).
hbm.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: This is flash memory (as in an ordinary SSD), but stacked in layers and connected almost as close to the processor as HBM. It gives 8–16x the capacity and reads almost as fast, but writes slowly — so it suits holding an already-trained model rather than training one. First inference hardware: early 2027.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: Complements HBM rather than competing with it. Volume production is Micron's (NASDAQ: MU) — the same winner as in HBM: for it this is one more growing product.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Modules of familiar memory (the same kind as in smartphones), but placed right against the processor. They give large capacity markedly cheaper than HBM, but several times slower. Their job is to hold what does not fit in HBM and relieve it on capacity.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: Does not affect the decision on a 2-year horizon. It is being developed by the same Samsung and SK Hynix — for them a far-off option, not a risk of losing the market.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: The idea of building simple computation into the memory chip itself, to move data to the processor less often and save energy. Technically elegant, but the timelines keep slipping by years, the software does not exist, and it is not deployed in real data centres yet.
hbm.roadmap.generations.0.note: The first volume generation (Nvidia H100); SK Hynix took nearly all of it.
hbm.roadmap.generations.1.note: Nvidia's Blackwell chip generation (2024). Samsung failed qualification and missed the cycle — a lesson in how share is lost here.
hbm.roadmap.generations.2.note: For Nvidia's new accelerators (Rubin) and AMD's (MI400). All three passed qualification for the first time — competition inside a generation.
hbm.roadmap.generations.2.spec: channel twice as wide; up to 2 TB/s
hbm.roadmap.generations.3.note: Memory turns from a commodity into a made-to-order product — the makers' margin rises further.
hbm.roadmap.generations.4.note: The harder the technology, the harder it is for new players to catch up — the leaders' protection only strengthens.
hbm.roadmap.takeaway: There is no replacement for HBM on a 2026–2028 horizon: every «competitor» either complements it or was created by the HBM makers themselves. The real technology risk is one maker failing qualification on a new generation (Samsung already lost a whole cycle that way).
hbm.scenarios.cases.0.name: Bear
hbm.scenarios.cases.0.note: the 2028 turn: new fabs from all three + CXMT qualifies, ordinary memory spot turns down, some contracts are renegotiated
hbm.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
hbm.scenarios.cases.1.note: the shortage holds through 2027, the market triples by 2028 ($35B → $100B), contracts protect the floor
hbm.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
hbm.scenarios.cases.2.note: HBM prices rise several-fold in 2027, memory has decoupled from the cycle, made-to-order HBM4E lifts ARPU
hbm.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~+12…+16%/yr (SK Hynix, probability-weighted) — asymmetric to the upside, but capped by the 2028 clock
hbm.scenarios.takeaway: The best set-up in all of memory, but not an endless one: the base case gives a solid ~15% while the shortage holds, and the bear case is gentler than in ordinary memory — contracts and prepayments prop up the floor. The decision turns on one thing: getting out before the 2028 turn rather than sitting through it.
hbm.supply.balance.2.note: «no visibility» on when supply catches up
hbm.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: Building the largest new memory campus at ~$89B — but meaningful output from it only arrives around 2030.
hbm.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: Expanding fabs for HBM: the target is roughly double the output by end-2026, with new buildings only coming online in 2028.
hbm.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: Building new fabs in the US and Singapore, ~$20B invested in a year; meaningful output only from 2027–2028.
hbm.supply.crowdingOut: Every wafer used for HBM yields a third as many gigabytes as one used for ordinary memory, and HBM already takes 22–30% of the industry's wafers. That pushes up the price of all other memory too (+90% in a quarter) — the same three makers earn twice.
hbm.supply.leadTime: A new memory fab takes 18–36 months from decision to product. Everything started now yields output no earlier than 2028: the shortage physically cannot be relieved before then.
hbm.supply.takeaway: The shortage is guaranteed through 2027 — that is what the whole thesis rests on. The dangerous window is 2028: new fabs from all three plus CXMT arrive at once. The exit signal is spot prices turning down and sector analysts using the words «market correction».
hbm.supply.utilization: Memory fabs are running flat out: every production line inside the fabs is fully loaded, none idle. So output cannot be added quickly without building new fabs.
hbm.thesis.bigIdea: The market prices HBM as ordinary cyclical memory about to collapse. But HBM has quietly decoupled from the commodity cycle: it is sold out years ahead on prepaid contracts with price floors, and its real constraint is not wafers but defect-free assembly yield. So both the high price and the record margin last longer than the market assumes — and the yield leader (SK Hynix) keeps extending its lead.
hbm.thesis.stream.0.t: Where the money in an AI chip actually sits
hbm.thesis.stream.1.t: An investor buying «Nvidia's suppliers» thinks they are buying compute. In fact they are buying memory. In the cost of a modern AI chip, 63% is HBM memory and only about 13% is the compute die itself. Over the past two years the value quietly moved from logic to memory: every accelerator carries 6–8 HBM modules worth $3–4K — more than the processor.
hbm.thesis.stream.10.items.0.note: all three makers fully sold out
hbm.thesis.stream.10.items.1.note: actively being contracted at floor-priced terms
hbm.thesis.stream.10.items.2.note: partly contracted — contracts keep reaching further out
hbm.thesis.stream.10.t: How far HBM is already sold out — by year
hbm.thesis.stream.11.items.0.l: of contracted future revenue at Micron
hbm.thesis.stream.11.items.0.n: several years of its revenue; 16 strategic agreements
hbm.thesis.stream.11.items.1.n: cloud giants pay up front to stake out volume
hbm.thesis.stream.11.items.2.n: more than it can physically produce
hbm.thesis.stream.12.t: When a customer puts down $22B of prepayments and fixes a price floor two years out, this is no longer an exchange-traded commodity but infrastructure designed into the project. That is what first partly decoupled HBM from the classic memory cycle.
hbm.thesis.stream.13.t: The real constraint is not wafers, it is scrap
hbm.thesis.stream.14.t: And it is not the wafers that cap output. The cap is final stack assembly: fine-drilling the channels through the layers, the queue for bonding machines and — above all — how many assembled stacks come out defect-free. Whoever assembles with fewer defects takes the margin.
hbm.thesis.stream.15.items.0.n: nearly every second die scrapped — which is why Samsung trails on margin
hbm.thesis.stream.15.items.1.n: thanks to its proprietary layer-bonding method; and it sheds heat better
hbm.thesis.stream.16.t: This is why SK Hynix leads — not on wafers, but on yield. And the advantage compounds: less scrap → lower unit cost → more margin to invest in the next generation's lead.
hbm.thesis.stream.17.label: HOW TO BUY THE CONSTRAINT ITSELF
hbm.thesis.stream.17.t: The pure play on the shortage is not memory but the layer-bonding machines: Hanmi and Besi. Their equipment is needed however the share split among the three makers lands.
hbm.thesis.stream.19.t: There are only three makers, and a single Nvidia order moves all of their shares at once.
hbm.thesis.stream.2.items.0.l: of an AI chip's cost is memory
hbm.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: the compute die itself is only ~13% (it was 52% two years ago)
hbm.thesis.stream.2.items.1.l: of HBM in a single accelerator
hbm.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: tripling; the hyperscalers pay for it
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.0.label: SK Hynix — the yield leader
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.0.note: ~90% of sales go to Nvidia; ~70% of the memory for the next accelerator generation
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.1.label: Micron — the only one listed in the US
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.1.note: grew from ~2% to ~21% in three years — the surprise of the cycle
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.2.label: Samsung — coming back
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.2.note: missed an Nvidia generation (Blackwell); recovering through AMD and Google
hbm.thesis.stream.21.t: What is already priced in — and where the anomaly is
hbm.thesis.stream.22.t: And here is the anomaly. A record 72% operating margin, years of prepaid backlog — and SK Hynix trades at 5–8x earnings, Micron at about 12x. A low multiple on a record margin is not cheapness, it is the market betting on an imminent profit fall. The market is pricing a cycle peak, not a growing business.
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.0.n: memory at a peak usually trades at 8–12x — this is cheaper still
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.1.n: the cheapest way in, and the only way to buy HBM on a US exchange
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.2.n: a record — and precisely what the market thinks cannot hold
hbm.thesis.stream.24.t: Our read: the argument is not about direction but about duration. Contract price floors, $22B of prepayments and the barrier of Nvidia qualification stretch the peak out. If the shortage holds through 2027 (and SK Hynix's chief says beyond 2030), then 5–8x is far too cheap. The market is looking at a quarter; we are looking at two contract cycles.
hbm.thesis.stream.26.t: The thesis rests on the shortage. Three signals would say it is over — and it is worth remembering that from 2027 growth rests increasingly on price, and price is the first thing to break when supply catches up:
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.0.1: Share redistribution and a price war — the leader's margin compresses
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.1.0: New fabs from all three + China's CXMT passes qualification (2028)
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.1.1: Supply catches demand — the shortage ends
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.2.1: The price floor the thesis stands on stops holding
hbm.thesis.stream.28.t: None of them is lit yet: contracts keep reaching further out, and Samsung has not closed the yield gap.
hbm.thesis.stream.29.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
hbm.thesis.stream.3.t: What HBM is, and why nothing works without it
hbm.thesis.stream.30.t: HBM triples to ~$100B by 2028, and it is paid for by the data centres of giants who have the money. Memory has quietly become the most expensive and the most heavily contracted part of an AI chip — and the market still prices it as a commodity on the edge of a crash.
hbm.thesis.stream.31.t: Compressed into one thought: the market is pricing a collapse, and the contracts say otherwise. The best-protected ways to buy it are the yield leader (SK Hynix) and the only maker available on a US exchange (Micron), for as long as the shortage holds, plus the bonding machines (Hanmi/Besi), which are needed however the shares fall. Samsung is a separate bet on a comeback and a share shift.
hbm.thesis.stream.4.t: HBM is several ordinary memory dies stacked on top of one another and threaded with vertical channels through the silicon (TSVs), so data travels up and down rather than around. The finished stack sits right against the compute chip on a shared substrate. Without it the accelerator «starves»: the compute core idles waiting for data. Each generation costs more than the last: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.thesis.stream.5.t: What the market thinks: «it's memory, it will crash»
hbm.thesis.stream.6.t: Memory has always been a brutal commodity cycle: boom → fab build-out → glut → price collapse. The market prices HBM by the same reflex. In July 2026 the makers' shares fell more than 20% — on record results. Everyone knows memory is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first.
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.l: earnings is what SK Hynix costs
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: on a record 72% operating margin — the market is pricing a profit fall, not growth
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.1.n: on a record quarter — the classic «this is the cycle peak» reaction
hbm.thesis.stream.8.t: Why HBM decoupled from the cycle
hbm.thesis.stream.9.t: But HBM is not traded on an exchange at a spot price the way ordinary memory is. It is contracted years ahead, prepaid, with a price floor, and co-designed with the customer. Commodities do not behave like that.
hbm.tldr.0: The best supply/demand set-up memory has seen in 40 years: three makers share the market (SK Hynix 56%, Samsung ~21%, Micron ~21%), all of 2026 is sold out, and the market goes from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028), growing ~40% a year.
hbm.tldr.1: The best return-for-risk is SK Hynix (the leader: ~70% of HBM4 supply — the newest generation of this stacked memory — is reserved for Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next accelerator generation, on a 72% operating margin). Micron is the cheapest way in (forward P/E ~12). Hanmi / Besi / TSMC supply the equipment and the final assembly for this link.
hbm.tldr.2: The main risk is cyclicality: memory gets cheaper the moment supply catches demand, and by 2027–2028 all three makers will have finished new fabs. The sector already fell >20% in July 2026. The question is whether multi-year contracts and prepayments hold the price when that new supply arrives.
hbm.unitEconomics.costCurve: SK Hynix produces at the lowest cost and with the least scrap, thanks to its proprietary layer-bonding method: on average ~20% less scrap and better heat removal than the method its competitors at Samsung and Micron use.
hbm.unitEconomics.grossMargin: HBM costs 5–6x more than ordinary memory per gigabyte. The 2026 paradox: ordinary server memory rose so far that it became more profitable per wafer than HBM — a sure sign HBM prices will be raised in 2027.
hbm.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: One multi-layer HBM4 chip costs ~$500–550, and an accelerator carries 6–8 of them (i.e. $3–4K of memory in every chip). Each generation costs more: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.unitEconomics.takeaway: The share of chips assembled defect-free is the main hidden profit lever: whoever assembles with less scrap takes the margin. Today that is SK Hynix. The main share-shift scenario is a Samsung breakthrough on scrap; watch its quarterly margin for it.
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.0.label: Samsung — HBM4 memory
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.0.value: ~50% defect-free (Jan 2026) → ~60% (mid-2026). Nearly every second die is scrapped — which is why Samsung trails on margin.
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.1.label: Samsung — new bonding (hybrid bonding)
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.1.value: ~10% defect-free on prototypes — the future technology is not yet ready to sell.
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.2.value: the figures are not disclosed, but SK Hynix runs a proven combination (mature memory + a TSMC base die) — lower scrap risk.
hbm.universe.0.note: The leader at 56%; +571% over 52 weeks. The most confident single bet in this link.
hbm.universe.1.note: The cheapest way in; ~$100B of future revenue contracted. Reports 22 Sep 2026.
hbm.universe.2.note: The purest picks and shovels: layer-bonding machines, ~71% of the market; qualified for HBM4.
hbm.universe.3.note: Micron's TCB vendor for HBM4; the hybrid-bonding leader for 16-hi and above.
hbm.universe.4.note: ~100% of AI-class CoWoS; foundry for the HBM4 base die.
hbm.universe.5.exposure: memory is one part of the conglomerate
hbm.universe.5.note: Recovering in HBM; turnkey HBM4 (its own foundry).
hbm.universe.6.note: Less re-rated; each chip needs ever more substrate layers.
hbm.update.bottomLine: Not nothing, but not a break either: Hynix's profit was trimmed slightly, efficiency is real, China is coming, capacity is being built — but demand has not broken. What the market re-rated is less the profit than the duration: investors are no longer willing to pay years ahead for peak margins (everyone knows the sector is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first). Only facts will settle the argument — durable orders, prices that hold, and profit. The nearest clean demand signal is TSMC's report; Hynix reports in about two weeks, into an already lowered bar.
hbm.update.headline: Is July's memory panic worth believing?
hbm.update.stories.0.detail: Hynix's Q2 profit guidance came in ~8% below expectations, and 2026–27 estimates were cut 9–11%. But the cause is company-specific: Hynix has more HBM in its revenue mix, and HBM under long contracts rises in price more slowly than ordinary memory, so its average selling price lagged the market. Meanwhile the margin is a record (~75%), profit is up 500% year on year, and by Q3 pricing catches up with the market as HBM4 ships. This is a Hynix quirk, not weak demand.
hbm.update.stories.0.title: SK Hynix's «miss»
hbm.update.stories.1.detail: Nvidia's platforms (Grace Blackwell and the coming Vera Rubin) face a direct competitor for the first time: AMD's Helios rack bets on an HBM4 memory advantage, and Microsoft has joined the project. For the memory makers this is a second large accelerator buyer besides Nvidia — HBM demand stops resting on a single customer and becomes more durable.
hbm.update.stories.1.title: AMD's Helios rack challenges Nvidia through HBM4; Microsoft is a new customer
hbm.update.stories.1.verdict: HBM demand extends beyond Nvidia — a plus for the three
hbm.update.stories.2.detail: Hynix's record $26.5B equity raise pulled in a lot of memory-dedicated capital, leveraged Korean funds amplified the move, and geopolitics added to it. Tellingly, the biggest fallers were the NAND names — the ones least connected to Hynix's issue, to efficiency, or to HBM supply. This looks like an overcrowded position unwinding, not demand breaking.
hbm.update.stories.2.title: The share-price fall itself
hbm.update.stories.3.detail: A startup compressed a model from ~54 to ~3.9 GB — impressive. But in practice it still needs ~9.4 GB of memory (with overhead), and answer quality falls. This continues a years-long compression trend rather than a sudden «HBM is no longer needed». The question is which moves faster: memory saved, or query volume. So far, the cheaper inference gets, the more inference there is. It matters over years, but it is not a reason to cut forecasts now.
hbm.update.stories.3.title: Model compression (efficiency)
hbm.update.stories.3.verdict: the trend is real, but not a collapse
hbm.update.stories.4.detail: ASML (which makes the machines for memory fabs) expects +75% memory revenue this year and +30% machine output by 2027 — the makers are genuinely investing in build-out. But upgrading existing machines adds only ~4.5% of throughput; serious growth takes new fabs, new machines and time. This is the future supply response (2027–28), not July's shock. Good for equipment demand now, but it pressures the duration of the cycle later.
hbm.update.stories.4.title: ASML's equipment signals
hbm.update.stories.4.verdict: supply is growing, but only by 2027–28
hbm.update.stories.5.detail: Two independent research teams, in Korea and Japan, showed new ways to integrate memory that route around HBM's thermal limits. As layer counts rise, pulling heat out of the stack becomes an ever more serious problem and one of the main engineering barriers for HBM4 and the generations after it. This is a question of future chip design, not of current demand.
hbm.update.stories.5.title: New memory architectures against HBM overheating
hbm.update.stories.5.verdict: heat is a growing engineering constraint, not a risk today
hbm.update.summary: Three weeks ago memory was in high demand — now it is being avoided: the leaders are down 20%+ from their late-June highs and ~$1.5T has left semiconductors, while the S&P barely moved. Below: which of July's fears actually change supply and demand, and which only explain the share prices.
hbm.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: The binding constraint moves to TSMC's fab (NYSE: TSM): from the HBM4 generation the bottom logic die of the chip is made on its capacity, and it is that capacity (plus the defect-free share on new generations) that will be short in the next cycle.
hbm.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Output is capped not by the wafers themselves but by final assembly of the multi-layer chip: fine-drilling the channels through the layers, the queue for bonding machines, and the share of assembled chips that come out defect-free. The money in that goes to the makers of the assembly machines — Hanmi (KRX: 042700) and Besi (AMS: BESI).
hbm.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Growth takes enormous capital: $75B at SK Hynix alone through 2028 (~80% of it in HBM), plus an $89B new campus. Good for the equipment suppliers; risky for the makers themselves if demand wobbles.
hbm.valueCapture.takeaway: The margin sits with the memory makers (70–85%) and in the key assembly constraints. The best-protected ways to buy it: the makers themselves during the short years, plus Hanmi/Besi, whose machines are needed however the shares split among the three.
hbm.verdict.bear.0: Oversupply in 2028: the new fabs together (three makers plus China's CXMT) outrun demand growth, and analysts start talking about a «market correction».
hbm.verdict.bear.1: China (CXMT — a new Chinese memory maker) breaks the trio's market: its memory passes qualification at a Western giant, its defect-free share rises, and it completes an $8.55B IPO.
hbm.verdict.bear.2: The ordinary memory cycle returns: spot prices turn down, inventories build, and margins come off the 85–92% peak.
hbm.verdict.bull.0: The shortage holds to 2028: on the Q3–Q4 2026 calls the makers say «sold out» again, and final chip assembly at TSMC stays short.
hbm.verdict.bull.1: HBM (stacked memory) prices rise several-fold in 2027: visible in contract pricing (TrendForce data) and in the average selling prices the makers disclose in H2 2026.
hbm.verdict.bull.2: HBM profits have decoupled from the old memory cycle: contracted commitments and prepayments keep growing (~$100B at Micron), and the price floors written into contracts hold.
hbm.verdict.horizon: about 2 years — the window of HBM shortage and high prices (2026–2027); by 2027–2028 new fabs catch demand and the cycle turns down.
hbm.verdict.keyQuestion: Will HBM demand absorb the 2027–2028 fabs — or will overbuild collapse prices the way it did in 2018 and 2022?
hbm.verdict.summary: A strong structural story: memory is acutely short, only three companies make it, and demand is contracted years ahead — hence the record prices and margins. But memory carries a built-in risk: by 2027–2028 all three makers (plus the Chinese newcomer CXMT) will have finished new fabs. When that supply arrives and catches demand, memory prices fall and profits with them — that is how every previous cycle ended. Hence a 7, not a 9.
hbm.whatIsIt: Memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin dies and placed right up against the compute chip. A large AI model sits idle not for lack of arithmetic speed but because ordinary memory cannot feed it data fast enough; this stack feeds it through a far wider pipe over a very short distance. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without it — it is the most expensive and the scarcest part of the chip.
ip.picks.0.note: Technology that has to be used again and again across many competing chips. Little capital, high switching costs, low cyclicality.
ip.picks.0.rows.0.exposure: EDA software, system design tools and IP; needed by any AI chip, whoever it belongs to
ip.picks.0.rows.0.priced: A premium valuation; less pure upside from any single bonding technology, but far less binary risk too.
ip.picks.0.rows.0.why: Revenue $5.3B (2025), operating margin 45%+, backlog $7.8B. The tools are wired into engineers' workflow — relearning is expensive. The best quality in the link.
ip.picks.0.rows.1.exposure: EDA + interface IP + engineering simulation (after the Ansys acquisition); ties chip design to the physics of the package and the system
ip.picks.0.rows.1.priced: More upside from integration, but more execution risk after Ansys; a high valuation.
ip.picks.0.rows.1.why: 2026 revenue guidance ~$9.67B; the EDA+IP market is put at ~$31B. Chiplets cannot be designed at the transistor level alone — thermal, power and mechanical simulation is required.
ip.picks.0.rows.2.exposure: licences on processor architectures and cores; royalties on every chip shipped
ip.picks.0.rows.2.priced: The valuation already assumes data-centre penetration and expensive designs; RISC-V pressure from below.
ip.picks.0.rows.2.why: Over the year, royalties ~$2.61B + licences ~$2.31B, with data-centre royalties doubling. An enormous software ecosystem — changing architecture once the software is written is expensive.
ip.picks.0.rows.3.exposure: memory-interface IP + physical chips between the processor and high-speed memory
ip.picks.0.rows.3.priced: Almost half the revenue is physical chips, which makes it more cyclical than a pure licence (inventory, product cycles).
ip.picks.0.rows.3.why: A direct bet on the memory-bandwidth shortage in AI servers. Q2 2026: $207M of revenue, of which $84M royalties.
ip.picks.1.group: Bonding and patents — more upside, more risk
ip.picks.1.note: Maximum operating leverage, but cyclical demand and volatile orders. Hold as a small position — all the more after hybrid bonding in HBM was pushed to HBM4E/HBM5.
ip.picks.1.rows.0.exposure: equipment for hybrid bonding and die attach; the most concentrated listed bet on this technology
ip.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Demand is not linear and orders are volatile; adoption in HBM has been deferred from HBM4 to HBM4E/HBM5 — dangerous at a valuation that assumes instant mass adoption.
ip.picks.1.rows.0.why: Revenue €166M at a 63.9% gross margin; the long-term target is €1.5–1.9B of revenue at a 40–55% operating margin. Maximum leverage if adoption accelerates.
ip.picks.1.rows.1.exposure: a broad packaging portfolio: thermocompression, hybrid bonding, flip-chip, photonics; the Lithobolt platform for die-to-wafer bonding
ip.picks.1.rows.1.risk: A less pure bet; lower group margin quality; commodity assembly segments dilute the growth from AI.
ip.picks.1.rows.1.why: A diversified alternative to BESI: it earns even if thermocompression wins. Revenue ~$570M for the quarter, and a bonding collaboration with IBM.
ip.picks.1.rows.2.exposure: patents on hybrid bonding and 3D integration; licenses the portfolio without manufacturing equipment
ip.picks.1.rows.2.risk: Lumpy revenue, dependent on renewals and negotiations; part of the business is media rather than semiconductors; patents expire over time.
ip.picks.1.rows.2.why: The most asymmetric IP bet: $105M of revenue in the quarter at a ~60% EBITDA margin, AMD and Microsoft signed, UMC's access extended. Cheap revenue once signed.
ip.picksTakeaway: The core is Cadence and Synopsys: EDA quality, recurring revenue and low cyclicality (the best risk-weighted economics in the link). Rambus is a direct bet on the memory-bandwidth shortage; Arm is the strongest architectural franchise, but sensitive to valuation and to RISC-V pressure. Hold bonding and patents as a small position: BESI has the greatest upside and the greatest risk (adoption in HBM deferred to HBM4E/HBM5), ASMPT is the diversified alternative, Adeia the asymmetric patent bet with lumpy revenue. The key KPI is the shift from pilot-machine orders to volume orders.
ip.thesis.bigIdea: «Licences and bonding» is two different businesses under one heading, and both grow on the same shift: the AI chip has become too big to make in one piece, so it is cut into chiplets and assembled in a stack (3D). The first business is licences on ready-made chip blocks and design software (Cadence, Synopsys, Arm): software-like margins (45%+), recurring revenue, little capital. The second is equipment for hybrid bonding of dies (BESI): maximum operating leverage, but cyclical. The conclusion: hold the quality (Cadence, Synopsys) as the base, and bonding as a high-risk bet — all the more so now that its adoption in HBM has just been pushed back from HBM4 to HBM4E/HBM5.
ip.thesis.stream.1.t: This section brings together two related but economically different businesses. The first is licensing intellectual property for chips: companies sell ready-made chip blocks, interfaces and patents, and charge one-off payments and royalties for them. The second is equipment and patents for hybrid bonding of dies: joining dies vertically at a very fine pitch. Both grow on the same shift — the AI chip has become too big to scale in one piece, so the industry is moving to chiplets, [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] and 3D assembly.
ip.thesis.stream.10.t: But here is the correction the market often misses: hybrid bonding is NOT yet mandatory for HBM. Both Samsung and SK hynix stayed on thermocompression bonding for HBM4, and pushed the switch to hybrid back to 16-layer HBM4E or HBM5. SK hynix is still developing its own MR-MUF technology. The reasons: JEDEC relaxed the package-thickness requirements, and demand for the very tallest stacks turned out weaker than expected. So hybrid bonding is a growing but deferred scenario, not a universal requirement today.

ip.thesis.stream.13.t: Break the link down by economics. The best risk-weighted position is EDA and IP: very high margin, little capital, recurring revenue, low cyclicality. Patent licensing (Adeia) has an extremely high margin once development is paid for, but the revenue is lumpy and tied to deals. Bonding equipment is high-margin but cyclical, with volatile orders; in exchange it carries the maximum operating leverage — the supplier moves from a handful of pilot machines to volume orders without needing fab-scale capital.
ip.thesis.stream.14.note: The best risk-weighted economics are in EDA and IP; the greatest operating leverage is in bonding equipment.
ip.thesis.stream.15.t: Why Nvidia will not replace its suppliers
ip.thesis.stream.16.t: Nvidia knows how its chip ought to work, but that does not mean it would build the equipment that assembles it better than anyone else. The competencies are different: Nvidia's are GPU architecture, software and networking; the bonding supplier's are precision mechanics, surface preparation, optics and alignment, yield and contamination control. The equipment has to work not for a single Nvidia design but for different customers, die sizes and materials, at high yield across millions of operations. And the main barrier is qualification: replacing a proven tool means re-tuning the process and going through certification again. Nvidia is better off keeping several suppliers than reproducing the whole precision stack itself.
ip.thesis.stream.18.t: The quality is concentrated in EDA. Cadence: revenue $5.3B (2025), operating margin 45%+, backlog $7.8B; Q2 2026 revenue $1.58B. Synopsys, after buying Ansys, raised its 2026 guidance to roughly $9.67B. Arm, in the year to March 2026: royalties ~$2.61B and licences ~$2.31B, with data-centre royalties doubling. Rambus in Q2 2026: $207M (almost half of it physical chips, which makes it more cyclical). Adeia: $105M in the quarter at a ~60% EBITDA margin, having signed AMD and Microsoft. BESI: €166M of revenue at a 63.9% gross margin; ASMPT around $570M for the quarter.
ip.thesis.stream.2.items.1.l: the EDA and IP market (Synopsys estimate)
ip.thesis.stream.20.t: Where it is heading — technology, money and the players' bets
ip.thesis.stream.21.t: Technology. Demand is being pulled by several lines at once. [[hbm|HBM4|decoupled from the cycle]] is moving to a TSMC logic base die on the 3 nm node (first on the Rubin platform), and stacks are growing towards 16 layers and beyond — which needs denser assembly and tighter control. Chiplets are spreading beyond AMD: the UCIe 3.0 die-to-die standard has raised speed to 64 GT/s and is becoming the de facto industry standard (in the ecosystem of Arm, Cadence, Synopsys, Marvell). Beyond that comes 3D assembly of logic on logic and memory on logic, where hybrid bonding is needed most, plus co-packaged optics. Nvidia has already laid out a [[pkg|packaging|became the main event]] roadmap to packages of 14+ reticles and 24 HBM stacks by 2029.
ip.thesis.stream.22.t: Money. Capital is going into packaging in enormous amounts. TSMC has budgeted $52–56B of capex for 2026, of which 10–20% goes to advanced packaging, testing and masks; CoWoS capacity is quadrupling to ~130k wafers a month by the end of 2026, and the Chiayi complex (AP7) will become the largest packaging hub in the world. Large deals are happening too: Synopsys closed its $35B acquisition of Ansys (July 2025), completing a «silicon to systems» link; Applied Materials holds ~9% of BESI as a strategic bet on hybrid bonding.
ip.thesis.stream.23.t: What the players are betting on. The most striking shift is at Arm: in March 2026 it released its first chip of its own (an AGI CPU for data centres) with Meta as lead partner — moving up out of licensing and into finished processors. The others are each on their own link of the complexity chain:

ip.thesis.stream.28.t: The main risk to the equipment bet is that hybrid bonding arrives more slowly than expected: thermocompression and improved solder balls may suffice for longer (the HBM4 → HBM4E/HBM5 postponement has already shown that). Then come yield problems at fine pitch; customer concentration (only a handful of fabs and memory makers buy the leading-edge machines, and one deferred programme dents a quarter); the cyclicality of packaging capex; the UCIe standard, which can widen the market and devalue part of the interface IP at the same time; RISC-V pressing on Arm from below; export restrictions on EDA and equipment into China; and high valuations — a correct thesis does not pay if the price already assumes flawless execution.
ip.thesis.stream.3.t: Why this link exists at all

ip.thesis.stream.32.t: AI is shifting the value in chips away from the simple transistor count towards reusable architecture, fast interfaces and physical assembly. The winners are those whose technology has to be used again and again across many competing chips. The IP companies earn on design complexity, the bonding suppliers on manufacturing complexity.
ip.thesis.stream.33.t: In order of preference: Cadence and Synopsys are the quality core (EDA, recurring revenue, low cyclicality). Rambus is a direct bet on the memory-bandwidth shortage. Adeia is an asymmetric bet on bonding patents, but the revenue is lumpy. Arm is the strongest architectural franchise, but the most sensitive to valuation. BESI has the greatest upside from hybrid bonding and the greatest expectations risk, all the more after the move to HBM4E/HBM5; ASMPT is the more diversified and less explosive alternative. Hold the quality as the base and bonding as a small position.
ip.thesis.stream.4.t: Performance used to grow simply through the number of transistors on a single die. That model hit its limits: the maximum area [[litho|lithography|impossible to replicate]] can print; falling yield on large dies; expensive leading-edge nodes; heat; and memory that cannot keep up with compute. The answer is chiplets: the processor is cut into several smaller dies and joined in one package — leading-edge compute dies, cheaper I/O dies, [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] stacks and networking blocks. The complexity does not disappear — it moves out of transistor scaling and into architecture, interfaces and [[pkg|packaging|became the main event]]. That is where the money is made now.
ip.thesis.stream.5.t: IP licences: what is sold, and why buyers do not do it themselves
ip.thesis.stream.6.t: What gets licensed is ready-made, proven blocks: processor architectures and cores, memory controllers and interfaces (DDR/HBM, PCIe, CXL), die-to-die links, packaging patents. Even a hyperscaler designing its own [[asic|custom chip|earns on every chip]] takes the processor core from Arm, the interfaces from Synopsys or Cadence, the memory from Rambus, the bonding patents from Adeia. Doing it in-house means years of development and carrying the risk of a failed tape-out. Licensing economics are like [[eda|software|impossible to route around]]: a one-off payment plus a royalty on every chip, while the next customer adds almost no cost. Hence margins of 45%+ and recurring revenue.
