ip.thesis.stream.8.t: Hybrid bonding — and an important correction
ip.thesis.stream.9.t: An ordinary stack of dies is joined with micro solder balls. As the pitch shrinks, the balls run into a limit: too few connections, higher resistance, extra height, heat. Hybrid bonding joins dies directly — copper to copper, without solder — and gives many times more connections in a smaller area. It is the key to 3D assembly: logic on logic and memory on logic.
lab.competition.concentration: The top three control ~88% of enterprise LLM spending: Anthropic 40%, OpenAI 27%, Google 21% (Menlo Ventures, Dec 2025). Closed-source is 87% of enterprise workloads. Consumer: ChatGPT holds ~57–67% of web traffic share (declining), while Gemini grows via Android and Search defaults.
lab.competition.entryBarrier: Extreme at the frontier: capital ($100M+ per training run, heading toward $1B+), electricity (5–7 year queues), talent (a few hundred researchers on packages of up to $1.5B), and GPU access. But DeepSeek showed that the frontier can be approached at roughly a twentieth of the cost.
lab.competition.players.1.edge: consumer scale (1B+ MAU); brand recognition; Stargate ($400B); ~$1.4T of compute commitments; custom silicon (Broadcom)
lab.competition.players.3.edge: the largest talent acquisition; open-weight ecosystem dominance; $115–145B of capex; 3B+ app users for distribution
lab.competition.players.4.edge: V3 at a ~$5.6M marginal cost; near-zero historical revenue; an efficiency icon forcing an industry-wide cost reset
lab.competition.shareTrajectory.0.detail: The enterprise leader; Claude Code holds ~54% of the coding market. A confidential S-1 (June 2026). It grew enterprise share 12%→24%→40% over two years
lab.competition.shareTrajectory.1.detail: The consumer leader (900M WAU, 1B+ MAU). But it has lost half its enterprise share (50%→27%). S-1 filed, targeting a ~$1T IPO
lab.competition.shareTrajectory.3.detail: A talent-buying spree; Scale AI at $14.3B; pivoting toward proprietary (Muse Spark). Rationing Gemini access
lab.competition.shareTrajectory.4.detail: The gap has collapsed to 39 Arena points (2.7%). DeepSeek V3 cost ~$5.6M. The Four Dragons carry ~$140B of combined valuations
lab.competition.switchingCost: Low and falling: every lab's API is similar — a customer can switch between models in minutes. Open models can be downloaded and run anywhere. It is higher for enterprise customers who have fine-tuned a model on their own data and passed regulatory review — for them moving is expensive and slow.
lab.competition.takeaway: The top three's 88% concentration masks rapid commoditisation from below. Open-weight is ~45% of OpenRouter, and the Chinese gap is 2.7%. The moats are distribution and capital access, not capability.
lab.demand.backlog: OpenAI's compute commitments are ~$1.4T (by vendor: Broadcom ~$350B, Oracle ~$300B, Microsoft ~$250B, NVIDIA ~$100B, AMD ~$90B). Anthropic carries a $965B valuation (Series H). Not a traditional revenue backlog — these are capital commitments.
lab.demand.contractStructure: Consumer subscriptions: $20–200/month (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini). Enterprise API: usage-based plus volume commitments. Government: a DoD CDAO $200M ceiling × 4 labs ($800M total); GSA at $1 per agency (land-grab loss leaders).
lab.demand.customerConcentration: Medium: enterprise is distributed (2M+ OpenAI business clients), but revenue is concentrated in hyperscaler subsidies. OpenAI → Microsoft/Amazon/NVIDIA capital. Anthropic → AWS/Google. A circular dependency.
lab.demand.pricing: Frontier API: Claude Opus $5/$25, Gemini 3.1 Pro $2/$12, GPT-5.5 ~$2.50/$15 per M tokens. The GPT-4 equivalent fell from ~$20/M (2022) to ~$0.40/M (2026). A ~1,000x deflation in 3 years.
lab.demand.soldOut.0.note: Enterprise LLM spending tripled to ~$37B (2025). Inference has overtaken training as the dominant workload. 85K+ enterprises on Gemini, 2M+ on OpenAI, ~300K on Anthropic
lab.demand.soldOut.1.note: Agentic AI expands the TAM. IPOs (OpenAI, Anthropic) test public-market appetite. Inference volumes keep growing explosively
lab.demand.takeaway: Demand is explosive and real: enterprise tripled, and consumer crossed 1B MAU. But pricing has deflated ~1,000x in 3 years — volume has to compensate. The revenue gap against capex is the core thesis risk.
lab.intro:
AI labs build foundation models — large neural networks trained on an enormous corpus of data and then applied to hundreds of tasks: dialogue, programming, document analysis. This is the top, «intelligent» layer of the chain: chips, racks and data centres ultimately exist so that such a model can be trained and served.

How it works — training. The model «learns» by adjusting billions of numerical parameters so as to predict the next fragment of text ever more accurately; for that, tens of thousands of GPUs work on a single computation for weeks as one cluster. The cost rises with model size and data volume, and every new generation demands more computation: a single training run for a flagship model costs from $100M and is heading toward $1B and beyond. It is training, not the model's later operation, that consumes most of the capital.

How it works — serving, and the money. A finished model is monetised two ways: paid subscriptions ($20–200 a month) and selling API access, where the charge is per volume of text processed, broken into «tokens» (billed per million tokens). Serving requests itself yields a gross margin of 83–89%, like ordinary cloud software. But the price per token falls fast: the GPT-4 equivalent went from ~$20 to ~$0.40 per million tokens in three years — roughly a thousandfold — so revenue can only grow through volume.

The most critical property is access to computation and capital. Only about five Western labs can bear the cost of training at the frontier. The scale of the spending shows in the largest one's commitments: around $1.4T of contracted computation against ~$25B of revenue — a ratio of 56 to 1. The labs are structurally loss-making (losing around $1.22 for every dollar earned), so the constraint is not the product but continuous access to computation, energy and capital; add to that retaining a few hundred researchers on packages of up to $1.5B (an estimate).

Who invests, and why they pay. Most labs are private, with no direct listed stake — exposure runs through the strategic investors who hold stakes and supply the infrastructure (the hyperscalers and the GPU maker). Global corporate AI investment was $581.7B in 2025 (+130% in a year, Stanford HAI). They pay almost any price for two reasons: a frontier leader could take the entire market, and the infrastructure suppliers subsidise the labs to lock in their demand for computation.

A second paradox. Despite high serving margins, open models are catching the paid ones fast: DeepSeek V3 was trained for roughly $5.6M — thousands of times cheaper — and the gap between the best closed and the best open model has narrowed to 2.7%. Hence the central question: will the labs' revenue grow to the level of the infrastructure spending (around $1.5T a year) before hyperscaler and sovereign-fund financing contracts?

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

lab.supply.leadTime: A frontier training run: months (data prep + compute allocation + training + post-training). Forming a new lab: $1B+ minimum to reach the frontier. Power: 5–7 years for interconnection (ERCOT/MISO/PJM).
lab.supply.utilization: Inference has overtaken training as the dominant workload. GPU utilisation is high (the cloud providers report sold out). Google is already rationing capacity to Meta.
lab.thesis.bigIdea: AI labs sit at the top of the whole chain: chips, racks and data centres exist so that a single model can be trained and served. And they may be the worst place in the entire theme to invest. Nvidia squeezes them from above (taking ~75% of the margin and ~90% of the hardware money), while free open models squeeze from below, devaluing the frontier. Nobody is profitable: OpenAI loses $1.22 for every dollar of revenue. And private rounds value the labs at 20–150 times annual revenue on a bet on «permanent monopoly» — even though its very support, model superiority, is the fastest thing to erode. The theme is better played through liquid adjacent shares (Alphabet, Oracle) than through the loss-making labs directly.
lab.thesis.stream.0.t: The top of the whole chain — and possibly the worst place to invest
lab.thesis.stream.1.t: AI labs are the reason the whole stack exists: [[asic|chips|earns on every chip]], [[rack|racks|borrows to buy GPUs]] and [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]] are ultimately needed so that a single model can be trained and served. This is the summit. And it may be the worst place in the entire chain to put money: Nvidia squeezes from above, keeping ~75% of the margin, and free open models squeeze from below. Not one lab is profitable.
lab.thesis.stream.11.t: A lab sits in a vice. From above, [[asic|Nvidia|earns on every chip]] takes ~75% of the margin and ~90% of the hardware money — the computation the labs cannot do without. From below, free open models are catching up: DeepSeek trained a frontier-class model at a marginal cost of ~$5.6M and gave it away, forcing the whole industry to cut prices. And the price of inference (serving requests) has fallen roughly 1,000x in three years: the GPT-4 equivalent went from ~$20 to ~$0.40 per million tokens. The value a lab creates is squeezed from both ends.
lab.thesis.stream.12.items.0.l: Nvidia's margin and its share of the hardware money
lab.thesis.stream.12.items.1.l: the marginal cost of DeepSeek's model
lab.thesis.stream.12.items.1.n: given away free — a price reset across the industry
lab.thesis.stream.12.items.2.l: fall in the price of inference over 3 years
lab.thesis.stream.13.t: Who is winning the model war
lab.thesis.stream.14.t: Three labs lead. Anthropic has enterprise trust (~40% of the enterprise market, with Claude Code the leading coding tool and ~70% of head-to-head wins). OpenAI has consumer scale (1B+ users, the brand, Stargate). Google DeepMind is the integrated player: its own chips (TPU), distribution through Search and Android, and an unlimited balance sheet. Meta pushes open models, and DeepSeek is the icon of efficiency. But the protection — «being the best model» — erodes fastest of all: everyone converges on the same point, and open models catch up within months.
lab.thesis.stream.15.items.0.label: Anthropic — enterprise trust
lab.thesis.stream.15.items.0.note: the leading coding tool; ~70% of head-to-head wins
lab.thesis.stream.15.items.1.label: OpenAI — the consumer leader
lab.thesis.stream.15.items.2.label: Google DeepMind — the integrated one
lab.thesis.stream.15.items.2.note: own chips + distribution + an unlimited balance sheet
lab.thesis.stream.16.t: The durable advantage is not the model itself but distribution and the ability to absorb losses indefinitely. And that is exactly where Google (Search/Android + its own chips + cash) and the hyperscalers win, not the pure labs.
lab.thesis.stream.17.t: Who pays — and the circular financing
lab.thesis.stream.18.t: Who buys? Enterprises (2M+ business customers at OpenAI, 85K+ on Gemini, ~300K at Anthropic) — through the API on usage-based pricing; consumers — by subscription ($20–200/month: at OpenAI this is the most stable revenue, ~70% of the total, ~$17B); and governments (so far, little). But the real fuel is circular: OpenAI leans on capital from Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia, and Anthropic on AWS and Google. The customers and the investors are the same handful of giants.
lab.thesis.stream.19.items.2.n: the compute suppliers finance those who pay them
lab.thesis.stream.2.items.0.l: of lab revenue against >$700B of capex
lab.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: a thin slice of the whole theme
lab.thesis.stream.2.items.1.l: of every dollar spent on AI hardware goes to Nvidia
lab.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: the fattest margin — above the labs
lab.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: losing $1.22 on every dollar of revenue
lab.thesis.stream.20.t: What the market thinks: «the next platform»
lab.thesis.stream.21.t: The market treats the frontier labs as the next platform: revenue will grow into the capex, and private rounds «confirm» a $1T scale. Hence Anthropic is valued at $965B and OpenAI at $852B (an IPO target of ~$1T) — 20–150 times annual revenue depending on which revenue figure you believe. The circular financing of hyperscalers and sovereign funds is assumed to be durable.
lab.thesis.stream.24.t: The private marks embed a «permanent monopoly» outcome almost as fact — but its very support, model superiority, is the fastest-eroding advantage in technology. Everyone converges on the same benchmarks, open models catch up within months, and the falling price of inference turns today's premium into tomorrow's commodity. Paying 20–150 times revenue for a loss-making business financed in a loop, on a melting protection, is the definition of pricing for perfection.
lab.thesis.stream.25.t: So the right way to own the AI demand theme is not the labs themselves but liquid adjacent shares that capture the value the labs create without the loss-making risk: the compute landlords collecting on ~$1.4T of commitments (Oracle, Amazon), and the one integrated player that owns the whole stack and can absorb losses forever (Alphabet).
lab.thesis.stream.26.t: The very protection the labs' valuations rest on — model superiority — is the fastest to erode. It is more sensible to fund the theme through liquid adjacent shares.
lab.thesis.stream.27.t: What is priced in — and how to buy this properly
lab.thesis.stream.28.t: The labs directly embed flawless revenue scaling against ~$1.5T of infrastructure. The liquid proxies are markedly cheaper: Oracle at ~28x earnings for a $553B contracted order book; Amazon collecting through its stake in Anthropic; Alphabet, where the strongest lab (DeepMind) plus its own chips plus Search distribution come essentially «free» inside a diversified giant. You pay a fraction of the revenue multiple — and get distribution and cash flow.
lab.thesis.stream.3.t: What the labs do, and why it costs so much
lab.thesis.stream.30.t: Our read: the labs directly are expensive; the liquid proxies (Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon) are fair.
lab.thesis.stream.31.t: Where the technology is going — and where the money is going
lab.thesis.stream.32.t: The frontier is shifting from ever-larger training toward agents — models that do not merely answer but act (writing and running code, carrying out multi-step tasks). That expands the market (more inference per task) but also raises the reliability bar. Two forces pull in opposite directions: unit costs keep collapsing (~1,000x and continuing — through better chips, batching, sparse models and quantisation), devaluing the middle segment; while the frontier itself stays scarce and expensive, because only ~5 players can fund it. Open models (DeepSeek, Meta) keep the frontier honest by giving «good enough» away free.
lab.thesis.stream.33.t: Where the money is going: ~$1.4T of OpenAI compute commitments (Broadcom/Oracle/Microsoft/Nvidia/AMD), tens of billions of hyperscaler stakes to stake out demand (Amazon in Anthropic, Microsoft in OpenAI), and sovereign funds (the UAE, Saudi Arabia) financing national labs. This is the largest capital formation in the history of technology — and it is circular: the compute suppliers finance the labs that pay the compute suppliers.
lab.thesis.stream.34.items.1.l: the largest capital formation in history
lab.thesis.stream.34.items.1.n: the suppliers finance the very people who pay them
lab.thesis.stream.34.items.2.n: funds in the UAE and Saudi Arabia
lab.thesis.stream.35.t: What the players are betting on: the labs — on winning the model war before the money runs out and listing at their private marks. The hyperscalers — on owning the lab's demand (stakes) and renting it computation (the real profit). Google — on vertical integration (its own model + its own chips + its own distribution). The open players (Meta, DeepSeek) — on devaluing the frontier so nobody holds a monopoly. And the smartest investor bet is adjacency: the compute landlords and the integrated giant, not the loss-making summit. The main questions ahead are whether revenue catches the ~$1.5T of capex and whether the circular financing holds.
lab.thesis.stream.36.t: What would break — or confirm — the thesis
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.0: The revenue-to-capex gap fails to close
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.1: The circular financing cracks — the labs re-rate sharply (−50…−80%)
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.0: Open models close the frontier gap to <1%
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.1: Model protection disappears — the premium collapses
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.0: A lab lists below its last private mark
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.3.0: Agents deliver a real jump in enterprise revenue
lab.thesis.stream.37.rows.3.1: The bulls are right and the gap closes (bullish)
lab.thesis.stream.38.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
lab.thesis.stream.39.t: AI labs are the summit of the stack and the reason everything beneath them exists. But they are squeezed by Nvidia's margin from above and free open models from below, not one is profitable, and private rounds value them at 20–150 times revenue on a bet on «permanent monopoly» — the fastest-melting protection in technology.
lab.thesis.stream.4.t: A lab builds a foundation model — an enormous neural network trained on a large corpus of data and then applied to hundreds of tasks (dialogue, programming, document analysis). Training means adjusting billions of numerical parameters for weeks across tens of thousands of GPUs: a single training run for a frontier model costs $100M+ and is heading past $1B. Serving the model afterwards (answering queries) is a separate, permanent cost line. Only ~5 Western labs can afford the frontier.
lab.thesis.stream.40.t: The conclusion: own the AI demand theme through adjacency rather than the summit — the compute landlords collecting on ~$1.4T of commitments (Oracle, Amazon) and the integrated giant with model, chips and distribution that can lose money forever (Alphabet). The labs directly (Anthropic, OpenAI at 20–150x revenue) are venture bets priced for perfection, not a core holding. And the real profit from this whole wave accumulates below the labs — at Nvidia and the compute suppliers.
lab.thesis.stream.5.items.0.l: one training run for a frontier model
lab.thesis.stream.5.items.0.n: the cost per generation is rising fast
lab.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: the rest lack the capital and the energy
lab.thesis.stream.5.items.2.l: a package for one top researcher
lab.thesis.stream.6.t: Economics that do not add up
lab.thesis.stream.7.t: And here is the problem. Serving the model in isolation looks excellent — an 83–89% gross margin on the API. But add training, research and the talent war and the consolidated economics are catastrophic. OpenAI loses $1.22 for every dollar of revenue — a −122% operating margin on ~$25B of revenue and a ~$14B loss in 2026. Not one is profitable. What sustains them is not profit but capital from the very compute suppliers they are paying.
lab.thesis.stream.8.items.0.l: serving margin against the consolidated one
lab.thesis.stream.8.items.0.n: serving is profitable, the whole thing deeply loss-making
lab.thesis.stream.8.items.2.n: flowing back to Broadcom, Oracle, Microsoft and Nvidia
lab.thesis.stream.9.t: That ~$1.4T goes to Broadcom (~$350B), Oracle (~$300B), Microsoft (~$250B) and Nvidia (~$100B) — the same companies investing in the lab. The money goes round in a loop.
lab.tldr.0: The labs' combined revenue is ~$60–90B (mid-2026). OpenAI runs at ~$25B of annual revenue, Anthropic ~$47B (on a single source), and Google DeepMind sits inside Alphabet. But spending exceeds revenue several times over: OpenAI's compute commitments are ~$1.4T against ~$25B of revenue (56x). Hyperscaler capex is >$700B in 2026 and >$1.15–1.4T cumulatively across 2025–27 (Goldman Sachs).
lab.tldr.1: Market concentration: Anthropic has 40% of corporate LLM (large language model) spending, OpenAI 27%, Google 21% = 88% in the top three (Menlo Ventures). The unit cost of inference (serving a single request on a finished model) has fallen ~1,000x in 3 years. API margins (selling access to the model through a programming interface) run 60–89% at the serving level, but the total margin is deeply negative after training, R&D and talent ($1.5B packages). No lab has proven it can be profitable as a standalone business.
lab.tldr.2: Open models (free, open-source) as a commoditising force: DeepSeek V3 was trained for ~$5.6M; Chinese models are ~45% of OpenRouter traffic (an aggregator service for models; it was <2% a year ago). The gap between closed and open models has narrowed to 39 Arena points (a rating based on blind comparisons of answers). The key question: will revenue grow to the ~$1.5T/yr of infrastructure spending — before the circular financing (money going round in a loop) of hyperscalers and sovereign funds contracts?
lab.unitEconomics.costCurve: Training per generation: GPT-4 at ~$100M+; the next generation heading toward $1B+. DeepSeek V3's marginal cost was ~$5.6M. Four compounding factors: hardware (2–3x per generation), software and batching (2–3x), MoE (3–5x), quantisation (2–4x). Talent: packages of up to $1.5B (Meta → Andrew Tulloch).
lab.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Serving layer: 83–89% gross margin for frontier models (SemiAnalysis). Self-hosting open-weight: 25–60% (Bessemer). But blended margins are catastrophic: OpenAI runs a −122% operating margin at $25B ARR. Nobody is profitable standalone.
lab.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: Frontier API: Claude Opus $5/$25, GPT-5.5 ~$2.50/$15, Gemini 3.1 Pro $2/$12 per M input/output tokens. The GPT-4 equivalent: $20/M (2022) → $0.40/M (2026) = a ~1,000x decline. Consumer: $20–200/month.
lab.unitEconomics.takeaway: High serving margins mask catastrophic blended economics. The fundamental question: can a frontier lab be profitable standalone, or is the hyperscaler subsidy permanent?
lab.unitEconomics.yields.0.note: The most stable revenue. ChatGPT Pro at $200/month, Plus at $20/month
lab.unitEconomics.yields.3.note: Google: AI folded into a $300B+ base. Meta: strategic value, not direct model revenue
lab.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Talent (a few hundred elite researchers, on packages of up to $1.5B) and closing the revenue-to-capex gap. If revenue does not scale, the circular financing breaks.
lab.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Capital and power: only ~5 Western labs can afford frontier training runs ($100M+ per generation, heading toward $1B+). Power is the binding constraint (5–7 year interconnection queues)
lab.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Extreme: OpenAI's compute commitments are ~$1.4T; it raised $122B at an $852B valuation. Global corporate AI investment was $581.7B in 2025 (+130% in a year, Stanford HAI).
lab.valueCapture.margins.0.source: Data-centre revenue ~$93.7B (FY2026). ~90% of AI-accelerator spending. It captures the fattest margin
lab.valueCapture.margins.1.source: The API margin is high in isolation (SemiAnalysis). But the consolidated margin is deeply negative after training, R&D and talent. ~$47B of annual revenue (on a single source)
lab.valueCapture.margins.2.source: ~$25B of annual revenue, a projected ~$14B loss in 2026. Losing ~$1.22 on every dollar of revenue. 900M users a week
lab.valueCapture.margins.3.source: Bessemer State of AI 2025. Against 80–90% for traditional SaaS. A lower margin, but no vendor lock-in
lab.valueCapture.margins.4.source: AI folded into a $300B+ revenue base. It can absorb losses indefinitely. Monetised through advertising, cloud and Search
lab.valueCapture.takeaway: Value accrues disproportionately to the compute suppliers (NVIDIA). Labs capture value only through distribution (Google, Meta, OpenAI consumer) or a durable enterprise franchise (Anthropic in coding). Pure API-for-hire labs face the worst squeeze.
lab.verdict.bear.0: The gap between spending and revenue is unbridgeable: Bain sees a ~$800B revenue shortfall by 2030; Cahn puts the requirement at ~$3T of revenue against Anthropic and OpenAI's combined ~$80B; Allianz notes a 46% divergence between capex and revenue, above the 2001 telecom bubble's 32%. Circular financing — Nvidia→lab→Nvidia (money going round in a loop between the chip supplier and the customer) — masks the end demand (an echo of Lucent and Nortel).
lab.verdict.bear.1: Open models (free, open-source) crush prices everywhere but a narrowing frontier: DeepSeek, Qwen and Kimi are ~45% of OpenRouter (the aggregator that routes access to models). The hyperscalers are integrating vertically (Meta Muse, Google TPU, Amazon Trainium — their own chips) and are ceasing to subsidise external labs.
lab.verdict.bear.2: No lab has proven profitability: OpenAI runs at a −122% operating margin. If hyperscaler or sovereign-fund financing contracts (rates, a safety incident, disappointment in returns: MIT NANDA finds ~95% of corporate AI pilots produced zero return on profit), the valuations will be re-rated sharply.
lab.verdict.bull.0: Revenue is growing faster than any software category in history: OpenAI 0→$25B in ~30 months; Anthropic up 47x in 17 months. If the pace holds, the capex pays for itself and today's valuations turn out to be cheap.
lab.verdict.bull.1: Agentic and reasoning AI (models that carry out multi-step tasks themselves rather than merely answering) expands the market from «chat» to «replacing labour»: a market worth trillions with premium pricing and a growing advantage to the frontier leaders.
lab.verdict.bull.2: Distribution (the channels that deliver the product to users) plus enterprise trust prove durable: Google's 900M monthly active users, OpenAI's 1B+, Anthropic's 40% of the enterprise market — the winners capture cloud-software-like economics as the unit cost of serving requests falls ~10x a year.
lab.verdict.horizon: 5–10 years to the thesis resolving, but a sharp re-rating is possible sooner — within 12–36 months, on an IPO or a large round.
lab.verdict.keyQuestion: Will AI labs' revenue grow to the scale of the ~$1.5T/yr of infrastructure spending — before the financing contracts?
lab.verdict.sizing: Direct foundation-model revenue ~$60–90B (mid-2026). A 25x spread in TAM ($20B for the model layer → >$1.2T for the full stack). Hyperscaler AI capex >$700B (2026)
lab.verdict.summary: The fastest-growing software category in history (OpenAI: 0→$25B in ~30 months), but a structurally loss-making sector sitting on a ~$1.5T/yr stack of commitments. The competitive advantages are thin and reshuffle monthly: commoditisation by open models (turning free, open-source models into a cheap standard) is merciless (~45% of traffic on OpenRouter, the aggregator that routes access to different models), and only distribution — the channels that reach users (Google, Meta) — and enterprise trust (Anthropic) are holding so far. Investability is limited: predominantly private companies at extreme valuations (20–150x revenue). The recommendation: a high-conviction thematic position at a small weight through liquid adjacent shares (Alphabet, Amazon, Oracle, ASML). Direct private exposure (secondary-market stakes in OpenAI/Anthropic) only at <1% size and with readiness for a re-rating.
lab.whatIsIt: The companies that build the AI models themselves — large programs trained on enormous volumes of text and able to hold a conversation, write code and analyse documents. This is the top, «intelligent» layer of the whole chain: chips, cabinets and data centres ultimately exist so that such a model can be trained and can then answer people's queries. Training one frontier model costs hundreds of millions of dollars and requires tens of thousands of chips to compute as a single unit for weeks.
litho.competition.concentration: An oligopoly: Applied Materials + ASML + Lam + TEL + KLA = 56–66% of the market, ~70% of WFE (MarketsandMarkets)
litho.competition.entryBarrier: The highest in world industry: decades of R&D, exclusive supply chains (Zeiss makes optics only for ASML), thousands of qualified engineers, patent estates of tens of thousands of patents. No startup can enter — this is an oligopoly that took 50 years to form.
litho.competition.players.0.edge: 30 years of development + Zeiss (exclusive) + Cymer (owned). Not reproducible.
litho.competition.players.1.edge: the broadest portfolio: deposition, etch, implant, CMP, e-beam, packaging
litho.competition.players.2.edge: software + data; the harder the chip, the more inspection — its share grows automatically
litho.competition.players.3.edge: >100,000 chambers installed; dominant in 3D NAND and leading-edge logic
litho.competition.players.4.edge: a monopoly in photoresist coating and developing — a mandatory lithography step
litho.competition.shareTrajectory.0.deta: the monopoly is invulnerable; High-NA widens the advantage
litho.competition.shareTrajectory.1.deta: records; a >50% share in HBM packaging equipment
litho.competition.shareTrajectory.2.deta: +360 bps of share since 2021; seven times its nearest competitor
litho.competition.shareTrajectory.4.deta: the largest Chinese player; revenue ~$5.84B; limited to mature nodes
litho.competition.switchingCost: Extremely high: every machine is qualified at a specific fab for a specific process (months of work). The installed base creates lock-in through service contracts (recurring income). Replacing one vendor means re-qualifying the whole line.
litho.competition.takeaway: The best-protected oligopoly in technology. Five companies control all chip manufacturing in the world. Chinese competitors are growing but are confined to mature nodes and cannot reproduce EUV, leading-edge etch or defect inspection. The leaders' positions strengthen with every new technology generation.
litho.demand.backlog: ASML: ~€39B (more than a year of revenue). Lam: a record $5.84B in a quarter, guiding $6.6B. AMAT: a record $7.91B, guiding $8.95B.
litho.demand.contractStructure: Long-term orders for EUV systems (12–18 month lead times; High-NA takes up to a year to qualify). Service contracts on the installed base are recurring income: ASML €2.76B/qtr, Lam $2.1B/qtr (a record, +25% y/y), AMAT $1.67B/qtr (+17%).
litho.demand.customerConcentration: High: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron are ~80% of demand. Those five companies' capex sets the whole market. TSMC 2 nm/A16, Intel 18A/14A and SK Hynix HBM are the main drivers for 2026–2027.
litho.demand.pricing: EUV 0.33 NA: ~$200M each. High-NA EUV: ~$380–400M each. Etch/deposition: $5–50M. Prices rise with every generation.
litho.demand.soldOut.0.note: ASML: a ~€39B order book (> a year of revenue); AMAT: 8 quarters of visibility; 100+ fab projects
litho.demand.soldOut.1.note: SEMI: a record $156B of total equipment; ASML plans ~80 EUV systems
litho.demand.takeaway: Demand is confirmed by record order books and fab capex. AI is the structural driver: HBM consumes 3x more wafers, GAA adds +15–25% process steps, and packaging grows >50%. But concentration in 5 buyers is a risk: if any one of them cuts its budget, the whole market feels it.
litho.dependencies.correlation: High correlation with fab capex (cyclical). But AI lengthens the cycle: fab programmes now run 3–5 years rather than the 1–2 of the past.
litho.dependencies.downstream: Fabs and memory makers: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron — their capex is demand, directly. Leading-edge logic + DRAM + packaging = >80% of 2026 growth (AMAT). Data centres = 30% of leading-edge wafer consumption.
litho.dependencies.takeaway: Equipment depends on two things: the capex of the 5 largest fabs (demand) and exclusive subsystem suppliers (supply). Zeiss to ASML is the most critical dependency in the whole chain: without that optics there are no EUV tools.
litho.dependencies.upstream.0.note: the 0.55 NA anamorphic column for High-NA — the world's only supplier
litho.dependencies.upstream.1.note: EUV sources are part of ASML's vertical integration
litho.dependencies.upstream.2.note: RF/DC power, gas delivery, vacuum, filtration — thousands of components
litho.dependencies.upstream.2.supplier: MKS (>85% of the market), Advanced Energy, Ichor, VAT, Entegris
litho.expectations.impliedGrowth: ASML at ~42x forward earnings embeds continued double-digit growth and a successful High-NA transition. Onto at ~150x embeds perfection. But SOX has already entered a technical bear market (−20% from its June 2026 peak) — the market has taken back part of the cycle premium despite record order books.
litho.expectations.marketBelieves: Monopolies deserve to be expensive, but the market fears the cycle more than it believes in structural growth: the SOX index fell 20% even as all five WFE leaders reported records (ASML's €39B order book, AMAT's $7.91B, KLA's 62.6% margin). A classic fear of an air pocket after the peak.
litho.expectations.metrics.0.history: expensive, but the only EUV maker
litho.expectations.metrics.0.note: the premium is justified by a 100% EUV monopoly; drawdowns of 15%+ (as in July 2026) have historically been entry points
litho.expectations.metrics.1.history: the best in the big five
litho.expectations.metrics.1.label: Gross margin · KLA
litho.expectations.metrics.1.note: software + data + automatic share growth; a 43% operating margin — the most resilient in downturns
litho.expectations.metrics.2.note: the shares are +234% in a year; any capex slowdown means a collapse. Metrology is valuable, but overheated
litho.expectations.metrics.3.history: more than a year of revenue
litho.expectations.metrics.3.label: Order book · ASML
litho.expectations.metrics.3.note: 2+ years of visibility; ASML has moved to annual disclosure — less transparency, but unchanged fundamentals
litho.expectations.metrics.4.label: Index · SOX
litho.expectations.metrics.4.note: a technical bear market on record metrics — a divergence between the share price and the business's fundamentals
litho.expectations.takeaway: The market prices this sector through fear of the cycle rather than through the quality of the monopolies. The divergence is in ASML and KLA: record order books against −20% in the shares means the price reflects a future air pocket that is not yet in the data. That is where the market's expectations have parted from the fundamentals.
litho.expectations.verdict: On a drawdown — fair (for a monopoly, closer to cheap); at the cycle peak — expensive
litho.expectations.weThink: AI lengthens the cycle — fab programmes run 3–5 years, and AMAT has 8 quarters of visibility. A −20% drawdown on a record €39B order book (more than a year of revenue) is a gap between price and fundamentals. ASML at a 15–20% drawdown is an entry into an insurmountable monopoly, not a signal to run. It is almost never absolutely cheap.
litho.intro:
Lithography and the related equipment are the machines that physically make every chip. Manufacturing proceeds layer by layer: on each layer, some tools grow ultra-thin films, the lithography tool transfers the transistor pattern onto them with light, others etch away the excess, and inspection systems hunt for defects a few atoms across. A single leading-edge chip goes through these cycles dozens of times. The hardest and most expensive step is lithography in extreme ultraviolet (EUV), and exactly one company in the world makes those machines.

How EUV works. The finer the transistor, the shorter the wavelength of light needed to «print» it: ordinary lithography works at 193 nm, but nodes of 7 nm and below need 13.5 nm — almost 14 times shorter. That light is produced like this: droplets of molten tin are fired into a vacuum chamber tens of thousands of times a second, and each is struck twice by a powerful laser — the first pulse flattens the droplet, the second turns it into plasma, and the plasma radiates the required 13.5 nm. The difficulty is that light of this wavelength is absorbed by almost everything, including air and glass. So the whole system runs in vacuum, and instead of lenses the light is guided by reflection off a set of ultra-smooth mirrors — each loses some of the light, so only a small fraction of the original reaches the wafer. The mirrors are polished to atomic smoothness; a single supplier makes them, exclusively for one lithography-tool maker. Finally the light reflects off a mask carrying the circuit pattern and transfers it onto a silicon wafer coated with a photosensitive layer.

Why one machine costs $200–400M. Behind it sit around 30 years of development and more than $10B of investment, exclusive optics, and a proprietary light source that has to ignite tin tens of thousands of times a second, reliably, for years. The precision is at the limit of physics, and nobody has managed to replicate that combination of mirrors, source and droplet delivery — Canon and Nikon dropped out of the EUV race, and simpler techniques stalled at the previous generation. The next generation with sharper optics (High-NA) already costs $380–400M a machine. No fab prints nodes of 7 nm or below without EUV — which makes this the deepest physical constraint in the whole AI chain.

Who pays, and how much. Demand comes from just five fabs, which account for ~80% of purchases; each has capex of $10–30B, and 70–80% of that money goes to the tools themselves. They pay almost any price, because without a lithography tool a new leading-edge fab simply cannot be built, and the lead time is 12–18 months: a place in the queue matters more than the price. The sole EUV maker's order book stands at around €39B — more than a year of its revenue.

The chip-manufacturing equipment market was around $135B in 2025 (heading toward ~$150B in 2026), and five companies control 56–66% of the total; in EUV lithography the monopoly is single and complete.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.
litho.marketSizing.bomShare.note: equipment is not part of the chip but the means of producing it. Yet every fab costs $10–30B, of which 70–80% is buying machines
litho.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice: Growth comes both through volume (more plants: 100+ active projects) and through price per machine (EUV: $200M → High-NA: $400M). Plus a structural shift: new technologies (GAA, HBM, advanced packaging) add ~$1B of additional market for every 100,000 wafers a month.
litho.mentalModel.chain.0: Chips get harder (GAA, HBM, backside power) → more process steps
litho.mentalModel.chain.1: every leading-edge node needs EUV — and only ASML makes EUV
litho.mentalModel.chain.2: a fab physically cannot print ≤7 nm without an ASML tool ($200–400M)
litho.mentalModel.chain.3: more steps = more inspection (KLA) and more etch (Lam) per wafer
litho.mentalModel.chain.4: fab capex of $10–30B → 70–80% on machines → leader margins of 50–65%
litho.mentalModel.drivers.0.note: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron = ~80% of demand. Their budgets set the whole market: TSMC 2 nm/A16, Intel 18A/14A and SK Hynix HBM are the 2026–2027 drivers.
litho.mentalModel.drivers.1.note: GAA transistors add +15–25% process steps, backside power delivery adds +$1B of market per 100k wafers/month, and HBM consumes 3x more wafers per bit. Harder chip, more equipment.
litho.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: the EXE:5200 costs ~$400M each (2.5x an ordinary EUV tool), with fewer than 12 systems in the world. Volume production in 2027–2028 is the next ASP jump and a new level of monopoly.
litho.mentalModel.framework: ASML is the single binding constraint on the whole AI chain: no leading-edge chip is produced without its EUV tool, and it cannot be replicated (30 years of development, ~$10B, exclusive Zeiss optics, Cymer light sources). But demand is cyclical — so this is a bet on an irreproducible monopoly bought at the right point in the cycle. Deposition (AMAT, Lam), inspection (KLA) and etch tools earn by the same mechanism: the harder the chip, the more steps and checks per wafer.
litho.mentalModel.revenueFormula: ASML revenue = number of EUV systems (~65 in 2026 → ~80 in 2027) × price ($200M EUV / $400M High-NA) + service on the installed base (€2.76B/qtr)
litho.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: a 100% share, 30 years of development and >$10B invested. No competitor has come close. High-NA EUV (~$400M each) widens the lead. Not one leading-edge chip on the planet is made without this machine.
litho.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: Zeiss makes optics only for ASML (the 0.55 NA anamorphic column for High-NA has one supplier in the world), and Cymer's light sources are ASML-owned. The most critical dependency in the whole chain — and it is closed.
litho.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: ~57% of the market, seven times its nearest competitor, +360 bps of share since 2021. The only category where share grows automatically: the harder the chip (GAA, BSPDN), the more inspection points — 10–100x more.
litho.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: every machine takes months to qualify at a specific fab for a specific process. Replacing a vendor means re-qualifying the whole line. Service contracts on the installed base lock the customer in (recurring income).
litho.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: ASML spends ~€1.2B/qtr on R&D (~13–15% of revenue); patent estates run to tens of thousands of patents. Every next generation costs more than the last — which protects those already inside.
litho.moatBreakdown.components.5.factor: Protection of mature nodes from China
litho.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the only crack: NAURA/AMEC/ACM have taken 6.5% of the Chinese market (up from 1.2% in 2021), with a ~50% localisation target; foreign suppliers' share of China's imports fell from 77% to 65%. Leading-edge nodes are out of their reach, but mature ones are eroding.
litho.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The deepest protection in technology — resting on a combination: ASML's EUV monopoly + Zeiss's exclusive optics + KLA's automatically growing share. Five of the six factors score 8–10. The one weakening component is mature nodes in China, and it does not touch the leading edge, where ASML and KLA are monopolists and invulnerable.

Besi and Camtek are the best asymmetric bets on packaging/HBM. Drawdowns of 15–20% (as in July 2026) are normal entry points for this sector.
litho.problems.items.0.gap: An EUV machine cannot be replicated: behind it sit ~30 years of development, >$10B of investment, exclusive Zeiss optics and a proprietary light source. Canon and Nikon abandoned EUV development, and China's SMEE is stuck on the older DUV technology (lithography at a longer wavelength, for larger transistors). Even with the money, a competitor is decades behind, while a buyer waits 12–18 months for a finished machine plus up to a year to tune a High-NA one.
litho.problems.items.0.problem: No chip at 7 nm or below can be printed without an EUV tool (the machine that prints a chip's pattern in extreme ultraviolet), and only one company in the world makes it — ASML. In 2026 it ships ~65 systems (+25% on 2025), but demand from the five fabs (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron) grows faster than output. Each machine costs $200M (ordinary EUV) or $380–400M (the new High-NA generation, with sharper optics), and the lead time is 12–18 months. While lithography tools are short, the fabs cannot raise leading-edge chip output — this is the deepest physical constraint in the whole AI chain.
litho.problems.items.0.solution: ASML is expanding EUV production (printing in extreme ultraviolet) by roughly +30% a year and plans to reach a fleet of ~80 systems by 2027; another +30% is under study for 2028. In parallel High-NA EUV is arriving — a new generation with sharper imaging for nodes of 2 nm and below (volume production 2027–2028). The physical ceiling on expansion is not money but cleanroom floor space (dust-free production halls) at the fabs: the market ceiling is estimated at ~$150B in 2026. So the problem is solved by years of planned build-up, not by a fast jump.
litho.problems.items.0.winners: ASML is the sole beneficiary: 100% of the EUV market (printing in extreme ultraviolet) and ~90%+ of all lithography, so any capacity expansion runs only through it. Its exclusive suppliers earn alongside it: Zeiss makes the ultra-smooth optics only for ASML, and the Cymer light source is a division inside ASML. Among the buyers, TSMC gains most — as the largest customer it gets priority access to new machines ahead of its competitors.
litho.problems.takeaway: Relieving this shortage only strengthens the incumbent monopolist: only ASML can expand EUV output, so all the growth in demand for leading-edge chips converts automatically into its revenue and reinforces a position nobody can contest.

litho.thesis.bigIdea: The market prices chip-making machines, over and over, as an ordinary cyclical business — and sells them off on fear of «peak capex» (the semiconductor index down 20% on record order books). But underneath the sector lies the least reproducible monopoly in technology: no leading-edge chip exists without ASML's EUV machines (which print the finest lines on a chip), and nobody else can build them. Every drawdown in that monopoly has been an entry point, AI lengthens the cycle, and the next-generation machines (High-NA — a still more precise and expensive version of the same tools) extend the monopoly by another decade.
litho.thesis.stream.0.t: The toll gate every chip passes through
litho.thesis.stream.1.t: Every transistor on every leading-edge chip was physically «printed» onto silicon by someone. And the machine that prints the finest lines is made by exactly one company on the planet — ASML. A new fab costs $10–30B, and 70–80% of that is buying machines from a handful of suppliers. A chip can be designed anywhere, but it can only be manufactured by buying equipment from these companies.
litho.thesis.stream.11.t: The margin goes to whoever owns a mandatory step. And the harder the chip, the more steps and checks there are — the market grows by itself. KLA (inspection) and Besi (packaging) are the margin champions (62–65%): the denser the transistors, the more there is to inspect.
litho.thesis.stream.12.t: Who buys — a narrow circle of giants
litho.thesis.stream.13.t: This market has only five serious buyers. TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron account for ~80% of all demand — their capital spending sets the whole sector. Revenue is concentrated but also predictable: these fabs' plans are known years ahead. The main drivers for 2026–2027 are TSMC's move to 2 nm, Intel's to 18A, and SK Hynix scaling [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]]. And the end customer is the data centre: it already takes ~30% of leading-edge wafer consumption.
litho.thesis.stream.14.items.0.l: of demand comes from just five buyers
litho.thesis.stream.14.items.1.l: of leading-edge wafers go to data centres
litho.thesis.stream.14.items.1.n: the end customer of the whole build-out
litho.thesis.stream.14.items.2.n: AI pulls all three at once (AMAT)
litho.thesis.stream.15.t: And demand multiplies structurally: [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] consumes 3x more wafers per bit, the new transistor structure (GAA) adds +15–25% process steps, and [[pkg|advanced packaging|became the main event]] grows by more than 50%. Every chip for [[asic|custom AI accelerators|earns on every chip]] passes through these same machines — and needs more of them.
litho.thesis.stream.16.t: The hidden engine: service on the installed base
litho.thesis.stream.17.t: But the most underrated part is not selling machines — it is servicing them. Every machine sold generates income for years: upgrades, spare parts, support. Lam has >100K chambers installed, and ASML's service brings ~€2.76B a quarter — 25–30% of revenue, recurring and high-margin. Service is exactly what smooths the cycle: even when fabs slow their purchases of new machines, the installed ones keep paying.
litho.thesis.stream.18.items.2.n: each generating service income for years
litho.thesis.stream.2.items.1.l: of a new fab's cost is equipment
litho.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: only it makes the machines for the finest lines
litho.thesis.stream.20.t: The sector's financial condition is at records, and it shows in the numbers. ASML's order book is ~€39B (more than a year of its revenue). Lam's quarterly orders are a record $5.84B, and Applied Materials' $7.91B. A single machine costs more with every generation, while the installed base generates service income for years.
litho.thesis.stream.22.t: Operating leverage is high: KLA's operating margin is 43%, Lam's 35%, Applied Materials' 32%. Service is 25–30% of revenue and grows with the number of installed machines, smoothing the cycle. That is how a one-off machine sale turns into a multi-year annuity.
litho.thesis.stream.23.t: What the market thinks: «it's a cycle, and it's at the peak»
litho.thesis.stream.24.t: Equipment has always been a cycle: fabs buy machines in waves, and a peak is followed by an air pocket. In 2022 the shares fell 55–60% (Applied Materials −57%, Lam −59%). The market prices the sector by that reflex. In 2026 the semiconductor index fell 20% from its peak — even as all five leaders reported records: ASML's €39B order book, KLA's 62.6% margin, and AMAT above 50% for the first time in 25 years.
litho.thesis.stream.25.items.0.l: the semiconductor index from its 2026 peak
litho.thesis.stream.25.items.0.n: on record order books and margins — fear of an air pocket
litho.thesis.stream.25.items.1.n: larger than a year of its revenue
litho.thesis.stream.25.items.2.n: for the first time in 25 years
litho.thesis.stream.26.t: Why this is a monopoly, not a cycle
litho.thesis.stream.27.t: But AI lengthens the cycle. Fab programmes run 3–5 years, Applied Materials has 8 quarters of visibility, and ASML's order book is more than a year of revenue. This is not a spot market that collapses overnight.
litho.thesis.stream.28.t: And the main point: every drawdown in this monopoly has historically been an entry point. ASML falling 15–20% is an entry into a business that cannot be reproduced, not a signal to run. A monopoly like this is almost never absolutely cheap. Demand is structural: leading-edge AI chips, more inspection per chip, a rising price per machine with High-NA, and a new equipment market for packaging and HBM.
litho.thesis.stream.29.t: The market is pricing a cyclical semiconductor business. In fact you own a toll gate on all leading-edge computing — with growing service income on top.
litho.thesis.stream.30.t: Where the sector is going — and where the money is going
litho.thesis.stream.31.t: Technically the sector is heading toward still greater complexity, and complexity is the equipment maker's friend. High-NA is entering volume (the next decade's monopoly), transistors of a new structure (GAA) are arriving, and [[pkg|advanced packaging|became the main event]] plus [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] add ~$1B of new equipment market for every 100K wafers a month. Every new turn demands new machines and more inspection.
litho.thesis.stream.32.t: Where the money is going: TSMC, Samsung and Intel queue for the same machines, and their capital spending ($10–30B per fab) flows straight into the big five's order books. A place in the queue cannot be bought: a machine takes months to build, and priority goes to whoever ordered earlier. China is a separate story: export restrictions close leading-edge machines to it (a revenue risk), but at the same time create demand for domestic equipment (which is what NAURA grows on).
litho.thesis.stream.33.t: What the fabs are betting on: staking out machines years ahead — whoever did not join the queue will not build a plant. What the investor should bet on: the toll gates themselves. ASML is the purest (100% of EUV + service + High-NA ahead); KLA and Besi are the margin champions; the inspection and packaging specialists (Camtek, Onto, Nova) are riskier leverage on the same complexity.
litho.thesis.stream.35.t: ASML trades at ~42x earnings — a premium, but one justified by a 100% EUV monopoly. The key observation: drawdowns of 15%+ (as in July 2026) have historically been entry points rather than turns. The market keeps hanging a «cyclical discount» on this monopoly at every downturn — and keeps being wrong.
litho.thesis.stream.36.items.0.n: the premium is justified by a 100% monopoly; 15%+ drawdowns have historically been entries
litho.thesis.stream.36.items.1.n: the best of the five — software and data
litho.thesis.stream.36.items.2.n: at the trough it falls to 20–25x, at the peak it reaches 42–45x
litho.thesis.stream.38.rows.0.0: A fab cancels or postpones a large project
litho.thesis.stream.38.rows.0.1: A capex air pocket — a drawdown like 2022's (−55–60%)
litho.thesis.stream.38.rows.1.1: A bigger revenue hit than the manageable loss today
litho.thesis.stream.38.rows.2.1: ASML's monopoly under threat — but in 30 years nobody has come close
litho.thesis.stream.39.t: The first signal is a real and recurring cycle risk; the other two are still distant. Which is exactly why the entry is on drawdowns rather than at the peak.
litho.thesis.stream.4.t: An EUV machine prints a chip's pattern in extreme ultraviolet (13.5 nm wavelength) — light so fine that air and ordinary lenses absorb it. So everything happens in vacuum, and the light is guided not by lenses but by ultra-precise Zeiss mirrors; the light itself is born from tin droplets struck twice in succession by a laser. This is not one instrument but a whole chain of unique technologies that only ASML assembles: Zeiss's optics and Cymer's light source are each a monopoly in their own right.
litho.thesis.stream.40.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
litho.thesis.stream.41.t: Lithography is not a cyclical business but the least reproducible monopoly in technology: no leading-edge chip appears without ASML's EUV machines, and nobody else can build them. The market keeps selling this monopoly as an ordinary cycle at every «peak capex» scare — and keeps being wrong.
litho.thesis.stream.42.t: The conclusion: every 15–20% drawdown has historically been an entry point rather than a turn. ASML is the purest expression of the thesis (100% of EUV, a service annuity, High-NA ahead); KLA and Besi are the margin champions; and the whole big five is a toll gate on the entire AI build-out that cannot be routed around.
litho.thesis.stream.5.items.0.n: the next generation (High-NA) costs twice as much
litho.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: Canon and Nikon tried and gave up
litho.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: each generation costs more — which is what protects the leader
litho.thesis.stream.6.t: High-NA is the next rung of the same monopoly: a still harder machine, still more expensive, still further from competitors. It extends ASML's lead by another decade.
litho.thesis.stream.7.t: Not just ASML: five companies, each on its own step
litho.thesis.stream.8.t: Lithography is the most visible barrier but not the only one. Making a chip takes hundreds of steps, and almost every mandatory step has its own dominant company that cannot be skipped.
litho.thesis.stream.9.t: To read the table, a brief word on how a chip is actually made. Ultra-thin films of material are laid onto a silicon wafer layer by layer — that is deposition. The pattern of the future circuit is then «printed» onto them with light (lithography) and everything unwanted is etched away with acid or plasma — that is etch. This repeats dozens of times until a multi-layer structure of billions of transistors has been grown. And before each print the wafer is coated with a photosensitive lacquer — photoresist — which is then developed like photographic film. Each of these steps has its own dominant company:
litho.tldr.0: The chip-manufacturing equipment market grew to a record $135B (2025) and is heading for $145–170B in 2026. AI, HBM memory (ultra-fast memory next to the chip) and advanced packaging are >80% of the growth.
litho.tldr.1: ASML is a 100% monopoly in EUV lithography (printing chips with extreme ultraviolet). Its order book of ~€39B is larger than a year of revenue. The new High-NA EUV (the next generation with sharper optics) costs ~$400M each, and fewer than a dozen exist worldwide.
litho.tldr.2: KLA has the best combination of margin (62–63%) and protection: defect inspection is ~57% of the market, seven times its nearest competitor. Its share grows because every new chip generation needs more inspection.
litho.tldr.3: The main risk: China is simultaneously the largest buyer (~40% of the market in 2024, falling toward ~20%) and a growing competitor (NAURA, AMEC and ACM have taken 6.5% of the Chinese market and keep gaining).
litho.unitEconomics.costCurve: R&D is the critical line: ASML spends ~€1.2B/qtr (~13–15% of revenue). The cost of entry: ASML spent >$10B and 30 years creating EUV. Every next generation costs more than the last — which protects the leaders' positions.
litho.unitEconomics.grossMargin: KLA: 62–63% (the best). Besi: 64–65% (packaging). ASML: 54% (guiding 55–57%). AMAT: ~50% (a first in 25 years). Lam: ~50%. TEL: ~45%.
litho.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: EUV 0.33 NA: ~$200M each. High-NA EUV (EXE:5200): ~$380–400M each (confirmed by Reuters/imec). One High-NA exposure costs ~2.5x an ordinary EUV one. Etch/deposition: $5–50M.
litho.unitEconomics.takeaway: The economics improve with every generation: the price per machine rises (EUV $200M → High-NA $400M), margins expand (AMAT above 50% for the first time), and the service base generates recurring income. The harder the chips, the more the equipment makers earn.
litho.unitEconomics.yields.0.note: share of revenue; high margin; grows with the installed base
litho.update.bottomLine: Records on every metric (revenue, margin, order books) against falling shares is the condition under which a long-term investor usually enters. ASML + KLA as the core, AMAT for value, Besi/Camtek as satellites. A 15–20% drawdown on record orders is an opportunity to add, not a reason to sell.
litho.update.headline: Records across the whole big five — yet SOX has entered a bear market

litho.update.stories.0.verdict: Rotation plus geopolitics, not a fundamental reversal. Order books are at records. Historically, drawdowns of 20–30% have been the best entry points.

litho.update.stories.2.title: Global equipment billings Q1 2026: $36.55B (+14% y/y)
litho.update.stories.2.verdict: Equipment demand has risen for a fourth quarter running.
litho.update.stories.3.detail: HBM packaging: revenue up ~6x in a year to more than $600M. 100+ active fab projects. 8 quarters of order visibility.

litho.update.stories.5.detail: First users: Intel (14A), SK Hynix (DRAM), Samsung (SF1.4), TSMC (A14 from 2028).
litho.update.stories.5.title: High-NA EUV (EXE:5200) installed at imec — cost ~$400M
litho.update.stories.5.verdict: Confirmation of the next generation of ASML's monopoly. <12 systems worldwide. Throughput ~175 wafers/hour, precision 0.7 nm.
litho.update.summary: The paradox of July 2026: all five WFE leaders reported records (ASML's €39B order book, AMAT $7.91B, Lam $5.84B, TEL ¥2,443B, KLA's 62.6% margin), but the SOX index fell 20% from its high into a technical bear market. The causes: rotation out of semiconductors, the Kimi K3 shock to the adjacent EDA sector, and geopolitical worries. Fundamentally nothing changed — demand is confirmed 2+ years out.
litho.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Defect inspection (KLA): with every new generation (GAA, HBM, BSPDN) 10–100x more points on a wafer have to be checked. KLA is already seven times its nearest competitor and keeps pulling away.
litho.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: ASML is an absolute monopoly in EUV: a 100% share, 30 years of development, >$10B invested, exclusive Zeiss optics and its own Cymer light sources. No competitor can reproduce it. High-NA EUV (~$400M each) is the next level of the monopoly.
litho.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: High for the equipment makers: ASML spends ~€1.2B/qtr on R&D (~13–15% of revenue). But higher still for the buyers: one fab means $10–30B of capex.
litho.valueCapture.margins.1.source: the best of the big five; software + data
litho.valueCapture.margins.3.source: above 50% for the first time in 25 years
litho.valueCapture.takeaway: Margins are rising across the whole big five — a sign of a healthy cycle and strengthening pricing power. Service and the installed base (>100,000 chambers at Lam, €2.76B/qtr at ASML) turn into recurring income. KLA and Besi are the margin champions (62–65%).
litho.verdict.bear.0: Cyclicality: in 2022 SOXX (the semiconductor share index) fell 46%, AMAT ~57%, Lam ~59%, ASML ~55–60%. In July 2026 SOX entered a technical bear market (−20% from its high).
litho.verdict.bear.1: China is a double blow: the largest customer ($41B, 40% of the market in 2024) is leaving (toward ~20% in 2026) AND building its own industry at the same time (NAURA, AMEC, SiCarrier). AMAT has already paid a $253M fine for export violations.
litho.verdict.bear.2: Valuations: ASML ~42x forward earnings, Onto ~150x, ACMR above its DCF fair value. If fab capex slows, the multiples compress first.
litho.verdict.bull.0: Record order books: ASML at ~€39B, Lam at a record $5.84B in a quarter, AMAT at a record $7.91B. Visibility 8 quarters out, with 100+ active fab projects.
litho.verdict.bull.1: AI structurally raises equipment intensity: GAA transistors (a new three-dimensional transistor structure) add +15–25% process steps, HBM (ultra-fast memory) consumes 3x more wafers per bit, and advanced packaging grows >50% in 2026.
litho.verdict.bull.2: The monopolies are insurmountable: ASML spent 30 years and >$10B on EUV (printing with extreme ultraviolet), plus exclusive Zeiss optics and its own Cymer light sources. It cannot be reproduced.
litho.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — tied to the AI capex cycle and the node transition (2 nm and beyond), where ASML's EUV machines are mandatory.
litho.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the fabs keep raising capex — or will capacity be overbuilt, as in every past cycle?
litho.verdict.sizing: The WFE market: $104B (2024) → $135B (2025) → $145–170B (2026) → up to $200–210B (2028). All equipment (including test and packaging): a record $156B in 2027.
litho.verdict.summary: The deepest monopolies in technology: ASML (100% of EUV — lithography in extreme ultraviolet), KLA (57% of defect inspection, a 62–63% margin), Applied Materials (the largest by revenue). Growth is double-digit and confirmed by order books and fab capex. But equipment is the most cyclical part of the chain: in 2022 the SOX index (of semiconductor shares) fell 46%, and individual names 55–60%. Valuations are high (ASML at ~42x forward earnings), and China is a double risk: both the largest customer and a rising competitor.
litho.whatIsIt: These are the machines that physically make every chip. A leading-edge chip is built in layers: some tools deposit ultra-thin films, others transfer the pattern of the future transistors onto them with light, others strip away the excess and hunt for defects a few atoms across — dozens of times over. The hardest and most expensive of these machines prints the pattern with a special short-wavelength light, and exactly one company in the world can build it.
nuc.picks.0.group: Operating capacity and equipment — money today
nuc.picks.0.note: They monetise AI demand right now — through contracts on operating reactors or through scarce equipment and fuel, without betting on any particular new design.

nuc.picks.0.rows.0.priced: P/E 26.7×; the AI premium is already substantial; regulatory risk and execution on large capital projects.
nuc.picks.0.rows.0.why: Operating round-the-clock generation plus the optionality of uprates, life extension and restarts. It moves output out of the spot market into long-term contracts with a premium for clean firm capacity.

nuc.picks.0.rows.1.priced: Concentration in a few assets and one customer; regulatory disputes over co-location; sensitivity to plant outages.
nuc.picks.0.rows.1.why: Smaller than Constellation, so a single large contract moves EBITDA, debt capacity and the valuation much more. Amazon as an anchor customer removes market risk.

nuc.picks.0.rows.2.priced: P/E 24.5×; a less pure nuclear bet — the outcome depends on gas, weather and retail margins.
nuc.picks.0.rows.2.why: An AI system does not run on nuclear alone: it needs baseload, peaking, reserve and storage. Vistra earns on the general rise in prices and consumption, not on a single contract.

nuc.picks.0.rows.3.priced: P/E 46×; a premium for scarce nuclear manufacturing; the commercial upside may come slowly.

nuc.picks.0.rows.4.why: Diversified Western exposure: it earns not only on the uranium price but on the industry's expansion (equipment and service through Westinghouse).

nuc.thesis.bigIdea: The market reads «AI + nuclear» as a reactor renaissance and buys everything in sight — small reactor startups, uranium, enrichment. But the scarcest thing here is not fission technology or a new reactor: it is a gigawatt of round-the-clock capacity that is already built, licensed and connected to the grid. A new unit would deliver the same electricity, but in 7–15 years and for $6–10B; an operating one can be recontracted today — which is exactly what Microsoft, Meta and Amazon are doing, signing 15–20 year contracts. So up to 2030 the money goes to the owners of working plants (Constellation, Talen), to the fuel bottleneck (Centrus) and to equipment manufacturers (BWXT), not to futuristic reactors — and much of it is already in the price.
nuc.thesis.stream.0.t: A single AI campus is now an energy facility
nuc.thesis.stream.1.t: A modern AI campus needs anything from a few hundred megawatts to several gigawatts. A 1 GW campus consumes about as much in a year as one large nuclear reactor produces. So building a data centre is now not only GPUs and networking but negotiation with generating companies, [[power|grid operators|not generation, but connection]], regulators and [[transformers|transformer|the steel inside it]] suppliers. And the key metric is no longer the price of electricity per MWh but time to power: how many years it will take actually to connect the site.
nuc.thesis.stream.10.t: A plant's revenue is simple: MWh produced × price. A 1 GW reactor at a 92% capacity factor delivers ~8.06 million MWh a year. At $60/MWh that is ~$484M of revenue, at $100/MWh ~$806M. The difference between $60 and $100 is more than $320M of additional annual revenue from a single gigawatt of continuous capacity. That is exactly why a long-term AI contract can radically revalue an already-built nuclear asset: the owner gets high utilisation, predictable revenue, less commodity risk and a higher residual value for the plant.

nuc.thesis.stream.12.t: Fast megawatts: licence extension, uprate, restart
nuc.thesis.stream.13.t: New reactors take a long time to build, so the relatively fast source of additional megawatts is the existing fleet, through three mechanisms. Licence extension: many units can run for 60–80 years after modernisation. An uprate is an upgrade that adds capacity (more efficient turbines, pumps, fuel): even +5% on a 1 GW reactor gives 50 MW — enough for a large AI site. Restarting closed units: the site, the interconnection and part of the staff already exist — cheaper than a new reactor, but with risk around equipment condition and licensing.

nuc.thesis.stream.15.t: Why new large reactors will not save the day before 2030
nuc.thesis.stream.16.t: Conventional nuclear's main problem is not reactor physics but project execution: complex engineering, a shortage of skilled staff, expensive financing, weak serial production, lengthy licensing. The US Department of Energy puts a first-of-a-kind advanced reactor at $6,000–10,000 per kW — that is $6–10B for a 1 GW unit, and that is the overnight cost, before interest over the years of construction, delays and interconnection. Serial construction theoretically cuts that by ~40%, but a successful series has to be built first. Time to start-up is 7–15 years. So before 2030 a new large reactor physically does not solve the problem.

nuc.thesis.stream.18.t: Fuel is a scarcer link than uranium itself
nuc.thesis.stream.19.t: Investors often look only at the uranium price, but the strategic shortage is not in the ore — it is in conversion and enrichment. Many new reactors require HALEU, more highly enriched uranium; the Western commercial HALEU chain is limited, and historically the expertise sat with Russia. That creates a circular problem: without reactors there is no demand for HALEU, and without guaranteed fuel the reactors cannot be financed. State contracts are the attempt to break it.
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: +465 TWh — the equivalent of ~53 GW of continuous generation
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: the same as one large reactor produces
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: data centres' share of world electricity by 2030
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: and the AI part of it will triple over that time
nuc.thesis.stream.20.t: The scale of the gap shows in the numbers. Even on a conservative estimate — counting only the reactors already planned — the US will need around 50 tonnes of HALEU a year by 2035, while only ~1 tonne is produced commercially today: a shortfall of almost 98%, meaning roughly 50 times more capacity is required. The most direct listed way to bet on this is Centrus Energy: effectively the only commercial HALEU producer in the US (it has already delivered ~900 kg to the Department of Energy), with a contract backlog of ~$2.3B and a $900M DoE contract; but even the expanded Piketon plant will only reach ~12 tonnes a year — so the gap is structural, not temporary. The second, early player is General Matter: a new entrant with DoE backing, but the company is private, so there is no direct access on the exchange.

nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.0.n: a ~98% shortfall; roughly 50× more capacity is needed
nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.1.l: Centrus's ceiling with an expanded Piketon

nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: the market does not finance enough capacity on its own
nuc.thesis.stream.22.t: Equipment and service: a bet that requires no guess about the reactor
nuc.thesis.stream.23.t: The best-protected position is not to guess which reactor design wins but to supply what any of them needs: reactor vessels, valves, pumps, steam generators, fuel, inspection and service. That kind of nuclear-grade manufacturing requires certification and years of experience — not just any factory can enter. The key listed player is BWX Technologies: Q2 2026 revenue of $901.6M, net income of $89.1M, a backlog of ~$8.4B (plus the defence naval business as a foundation). The diversified analogue in fuel is Cameco (uranium + the fuel cycle + a stake in Westinghouse).
nuc.thesis.stream.25.t: The hidden risk: co-location and the allocation of grid costs
nuc.thesis.stream.26.t: Many of the deals are co-location: the data centre is placed right next to the plant to bypass the interconnection queue. The upsides are fewer new lines, a short path and high reliability. But that is also the source of the main regulatory argument: should such a customer pay for the shared grid; what about the electricity that previously went to other consumers; will household tariffs rise; will a giant block others' access to the plant. The allocation of system costs is one of the key constraints on the «nuclear → data centre» model. So future deals will probably be hybrids: a PPA + grid supply + transmission charges + reserve + customer investment in infrastructure.
nuc.thesis.stream.27.t: Where it is heading — and where the money is going
nuc.thesis.stream.28.t: Capital is already going into acquiring and revaluing operating generators, long-term PPAs, life extension, uprates, restarts, uranium enrichment, nuclear manufacturing, [[transformers|transformers and substations|the steel inside it]] and transmission. Global nuclear spending is still far below spending on renewables and fossil fuels: to meet the stated targets, annual nuclear investment would have to rise from roughly $75B to $250B.
nuc.thesis.stream.29.t: Over a 5–10 year horizon come the first commercial small reactors, HALEU plants, TRISO fuel production, standardised nuclear components, the conversion of coal sites to nuclear, and private microgrids for AI campuses. Small reactors (Oklo, NuScale, X-energy, Kairos) are probably the next big cycle, but after 2030; today they are technological and financial optionality, not cash flow.
nuc.thesis.stream.3.t: The scarcity is not energy in general, but round-the-clock power in the right place
nuc.thesis.stream.30.note: State programmes + direct corporate investment. The LPO's >$300B is a lending limit, not money disbursed.
nuc.thesis.stream.31.t: What is already in the price
nuc.thesis.stream.32.t: The AI-energy thesis is no longer a secret — much of it is already in the quotes. So simply buying «all of nuclear» can deliver poor risk-adjusted returns even if the sector forecast is right. The right question is not «is the forecast correct» but «will earnings grow faster than the market already expects».

nuc.thesis.stream.36.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
nuc.thesis.stream.37.t: AI is not creating the nuclear industry from scratch — it is raising the value of round-the-clock capacity that already exists and giving the industry a new customer who can pay. Before 2030 the main benefit goes to the owners of operating plants and to suppliers of fuel, equipment and grid infrastructure. Small reactors are probably the next big cycle, but after 2030; today they are optionality, not guaranteed cash flow.
nuc.thesis.stream.38.t: The conclusion: the scarcest thing here is neither uranium nor fission technology, but a licensed, grid-connected and physically available gigawatt of round-the-clock capacity. Constellation and Talen are the most direct bets on that today; BWXT and Cameco are the picks and shovels that require no guess about the reactor; Centrus is the strategic fuel bottleneck (but expensive); small reactors (Oklo, NuScale) are a small optional position, not the core. And almost everywhere the thesis is already partly in the price.
nuc.thesis.stream.39.head.1: What to cover the theme with
nuc.thesis.stream.39.note: Not a recommendation — a match of instrument to style; the decision is the investor's.

nuc.thesis.stream.4.t: AI's problem is not producing more kilowatt-hours. The value lies in the ability to deliver a lot of energy, round the clock, at a specific point and within an acceptable timeframe. Nuclear fits that: the US nuclear fleet's capacity factor is above 90% (it runs almost without stopping), a single site delivers 1–2 GW on a small footprint, and fuel is a small share of the cost — which makes an already-built, partly depreciated reactor extremely valuable. Sun and wind are cheaper, but they do not provide guaranteed round-the-clock firm power without a multiple of surplus generation, batteries, gas backup and new lines.

AI has changed their owners' negotiating position: the hyperscalers are willing to sign 15–20 year contracts for guaranteed access to capacity. Below are the actual deals, not intentions.

Fabrinet (an agnostic assembler) and MACOM (components, a 58.5% margin) give the same theme more cheaply.
photonics.intro:
Optics is needed in an AI cluster because copper has physically stopped coping. At 200 Gbit/s per lane an electrical signal on a copper wire decays within tens of centimetres, while servers have to be connected across metres and hundreds of metres. So data inside the cluster is converted into light: it travels through glass fibre with almost no loss and no distance limit. The device that performs that conversion is an optical transceiver; a scale-out network uses about six of them per GPU.

How it works. The signal passes through a chain of physical conversions. First a laser emits a continuous beam of light — made not on silicon but on indium phosphide (InP), because silicon barely emits light at all. A modulator then switches that beam on and off in time with the data bits, up to 200 billion times a second; in an EML design the modulator is built into the laser itself. A silicon-photonic die then combines several light channels of different wavelengths into one fibre. At the far end a photodetector turns the light back into a weak electrical signal, and a separate chip (an optical DSP) cleans it up and reconstructs it. The newest architecture is co-packaged optics: the optics sits right against the switch chip, removing the long electrical path to a pluggable module and saving up to 70% of the transmission energy.

The narrowest and most expensive point is the laser and its yield. Silicon does not emit light by its own physics, so the light source has to be made on indium phosphide wafers — a temperamental material with low yield, and only a handful of fabs worldwide can produce it in volume. Demand for such lasers exceeds supply by roughly 30% (LightCounting), and a production 200 Gbit/s-per-lane laser is essentially available from one supplier today. It is the laser that sets how many transceivers can physically be built: without it the finished silicon photonics, optical DSP and assembly all sit idle. This cannot be relieved quickly — moving from 3-inch InP wafers to 6-inch (4x+ more devices at half the cost per device) takes years of process development, not quarters.

Who pays, and how much. The shortage is so critical that in March 2026 Nvidia invested $2B directly into each of two key laser suppliers ($4B in total) — into light production specifically, not assembly. For the buyers this makes sense: optics is only ~3–5% of a compute node's cost, but without it the expensive GPUs cannot exchange data and sit idle, so lasers are paid for with almost no haggling. The modules themselves get cheaper as volume ramps (800G ~$360–450, 1.6T ~$1,300–1,500), but the value settles in the laser and the optical DSP rather than in assembly, where margins are thin.

The AI optics market: $16.5B (2025) → ~$26B (2026, +60%, LightCounting); the laser shortage is forecast to ease by late 2026 or early 2027.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.
