photonics.moatBreakdown.components.1.not: Marvell ~60–70% + Broadcom >30% = >90% of high-end PAM4. A 3 nm tape-out at $500M+ is an entry barrier. But LPO (modules without a DSP, 40–50% less power) takes a bite out of demand at the low end.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.2.not: qualifying a transceiver at a hyperscaler takes months; customers certify at least 3 sources per speed grade. Patent royalties run up to ~8% of ASP. But module assembly itself is competitive, so switching is possible.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.3.not: vertical integration of silicon photonics (InnoLight at ~70% of high-speed on SiPh) and foundry capacity (TSMC's COUPE, mass production in 2026) raise the bar. CPO packaging is a new layer of complexity where value migrates to the lasers and the SiPh foundry.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.4.not: InnoLight supplies ~80% of the 1.6T modules for Nvidia's GB200; incumbency is sticky. Nvidia's $2B into Coherent and $2B into Lumentum lock in laser supply for both pluggable and CPO.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.5.not: the one obvious crack: assembly is commoditising. Chinese makers hold 7 of the top 10 places (63% of the market) at prices 20–25% below Western ones. China's share rose from 55.6% to 63.2% in a year. The «box» is getting cheaper — the value moves into the components.
photonics.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection rests not on the module but on what is inside it: EML/InP lasers and DSPs are physical and IP bottlenecks that China has not yet reproduced. Five of the six components are strong or strengthening; the weak link is assembly itself, and that is exactly what is being handed to China. The rule is simple: own the bottleneck (lasers, DSP), not the box.

photonics.problems.items.0.gap: Chinese module assemblers have grown explosively (InnoLight +192%, Eoptolink +187% of revenue), but the EML laser inside their modules is still Western or Japanese. Starting your own InP (indium phosphide) production at acceptable yield means years of process development and the capital for a fab; a qualified 200 Gbit/s laser cannot be replicated in a quarter or two. So the value settles in the laser rather than in assembly (assembly margins run ~8%, while Lumentum's laser margins are structurally higher and rising).
photonics.problems.items.0.problem: All of AI optics is constrained by one component — the EML laser on indium phosphide (InP, the material the light source inside every module is made from). Demand exceeds supply by roughly 30% (LightCounting), and at 200 Gbit/s per lane only Lumentum produces it in volume. Yield on InP wafers is low, and only a handful of fabs in the world can make them. Without the laser the rest of the module (silicon photonics, the DSP chip that reconstructs the signal, assembly) sits idle — it is the laser that sets how many modules can physically be built, and a scale-out network (linking servers) needs about 6 of them per GPU.
photonics.problems.items.0.solution: Moving from 3-inch InP (indium phosphide) wafers to 6-inch: a single wafer yields more than 4x the devices at half the cost per device. Coherent is building such a line in Sherman, Texas and in Zurich, and has tripled its InP output in a year with a plan to double again by end-2026. Lumentum is expanding EML laser capacity by more than 50% through its Japanese fab. LightCounting forecasts the shortage easing by late 2026 or early 2027. Beyond that, the co-packaged optics architecture (CPO — placing the light source right against the switch chip) removes part of the demand, but brings its own problem: yield and reliability in assembly (18 photonic dies in a single Quantum-X module).
photonics.problems.items.0.winners: Lumentum is the only supplier producing 200 Gbit/s per lane in volume, its Japanese fab is fully allocated, and its operating margin is rising toward 35–36%. Coherent is the only one with a full cycle (indium-phosphide lasers + silicon photonics + modules + CPO) and its own 6-inch InP lines. Both received $2B each from Nvidia in March 2026 — direct confirmation that the laser shortage is real and that the money is going straight to the scarcest link. They win because an indium-phosphide fab means decades of process development, not building a new hall.
photonics.problems.takeaway: Relieving the laser shortage strengthens the incumbent leaders: only Lumentum and Coherent have 6-inch indium-phosphide lines and a qualified 200 Gbit/s laser, and Nvidia's money goes straight to them. No newcomer appears here — the barrier is not assembly but the physics of producing indium phosphide.

photonics.thesis.bigIdea: The next constraint on AI is not computation but moving data between chips. At high speeds copper burns ever more energy and loses signal, while clusters grow toward a million accelerators — and when the network cannot keep up, expensive GPUs sit idle. Optics carries data as light rather than electricity: more data per pass, over greater distance, at lower energy. The thesis is not that «copper disappears» but that optics moves step by step closer to the chip itself — from pluggable modules to bonding beside the chip and on to optical I/O at the GPU. And since the AI build-out's scarcest resource is electricity (and it is the frontier of the US–China race), whoever makes the interconnect more energy-efficient wins. The core names are Broadcom, Marvell and Coherent; the riskier bets are packaging (TSMC) and optical I/O (Ayar Labs).
photonics.thesis.stream.0.t: AI's next constraint is not computation but interconnect
photonics.thesis.stream.1.t: In the boom's first phase, performance grew through GPU count and data-centre size. The next limit is different: thousands and tens of thousands of accelerators must work as one machine and constantly exchange weights, gradients and activations. When the interconnect cannot keep up, an expensive accelerator sits idle waiting for data — and that is not an abstraction: training GPT-4 across 25K accelerators saw real utilisation fall to 32–36%, and a 100K-GPU cluster running at 60% utilisation instead of 90% loses on the order of $300M a year (an H100 costs ~$3–4 an hour). The question shifts from «who has the fastest chip» to «who assembles the most efficient system as a whole».
photonics.thesis.stream.10.t: Optics is already widely deployed in data centres — but as pluggable modules on the front panel of a switch. A switch is the device that binds servers into one network and routes data between them; a pluggable module is a small insert that turns an electrical signal into light and back. That is how servers, racks and whole buildings are connected at 400 → 800G → 1.6T (the throughput of a single channel). Everyone uses these [[transceivers|modules|optical transceiver]] — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle, xAI, CoreWeave. But a plug-in module on a panel is not yet optics bonded to the chip itself. And here is what matters: optics is starting to move inward — into the tight accelerator-to-accelerator links that used to run on copper.
photonics.thesis.stream.11.items.1.n: 2.6x in a year; components are the constraint
photonics.thesis.stream.11.items.2.n: it became the main solution on cost and energy
photonics.thesis.stream.12.t: Where it is going — optics moves closer to the chip
photonics.thesis.stream.13.t: The transition is not one leap but a series of steps, and they all point the same way: optics moves ever closer to the chip itself. First the light is created in a pluggable module on the switch panel; then the module is simplified; then the optics moves onto the board beside it; then right up against the chip's package; then it is bonded directly to the switch chip (this is what CPO — «optics in one package with the chip» — means); the next step is optics right at the GPU; and eventually optical interconnect at the level of a whole rack and data centre. Each step removes part of the long copper path and cuts energy use.
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.0.1: pluggable modules dominate; 800G ramps and 1.6T goes on sale; copper still holds the short links
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.1.1: the first CPO in top-end switches (Nvidia, Broadcom); 51.2–102.4 Tbit/s switches strain the panel
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.2.1: the inflection: chip-bonded optics in top-end switches, optical accelerator links between racks, optics right at custom accelerators
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.3.1: optics beside the GPU; memory disaggregated over optics; optical chiplets
photonics.thesis.stream.16.t: The main argument is energy. Bonding optics to the chip (CPO) shortens the path: switch chip → a short link → an adjacent photonic engine → fibre. Nvidia claims 3.5x the energy efficiency and 4x fewer lasers on its Spectrum-X Photonics platform, and a fifth of the energy per 1.6T port compared with pluggable modules, plus several times the reliability. At the scale of hundreds of thousands and a million GPUs, powering pluggable modules becomes untenable — and that is where CPO has a clear economic argument.
photonics.thesis.stream.18.t: Why this is a strategic frontier — energy and the race with China
photonics.thesis.stream.19.t: The AI build-out's scarcest resource is [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]], and the interconnect takes a growing share of that budget. Whoever makes data transmission more energy-efficient fits more computation into the same megawatt — direct leverage in the US–China race, where energy is the constraint. The money confirms it: in just three months of 2026 Nvidia invested around $6.5B in photonics — $2B each into Coherent, Lumentum and Marvell (lasers and networking chips) and up to $3.2B into Corning (glass and fibre). The optical-I/O startup Ayar Labs drew competitors in together — Nvidia, AMD and MediaTek, in a $500M round. Strategics are entering optics before the winning standard is settled — a strong signal that everyone considers it strategically important.

photonics.thesis.stream.21.t: What it costs, what buyers will pay, and the order books
photonics.thesis.stream.22.t: The price of it. One 800G optical module costs roughly $900–1,300, and 1.6T about twice that; 2026 is being called «the year of 1.6T». Customers are willing to pay in advance: hyperscalers sign multi-year purchase agreements (Nvidia with Corning, up to $3.2B including purchases). Order books are already booked years out: Lumentum has more than $400M plus a separate several-hundred-million chip-bonded optics order for delivery in 2027; Coherent's orders run into 2028–2030 on a record book. So the demand is not a promise but contracted money.
photonics.thesis.stream.23.items.2.l: how far out Coherent's orders run
photonics.thesis.stream.24.t: Who is already using it, and what the leaders say
photonics.thesis.stream.25.t: CPO is no longer only a laboratory matter. Broadcom has assembled the Tomahawk 5-Bailly platform (a 51.2 Tbit/s switch with bonded optics) and calls it one of the first volume CPO deployments; its position is «the technology works, the question is the pace of adoption». Nvidia has built photonics into real platforms — Quantum-X (InfiniBand) and Spectrum-X (Ethernet) — meaning it treats CPO as part of the commercial roadmap rather than distant research. Marvell guides more cautiously — a meaningful inflection around 2028 — but has already shown 200 Gbit/s-per-lane optical engines and CPO for future switches. TSMC is building the COUPE packaging platform (photonic engine + SoIC + [[pkg|CoWoS|became the main event]]): its actions are a stronger signal than words.
photonics.thesis.stream.26.rows.0.1: switch + bonded optics (Tomahawk 5-Bailly); the first volume CPO · [[https://www.broadcom.com/company/news/product-releases|more]]
photonics.thesis.stream.26.rows.1.1: CPO in the Quantum-X and Spectrum-X platforms — as part of a complete AI system · [[https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/silicon-photonics/|more]]

photonics.thesis.stream.26.rows.3.1: the COUPE packaging platform — a photonic engine in an advanced package
photonics.thesis.stream.26.rows.4.1: lasers and components — needed under any standard · [[https://www.coherent.com/networking|more]]
photonics.thesis.stream.27.t: Who is betting on the future — optical I/O
photonics.thesis.stream.28.t: The most distant and most asymmetric link is optical I/O right at the compute chip. I/O is how a chip takes data in and sends it out; making it optical means converting data to light at the chip itself. Serious money has already arrived. Ayar Labs (the TeraPHY chiplet, mounted beside a GPU, CPU or [[asic|custom accelerator|earns on every chip]]) has raised $870M — $500M of it in 2026 at a $3.75B valuation — and is ramping volume production; its investors include Nvidia, AMD, Intel, GlobalFoundries, Applied Materials and MediaTek. Lightmatter (the Passage platform) has raised $850M at a $4.4B valuation, with Google and T. Rowe Price among its investors. And Celestial AI (optical links to memory) has already been bought by Marvell — for ~$3.25B, up to $5.5B on revenue milestones. Volume shipments are still small — these are bets on 2028–2030+ — but large capital and the buyers themselves are already in.
photonics.thesis.stream.3.t: Why copper is hitting its limit
photonics.thesis.stream.30.t: The most durable value is wherever it is needed under any standard. Lasers: every architecture needs light, so the laser makers (Coherent, Lumentum) are least dependent on who wins. Packaging is the main constraint: few can align optics and electronics to within fractions of a micron ([[pkg|TSMC, BESI, ASMPT|became the main event]]). Networking chips and SerDes (Broadcom, Marvell) benefit from co-designing the switch and the optics. [[test|Test|hardware and software]] gets more valuable, because one package now holds expensive electronics and optics together. And the modules themselves (Innolight, Eoptolink, Fabrinet) are the near-term beneficiaries — but they are precisely where CPO takes value away into integrated engines.
photonics.thesis.stream.31.t: With what confidence — a map of the bets
photonics.thesis.stream.32.rows.0.1: very high — a large, fast-growing market
photonics.thesis.stream.32.rows.2.0: Optics bonded to the switch chip
photonics.thesis.stream.32.rows.2.1: high — a clear argument on energy and density
photonics.thesis.stream.32.rows.3.1: medium-high — the hyperscalers redesign the whole system
photonics.thesis.stream.32.rows.4.1: medium — constrained by yield, lasers and standards
photonics.thesis.stream.34.t: Pluggable modules may get cheaper and better, delaying the move to CPO. Operators value serviceability: a failed module is swapped in a minute, while a failed photonic engine inside a package means an expensive repair of the whole switch. Then there is heat (optics is sensitive to warmth beside a hot chip), the yield of complex packages, vertical integration (Nvidia, Broadcom and the hyperscalers could take optics in house and squeeze the independents), module commoditisation against Chinese capacity, standards fragmentation, and high valuations — a correct thesis earns nothing if the price already embeds rapid adoption.

photonics.thesis.stream.36.rows.0.1: near-term demand confirmed (bullish for modules and lasers)

photonics.thesis.stream.38.t: The thesis is not that «copper disappears» but that interconnect becomes AI's constraint, and optics moves step by step closer to the computation — to the switch, to the accelerator, to memory. The optical content per system grows, and new pools of value appear: lasers, photonic engines, packaging, test, optical I/O. And since the frontier is energy, photonics is also strategic leverage in the US–China race; capital is already flowing there.
photonics.thesis.stream.39.t: There is no single «right» name here — there is an instrument to suit your style. Below is not an instruction to buy X through Y but a map: what to cover the theme with, depending on what you are willing to take on. One risk is common to all of them — that pluggable modules last longer and that Nvidia and the hyperscalers take optics in house.
photonics.thesis.stream.4.t: Copper does not stop working all at once — it just becomes harder and costlier to use. The industry is moving from 100 to 200 Gbit/s per electrical lane, and at those speeds attenuation, loss, crosstalk and heat all rise. Preserving the signal takes retimers, complex digital processing, thicker cables, shorter traces, more power and more cooling. In an ordinary switch the path is long: switch chip → a long board trace → a connector → a pluggable optical module → fibre. It is that electrical stretch that hits the limit.
photonics.thesis.stream.40.head.1: What to cover the theme with
photonics.thesis.stream.40.note: Not a recommendation but a match of instrument to style — the decision is the investor's.
photonics.thesis.stream.40.rows.0.0: Neutral — not guessing the winning standard
photonics.thesis.stream.40.rows.0.1: lasers and components: Coherent, Lumentum — light is needed under any architecture
photonics.thesis.stream.40.rows.1.1: networking chips: Broadcom, Marvell; Ethernet: Arista — they capture value whoever wins
photonics.thesis.stream.40.rows.2.0: A bet on packaging, neutral to the standard
photonics.thesis.stream.40.rows.2.1: TSMC — it fabricates and packages photonic engines for many customers
photonics.thesis.stream.40.rows.3.1: private optical I/O: Ayar Labs, Lightmatter — in small positions

photonics.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: each one adds power and heat
photonics.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: beyond that copper cannot carry it — only optics can
photonics.thesis.stream.6.label: ALTERNATIVES TO OPTICS
photonics.thesis.stream.6.t: Over short distances copper still holds: direct copper cables (up to ~2 m) and active copper cables are cheaper than optics. And «linear» optical modules — simplified and cheaper than the usual kind — delay the move to expensive chip-bonded optics. Those are optics' real competitors.
photonics.thesis.stream.8.t: Silicon photonics uses semiconductor manufacturing to build the parts that create, guide, modulate and capture light. Electrical data is turned into an optical signal: laser → modulator (encoding data into light) → waveguide → multiplexer (combining several wavelengths into one fibre) → fibre → photodetector → back to an electrical signal. Silicon itself emits light poorly, so the lasers are made from a different material (indium phosphide). A separate and hardest part is packaging: the photonic die, the electronic control chip, the laser and the fibres must be aligned to within fractions of a micron.
photonics.tldr.0: The AI/Ethernet optics market (Ethernet being the mass networking standard): $16.5B (2025) → $26B (2026, +60%). Shipments of modules at 800G and above (the number is speed, gigabits per second): 24M (2025) → 63M (2026, 2.6x). Three generations (800G/1.6T/3.2T) are ramping at the same time rather than in sequence.
photonics.tldr.1: The hyperscalers (the largest cloud companies) are integrating vertically: investing in module makers to lock in supply. That signals how strategically important optics is to AI clusters.
photonics.tldr.2: InnoLight is the world's no. 1 in optical modules (>23% share): ~80% of the 1.6T modules for Nvidia's GB200. Q1 2026 revenue +192% y/y. Chinese makers hold 7 of the top 10 places, but the EML lasers, the DSP (the chip that reconstructs the signal) and the TIA (the amplifier for the weak signal from the photodetector) inside their modules are almost all Western or Japanese.
photonics.tldr.3: Co-packaged optics (CPO — optics built right against the switch chip, removing the long electrical path to a pluggable module) is the next shift: Nvidia's Spectrum-X went into production (May 2026), and Broadcom has Davisson 102.4T. CPO cuts optics power consumption by ~70%, but the module leaders (Coherent, Lumentum) supply the lasers for CPO too. The main question: does the value stay in the module, or move into the chip package?
photonics.unitEconomics.costCurve: A 6-inch InP wafer yields >4x the devices at less than half the cost of a 3-inch one. SiPh: TSMC's COUPE lowers the cost of integration. LPO: 40–50% less power than DSP-based designs, so lower cost of ownership. CPO: 70% less optical power and 8x the silicon-area efficiency (Broadcom).
photonics.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Marvell DSP: ~58.9%. MACOM: ~58.5%. Eoptolink: ~47.8%. InnoLight: ~42.8%. Coherent: ~38–40%. Lumentum: expanding (+540 bps QoQ). The AI mix and 1.6T are accretive to margin.
photonics.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: An 800G module: ~$360–450. A 1.6T module: ~$1,300–1,500 (heading to ~$1,100). ~6 transceivers per GPU. Pluggable optics is >50% of a switch's cost and power. CPO: 70% less optical-interconnect power.
photonics.unitEconomics.takeaway: Margins are best in DSP (Marvell ~59%, MACOM ~59%) and lasers (Lumentum expanding). Module assembly is thinner, but InnoLight and Eoptolink hold 40–48% on SiPh integration. 1.6T is structurally accretive. CPO lowers the cost of optics, but the value migrates to lasers, SiPh and switch silicon.
photonics.update.bottomLine: AI optics is one of the fastest-growing subsegments (Ethernet +60%, 800G+ 2.6x). The EML bottleneck is confirmed by Nvidia's $4B. CPO is shipping but additive — the laser companies win in either scenario. Enter on drawdowns (as on 2 July): the fundamentals are at records, but 100x+ P/E means zero margin of safety.

photonics.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: CPO lasers and silicon-photonics packaging: as CPO scales (2028+), value migrates to the suppliers of external laser sources (Lumentum, Coherent), the SiPh foundry (TSMC COUPE), and switch silicon (Broadcom, Nvidia).
photonics.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: EML/InP lasers: demand exceeds supply by ~30% (LightCounting). Lumentum is the only supplier of 200G/lane EML in volume. Coherent: the InP imbalance persists into 2026–2027. Nvidia's $4B is direct confirmation.

photonics.verdict.bear.0: Co-packaged optics (CPO — optics built directly into the switch chip's package): Nvidia's Spectrum-X is in production and Broadcom has Davisson 102.4T; pluggable optics is >50% of a switch's cost and power consumption — and that is exactly the value CPO redistributes into the networking chip's silicon and into packaging at TSMC.
photonics.verdict.bear.1: Chinese commoditisation (turning it into a cheap mass-market product): 7 of the 10 largest makers are Chinese, at prices 20–25% below Western ones. InnoLight: the top-5 customers are 76% of sales and 90% is exported — fragile under export controls.
photonics.verdict.bear.2: Valuations: Coherent at a P/E of ~110–158x, Lumentum ~114–156x. On 2 July 2026: AOI −17%, Coherent/Lumentum −10% in a day. Linear optics (LPO — transmitting light without a DSP chip) threatens the DSP chip market.
photonics.verdict.bull.0: ~6 light converters per GPU in a scale-out network (linking servers and racks); the count per GPU rises with each generation (800G ~$400 → 1.6T ~$1,400). Three generations are ramping simultaneously — without the usual pause to clear inventory.
photonics.verdict.bull.1: An EML/InP laser shortage (indium-phosphide lasers, the light source in every module): demand exceeds supply by ~30%; Nvidia invested $4B in Coherent and Lumentum — direct confirmation of the shortage. The laser companies have the ability to set the price.
photonics.verdict.bull.2: Shipments of 800G+ modules: 24M → 63M (2026, 2.6x). The largest cloud companies' capex is ~$750B (2026, +67% y/y). Optics is ~$0.15–0.20 for every $1 of GPU compute.
photonics.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — the speed ramp from 800G → 1.6T → 3.2T and the shift to in-package optics (CPO).
photonics.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the value stay in the pluggable module (InnoLight, Coherent) — or move into co-packaged optics inside the switch or GPU?
photonics.verdict.sizing: AI optical modules: $16.5B (2025) → $26B (2026). DSP chipsets: ~$3.5B (2024) → >$11B by 2030. CPO: $46M (2024) → $8.1B by 2030 (Yole, a 137% CAGR). The total transceiver market: ~$24B (2025).
photonics.verdict.summary: One of the fastest-growing subsegments in semiconductors: AI optics +60% in 2026, Lumentum +90%, InnoLight +192%. Deep competitive advantages in EML/InP lasers (indium-phosphide lasers, which generate the light signal itself) and in the DSP duopoly (the chip that cleans up and reconstructs the signal on receive). But co-packaged optics (CPO — optics built into the switch chip's package) threatens pluggable modules after 2028, Chinese assembly dominates (63% of the market), and valuations are sky-high (Coherent/Lumentum at 100–158x forward earnings). The answer: own the scarcest link (lasers, DSP chip IP), not the box (module assembly).
photonics.whatIsIt: A small device that turns data into short flashes of light and sends them down a thin glass strand from one server to another. Copper wire cannot carry the signal at these speeds — it decays within tens of centimetres, while servers in an AI cluster have to be connected across metres and hundreds of metres, so data inside the cluster travels as light. Each compute chip needs about six of these light converters: without them the expensive chips cannot exchange data and sit idle.

pkg.intro:
Advanced packaging is the final assembly of an AI accelerator from several separate dies into one package. Processors used to be made as a single piece of silicon that got cheaper with every generation. That no longer works: transistors have all but stopped getting cheaper, and a lithography tool prints a rectangle of limited area in one pass (~858 mm²) — a large AI processor no longer fits inside it. So it is cut into several smaller dies and assembled together with HBM memory stacks on a shared base. Without this assembly a modern accelerator physically does not exist.

How it works. Compute dies and memory stacks are produced separately at leading-edge fabs, and then have to be joined to each other over a very short distance and at very high connection density. To do that they are mounted not directly on a board but on an intermediate silicon interposer. It carries tens of thousands of ultra-fine wires — denser than an ordinary board allows — and it is those wires that connect processor to memory at the required speed. The sequence runs: (1) the dies are mounted on the interposer, aligned to within microns and bonded across thousands of contacts at once; (2) the assembled block is seated on an organic package substrate; (3) the whole thing is encapsulated in a protective compound, ground flat and tested. Once encapsulated, a package cannot be taken apart.

Why this comes down to yield and capacity. What matters here is not the ability to assemble but the share of packages assembled without defects. The larger the interposer, the more it warps when heated and the more often contacts break: a large monolithic silicon interposer yields around 60% against ~90% for the version using local silicon bridges — which is why the industry is moving to bridges. The cost of a single error is high: if a package is scrapped, neither the processor nor the memory can be recovered from it — ~$4,000–4,600 of components are lost, and in the worst case the full chip value ($5,700–7,300). So the winner is whoever assembles most cleanly at maximum volume. The second constraint is capacity itself: there is essentially one assembly line for the whole leading-edge AI class, the queue for it runs from one to three years (52–156 weeks), and building a new line takes about 18 months.

Who pays, and how much. Demand has nearly tripled in two years: from 370K wafers (2024) to ~1M (2026). The price of assembling one wafer has reached ~$10K — as much as the leading-edge processor silicon itself costs — and was raised several times by 10–20% across 2025–2026. Customers pay in advance to stake out volume: in summer 2026 one of them put $1.5B of prepayments with a contractor against future deliveries. The holder of the key technology directs 10–20% of all its capex to packaging and related work — on a total 2026 budget of $60–64B, that is roughly $6–13B a year. They pay with almost no haggling: without this assembly a finished chip cannot be produced, and its share of the chip's cost (~15%) is in any case smaller than the cost of missing the delivery entirely.

Market structure. The high-end AI packaging segment grows about 23% a year and reaches ~$28B by 2030 (Yole estimate). Concentration is extreme: essentially the whole AI class is assembled by one player (TSMC, the CoWoS technology), with the simpler final part of the work handed to a few neutral contractors.

pkg.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Besi and ASMPT between them hold about half the bonding-machine market; Besi works alongside Applied Materials at TSMC. The larger the package, the more precision matters — this layer strengthens with every generation.
pkg.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the main crack: an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build (it used to be 3–5), Intel and Samsung are entering as alternatives, and the shortfall has already halved. pkg.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is real at TSMC (leadership on scrap and on the whole chain) and at the equipment and materials makers (Besi, Disco, Ajinomoto), but weak at the independent assembly houses, where the work is closer to contract labour. Unlike memory, supply here is relieved fast and paid for by the customers themselves — a less impregnable monopoly.

The re-rated assembly houses (ASE ~56x, Amkor ~37x) are a monopoly price for contract work and a crowded bet on a finite shortage; they fall hardest in a cycle.
pkg.problems.items.0.gap: Second suppliers are real but arrive slowly: Amkor's $7B Arizona plant yields output only from early 2028 and meaningful revenue from 2029; TSMC's US plant is also 2029. To hand assembly to a new contractor, the chip must be re-qualified — several quarters, plus the queue itself. TSMC's 12–24 month lead across the whole chain makes the core — large AI packages — nearly impossible to capture.
pkg.problems.items.0.problem: All AI-accelerator assembly comes down to one technology — TSMC's advanced CoWoS packaging (processor and memory assembled on a shared silicon substrate): without it an Nvidia accelerator physically cannot be built. TSMC holds nearly 100% of AI-class assembly, the queue runs from 52 to 156 weeks (up to three years), the price has reached ~$10K a wafer, and the shortfall in 2025 was ~20%. Demand has nearly tripled: 370K wafers (2024) → ~1M (2026). The most delicate point inside it is the large silicon interposer (an intermediate wafer carrying thousands of connections between chips): the bigger the package, the more it warps and the more scrap it produces — which is why Nvidia had to cancel the largest version of a future chip.
pkg.problems.items.0.solution: TSMC is expanding its 11 packaging plants in Taiwan: output rises from roughly 75K to 120–140K wafers a month across 2026. The key advantage over memory is that an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build rather than 2–3 years, so the shortage clears faster. The large-interposer problem is routed around with the CoWoS-L variant: instead of one monolithic silicon wafer, local silicon bridges are used (small silicon inserts only where dense connection is needed). Customers fund second suppliers with prepayments — Nvidia put $1.5B with Amkor against future volume. The assembly equipment itself is made by Besi and ASMPT (thermocompression and hybrid die bonding — joining chips under pressure and heat), the grinding and dicing by Disco, the encapsulation by Towa.
pkg.problems.items.0.winners: TSMC (NYSE: TSM) — holds nearly the whole AI class and is 12–24 months ahead of competitors across the chain of assembly + substrate + 3D bonding. But the main margin sits not in the assembly itself but in the equipment: Besi (AMS: BESI) at a 62% gross margin, and ASMPT (HKG: 522), where every bonding tool is a barrier of its own. The independent contractors Amkor and ASE take only the overflow that TSMC deliberately hands to «neutral» players, and earn just 14–26% gross on it — their work is closer to contract labour.
pkg.problems.takeaway: Relieving this shortage strengthens the incumbent leader — TSMC and the equipment makers (Besi, ASMPT) — not the independent assembly houses. But unlike memory, diversification has already begun and is paid for by the customer itself (Nvidia's prepayment), so this is a barrier that gradually weakens rather than one that holds forever.
pkg.risks.0.note: The main risk of the theme. Amkor +336% in a year, Ibiden ~+500%, AT&S ~+1140%, Besi on a forward P/E of ~55. The easy money is made; any disappointment brings a sharp fall.
pkg.risks.1.note: Nvidia is ~60% of demand, TSMC is nearly all of production. A double dependence: on one buyer and on one supplier.
pkg.risks.2.note: Nearly all AI-class assembly is physically in Taiwan. A stoppage would collapse accelerator output worldwide. Alternatives arrive slowly: Amkor in the US in 2028, TSMC in 2029.
pkg.risks.3.note: TSMC's expansion plus overflow to the contractors plus Intel and Samsung could level the market. The first sign is already there: output growth slows to ~26% a year.
pkg.risks.4.note: Calmer than memory, but the shares are high-beta: Amkor lost 34% in the 2025 tariff shock and 30% in a single month. The semiconductor index has fallen 30%+ in every cycle for 30 years.
pkg.risks.5.note: Failing to master the shift to panels, glass or still larger packages. The limit has already shown itself: Nvidia had to cancel the largest version of its chip.
pkg.risks.6.note: Practically ruled out: it takes enormous investment, years of learning through scrap, and scale. Customers prefer to pay in advance (Nvidia's $1.5B prepayment) rather than build their own.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: This is not a threat to packaging as a whole but a change of suppliers: the losers are the makers of today's substrates — Ibiden (TYO: 4062), Unimicron (TPE: 3037), AT&S (VIE: ATS) — which are precisely the names that rose most. An important risk if you hold them.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: At large package sizes the familiar organic substrate starts to warp and no longer holds its geometry. Glass is stiffer and flatter. Closest to volume is Absolics (an SKC division) with its Georgia plant, followed by Samsung (after 2027) and LG (2028); the glass itself comes from Corning, AGC and SCHOTT.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.0.tech: Glass bases instead of ordinary substrates
pkg.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: The main technology risk in this link. It undercuts the «bigger package = more revenue» growth plan, but at the same time raises the value of those who can solve the precision problem — Besi's and ASMPT's equipment, and glass bases.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: The larger the package, the more it warps under heat and the more scrap it produces. That is exactly why, according to one industry source, Nvidia cancelled the largest version of a future chip (4 dies) and replaced it with one half the size. This is the first case of packaging constraining chip architecture.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: Does not affect the decision. Cutting a chip into pieces is not the problem — it is precisely the industry's answer to the size limit.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: An alternative approach: rather than cutting the chip into pieces, make one enormous one. It works at individual companies but stays a niche — the volumes are not comparable to ordinary assembly and are unlikely to become so.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.3.angle: More of a plus: it makes assembly harder and raises its price, which increases this link's revenue. The same TSMC and its contractors win.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.3.detail: The light source is placed inside the package, next to the processor, so data leaves «straight from the chip» as light. TSMC begins volume production in 2026, and Amkor already has three such projects.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.3.verdict: a new market, not a threat
pkg.roadmap.generations.0.note: The Nvidia H100 and Google chip generation. Cheaper, but already at its size limit.
pkg.roadmap.generations.1.note: The current generation (Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin, AMD's MI400). It costs 3–4x the basic version — the main revenue driver of this link.
pkg.roadmap.generations.2.note: A bigger package still, and more memory. The larger the package, the more the precision-bonding equipment matters — Besi and ASMPT win.
pkg.roadmap.generations.3.note: This is where package warping physics starts: the technology risk is real (see the cancellation of the largest Rubin version).
pkg.roadmap.generations.4.gen: Panel assembly instead of a round wafer
pkg.roadmap.generations.4.note: On a round wafer the edges go to waste; a rectangular panel uses the area more fully. It reshuffles the balance of power in equipment.
pkg.roadmap.takeaway: The technology sells itself: each package generation costs 3–4x the last, so revenue grows even without more chips. But two warnings: the physical package-size limit has already shown itself, and the shift to glass bases could wipe out the advantage of today's substrate makers.
pkg.scenarios.cases.0.name: Bear
pkg.scenarios.cases.0.note: oversupply by 2027–2028: the shortfall drops below 5%, the queue shortens, Nvidia trims orders. Historically assembly houses fell 30–50% in a cycle, and the multiple halves from ~50x
pkg.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
pkg.scenarios.cases.1.note: the shortage holds through 2027 and melts gradually, package content grows (5.5 → 9.5 fields), TSMC holds its share. Revenue growth is eaten by the de-rating of high multiples
pkg.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
pkg.scenarios.cases.2.note: the shortage holds longer, packages grow to 14 fields, in-package optics and panels raise the assembly price; equipment (Besi, ASMPT) accelerates on orders
pkg.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~+5…+8%/yr (probability-weighted) — but with a wide spread and worse asymmetry than in less-played links
pkg.scenarios.takeaway: The upside is capped by the fact that the shares are already up 5–12x, while the downside from the re-rating is large — the asymmetry is skewed downward. The only way to soften it is name selection: TSMC and equipment (Besi, Disco, Towa) plus the laggards (Onto, Powertech) instead of the re-rated assembly houses.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: 11 packaging plants in Taiwan; output rises from roughly 75K to 120–140K wafers a month across 2026. A US plant only by 2029.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: A $7B Arizona campus: construction to mid-2027, output from early 2028, meaningful revenue from 2029. Funded in part by Nvidia's prepayment.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: Expanding in Taiwan and Malaysia, ~$6B invested over a year.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.3.detail: Building their own assembly as an alternative to TSMC: Intel expects first orders in H2 2026, and Samsung's plant is already fully loaded.
pkg.supply.crowdingOut: The first sign of a slowdown is already there: TSMC's assembly output growth slows to ~26% year on year in 2026, where volumes used to double.
pkg.supply.leadTime: The key difference from memory: an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build — it used to be 3–5 years. An ordinary chip fab takes 2–3 years. So an assembly shortage is far easier and faster to relieve than a memory shortage.
pkg.supply.takeaway: The shortage holds through 2027, but it is melting: the gap has already halved. This is not a «shortage forever» story the way memory is. The exit signal is the queue falling below 40 weeks or the shortfall dropping below 5%.
pkg.supply.utilization: The plants are running flat out: ~90% at the independent contractors, and TSMC's AI-class assembly is effectively at 100%, all of it booked.
pkg.thesis.bigIdea: Advanced packaging (CoWoS) is the real physical constraint on the whole AI build-out: without it no accelerator can be assembled, TSMC holds nearly 100%, and the queue is booked three years out. But the market overdid it: independent assembly houses are up 5–12x and trade at 50–70x earnings — as if the shortage were permanent. It is not; it clears faster than memory, and packaging's share of chip cost is actually falling (from 19% to 15%). The constraint is real — but it should be bought through whoever keeps the margin (TSMC and Besi's equipment), not through re-rated assembly contractors.
pkg.thesis.stream.1.t: You can design a chip (in [[eda|chip software|impossible to route around]]), print it on [[litho|ASML's machines|impossible to replicate]] and build [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory stacks beside it — and still not ship an accelerator. Because the last step — joining the compute die and the memory stacks on one substrate so data can fly between them — is exactly what became the constraint on the whole AI build-out. Demand for that assembly has nearly tripled in two years, and TSMC's queue for it is booked three years ahead.
pkg.thesis.stream.10.t: Who holds the market — and who gets TSMC's overflow
pkg.thesis.stream.11.t: TSMC does ~100% of AI-class assembly. Of Nvidia's ~595K wafers for 2026, TSMC assembles ~510K itself and deliberately passes the overflow to «neutral» contractors (Amkor, SPIL) — specifically so the orders do not go to its rival Samsung. Amkor is building a $7B plant in Arizona (output from 2028; Nvidia put down $1.5B of prepayments in July 2026). ASE/SPIL take 40–50% of the overflow on basic assembly.
pkg.thesis.stream.12.items.0.label: TSMC — nearly the entire AI class
pkg.thesis.stream.12.items.1.label: Amkor — overflow from TSMC
pkg.thesis.stream.12.items.1.note: the second source is real, but revenue only from 2029
pkg.thesis.stream.12.items.2.label: ASE / SPIL — basic overflow
pkg.thesis.stream.12.items.2.note: 40–50% of the overflow on basic assembly
pkg.thesis.stream.13.t: The customer pool is the most concentrated in the entire chain: Nvidia is ~60% of AI-class assembly demand, Broadcom (chips for Google/Meta/OpenAI — see [[asic|custom AI chips|earns on every chip]]) ~15%, AMD ~11%, Amazon ~5%. The top three are more than 85%.
pkg.thesis.stream.15.t: And here is what is interesting: the constraint is real, but the margin does not sit where the market is looking. Independent assembly houses (ASE, Amkor) run on gross margins of just 14–26% — their work is closer to contract labour. The real margin sits with the equipment maker Besi (62% gross) and with TSMC itself (66–68%).
pkg.thesis.stream.16.items.0.label: Nvidia — the accelerator itself
pkg.thesis.stream.16.items.1.label: TSMC — assembly done in house
pkg.thesis.stream.16.items.2.label: Besi — assembly equipment
pkg.thesis.stream.16.items.3.label: ASE — independent assembler
pkg.thesis.stream.16.items.4.label: Amkor — independent assembler
pkg.thesis.stream.16.items.4.note: closer to contract work than to a monopoly
pkg.thesis.stream.17.t: Assembly does not need ultra-expensive [[litho|lithography tools|impossible to replicate]], so equipment depreciation is lower, and Besi holds a near-software margin however the shares split. The independent houses only do the final mounting and test.
pkg.thesis.stream.18.t: What the market thinks: «the shortage is forever»
pkg.thesis.stream.19.t: The market saw a shortage and bought it as permanent pricing power. Assembly houses and materials makers are up 5–12x in a year (Amkor +336%, Ibiden ~+500%, AT&S ~+1140%) and now trade at 50–70x earnings (Besi ~55x, ASE ~56x, Ibiden ~70x). The bet is simple: constraint = forever.
pkg.thesis.stream.2.items.1.l: of the AI class is done by TSMC
pkg.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: 12–24 months ahead of competitors, 11 packaging plants
pkg.thesis.stream.20.items.0.l: share price gain over a year
pkg.thesis.stream.20.items.1.n: as if the shortage were permanent
pkg.thesis.stream.20.items.2.n: Nvidia booked more than half of the expansion
pkg.thesis.stream.22.t: Three things the euphoria misses. First: the shortage is finite and clears faster than memory. TSMC is doubling assembly capacity, Amkor and Intel add a second source from 2028, and new methods (silicon bridges, panel-level assembly) take part of the load off. Historically assembly houses fell 30–50% in a cycle.
pkg.thesis.stream.23.t: Second, and this is the main point: packaging's share of an AI chip's cost is not rising but falling — from 19% two years ago to 15% today, because [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory rose in price several times faster. The constraint is here, but the money accumulates in memory. You pay a scarcity premium on a shrinking share.
pkg.thesis.stream.24.t: Third, the margin structure: what rose most was precisely the assembly houses, and that is a low-margin contract layer (14–26%), not a monopoly. Buying ASE at 56x earnings is paying a monopoly price for contract work.
pkg.thesis.stream.25.t: The constraint is real — but the easy money is made. Our difference with the market is not about demand, but about the fact that the price already treats the shortage as permanent when it is finite.
pkg.thesis.stream.26.t: What is priced in — and how to buy this properly
pkg.thesis.stream.27.t: The verdict breaks down by layer. The assembly houses (ASE ~56x, Amkor ~37x) are priced for a permanent shortage that is finite — expensive. TSMC (66–68% margin, a genuine monopoly) and equipment (Besi, 62% margin, earning however the shares split) are the fair way to own the same constraint.
pkg.thesis.stream.28.items.0.n: a monopoly price for a 14–26% contract margin
pkg.thesis.stream.28.items.1.n: the best layer on margin, but the price already reflects it in full
pkg.thesis.stream.28.items.2.l: TSMC — at the whole company's multiple
pkg.thesis.stream.28.items.2.n: the best-protected way in, though a diluted one
pkg.thesis.stream.29.t: Put simply: own the constraint through the layer where the margin stays (TSMC and equipment), not through re-rated assembly houses priced as a permanent monopoly.
pkg.thesis.stream.3.t: What «packaging» is and why it became the main event
pkg.thesis.stream.30.t: Where the technology is going — and where the money is going
pkg.thesis.stream.31.t: Technically, packaging moves up a clear ladder, and every step reshuffles the winners. Today it is 2.5D assembly (chip and memory on a shared interposer). When a large monolithic interposer hits physics, the industry moves to silicon bridges, then to panel-level assembly (rectangular panels instead of round wafers — more area and cheaper per package) and glass substrates (flatter and larger, for giant packages). The end goal is 3D assembly (logic mounted directly on logic through direct bonding, with no solder). The larger and denser the package, the more it matters who mastered the next step first.
pkg.thesis.stream.32.t: Where the money is going: TSMC is doubling assembly capacity (~70K → ~140K wafers a month) and building several new packaging plants. Amkor is putting $7B into an Arizona plant, and Nvidia has placed $1.5B of prepayments there to stake out future volume. Intel is investing in its own packaging as a way back into the game — it talks of deals worth «billions a year». The equipment makers (Besi, ASMPT) are investing in direct bonding (hybrid bonding), the next big transition. And the hyperscalers pay up front to guarantee themselves a place in the queue.
pkg.thesis.stream.33.items.0.l: assembly wafers a month at TSMC
pkg.thesis.stream.33.items.1.n: a second source; meaningful output from 2028–2029
pkg.thesis.stream.33.items.2.n: content grows — revenue on the same number of chips
pkg.thesis.stream.34.t: What the key players are betting on: TSMC — on being first to master every next step (silicon bridges, 3D assembly) and staying a monopoly. Nvidia — on staking out capacity with prepayments while spreading orders across a second and third source (Amkor, Intel, Samsung) so as not to depend on one supplier. Intel and Samsung — on packaging as the route back to the top tier: you can compete here even while behind on transistors. The equipment makers — on direct bonding, which 3D assembly requires. The next battlefield is not the substrate itself but direct bonding and glass bases.
pkg.thesis.stream.35.t: The market's attention and its capital are converging here: packaging has gone from a boring finale to the place that decides how many AI chips exist at all. But the winner is not whoever's share price rose loudest — it is whoever masters the next step first and holds the margin, and that list can change at every transition.
pkg.thesis.stream.36.t: What would break the thesis — or confirm it
pkg.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.0: Nvidia trims orders, the queue shortens
pkg.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.1: Oversupply in 2027–28 — assembly houses fall 30–50%, the multiple halves from ~50x
pkg.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.1: TSMC's pricing power erodes — the end of the «permanent» shortage
pkg.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.0: The shortage holds and package size grows (5.5 → 9.5 fields)
pkg.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.1: The bull case — the assemblers justify their high multiple
pkg.thesis.stream.38.t: For now 2026 is 100% sold out, but what to track is the capacity relief and the second source, not the shortage headlines.
pkg.thesis.stream.39.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
pkg.thesis.stream.4.t: Packaging used to be the boring last step — «put the chip in a case». It is now the hardest stage. A modern accelerator is not one chip but a compute die plus 6–8 [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory stacks, which must sit millimetres apart on a shared silicon interposer (a tiny «board» cut from silicon) so data moves between them instantly. That assembly is what CoWoS means. Without it the fastest GPU and its memory simply cannot be joined, and with each generation the package gets larger and more complex.
pkg.thesis.stream.40.t: Advanced packaging is a real physical toll gate on the AI chip: without it no accelerator can be assembled, TSMC holds nearly all of it, and the queue is booked three years out. But the market has already priced that shortage as permanent — and it is finite, clears faster than memory, and packaging's share of chip cost is actually falling (19% → 15%). And what rose loudest was precisely the low-margin contract layer, not the monopoly itself.
pkg.thesis.stream.41.t: The conclusion: own the constraint through the layer where the margin stays — TSMC (a monopoly plus a fab) and the equipment makers (Besi, ASMPT), who earn however the shares split. The re-rated assembly houses (ASE, Amkor at ~50x for a 14–26% contract margin) are a crowded bet on a finite shortage, and they fall hardest in a cycle.
pkg.thesis.stream.5.items.0.n: as much as leading-edge silicon costs — packaging has caught logic on price
pkg.thesis.stream.5.items.2.l: of an AI chip's cost is packaging
pkg.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: physically critical, but a small share of the money
pkg.thesis.stream.6.t: Why it all comes down to scrap
pkg.thesis.stream.7.t: The whole economics of this link is about yield. A large monolithic interposer is hard to make without defects: ~60% yield against ~90% for the version using silicon bridges (small silicon links embedded in the substrate instead of one large monolithic wafer) — which is why the industry moved to silicon bridges at larger sizes. And the cost of one error is enormous: if a package is scrapped, neither the processor nor the memory can be recovered — $4,000–4,600 of components are lost, and in the worst case the whole chip ($5,700–7,300).
pkg.thesis.stream.8.items.0.n: the spread is enormous — and it is what decides the profit
pkg.thesis.stream.8.items.1.n: which is why the industry moved to embedded bridges
pkg.thesis.stream.8.items.2.l: lost on a single scrapped package
pkg.thesis.stream.8.items.2.n: neither the die nor the memory can be saved
pkg.thesis.stream.9.t: Whoever assembles most cleanly takes the profit — and that is TSMC: 12–24 months ahead, 11 packaging plants and the whole chain tuned. The next constraint will be physics itself: at very large package sizes the package starts to warp and scrap rises — according to an industry source, that is precisely why Nvidia cancelled the largest version of a future chip.
pkg.tldr.0: Advanced packaging (the final assembly of chip and memory into one package) is the real binding constraint on AI-chip output, and TSMC controls it (nearly 100% of AI-class assembly, a 52–156 week queue, ~$10K per wafer).
pkg.tldr.1: But here is the paradox: packaging's share of an AI chip's cost is shrinking (19% → 15%) while memory takes the money for itself (52% → 63%). The constraint is here and the profit goes there.
pkg.tldr.2: The theme is already heavily played: Amkor +336% in a year, Ibiden ~+500%, AT&S ~+1140%, Besi on a forward P/E of ~55. The best return-for-risk is equipment and materials (Besi, ASMPT, Disco, Towa) plus TSMC itself, not the re-rated assembly houses.
pkg.unitEconomics.costCurve: TSMC is the cheapest producer at volume: lower depreciation, better defect-free yield, and the whole chain tuned. For the independent contractors only the simpler part of the work pays — final mounting and test.
pkg.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Inside TSMC, packaging still earns less than the company average (66%), but it has a path upward: assembly does not need ultra-expensive lithography tools, so equipment depreciation is lower. At the independent contractors gross margin is only 14–26%.
pkg.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: Assembling one wafer costs ~$10K. It yields 25–28 finished interposers. Per chip that works out at ~$750 for the basic version of the assembly and ~$1,000–1,100 for the advanced one (nearly 50% more). In total, packaging is 10–15% of an AI chip's cost.
pkg.unitEconomics.takeaway: The economics of this link is about scrap: when an error costs thousands of dollars, the winner is whoever assembles most cleanly, and that is TSMC. The contractors have meaningful operating leverage too: ASE's profit grew 90% in a year on just 30% revenue growth — at full utilisation they earn disproportionately.
pkg.unitEconomics.yields.0.label: Advanced assembly (large packages)
pkg.unitEconomics.yields.0.value: 65–95% defect-free on Epoch AI's estimate — an enormous spread, and it is what decides the profit.
pkg.unitEconomics.yields.1.label: The large monolithic interposer
pkg.unitEconomics.yields.1.value: ~60% against ~90% for the version using embedded bridges. Which is why the industry moved to bridges at larger sizes.
pkg.unitEconomics.yields.2.label: The cost of a single error
pkg.unitEconomics.yields.2.value: If a package is scrapped, neither the processor nor the memory can be recovered from it: ~$4,000–4,600 of components are lost, and in the worst case the full chip value ($5,700–7,300).
pkg.universe.0.exposure: packaging is ~8–10% of revenue, but it is the constraint on the whole industry
pkg.universe.0.note: The highest-quality name: nearly 100% of AI-class assembly. The drawback is that packaging is only a tenth of the business, so the exposure is diluted.
pkg.universe.1.note: The best layer on margin, and it earns however the shares split. But the price is already high: +164% in a year.
pkg.universe.10.note: Up roughly 6x. A double risk: a high price plus the industry's possible shift to glass bases.
pkg.universe.11.exposure: package substrates, the only one in Europe
pkg.universe.11.note: Up roughly 12x while loss-making — the most speculative position in the link.
pkg.universe.12.note: Cheaper than the «pure» names, and works with TSMC on bonding. But packaging is dissolved in a vast business.
pkg.universe.2.note: The number two in bonding equipment, taking share from its Korean rivals on precision.
pkg.universe.3.note: Effectively a monopoly in high-precision dicing — an irreplaceable link whatever the assembly technology.
pkg.universe.4.note: The cleanest bet on package encapsulation; a narrow set of suppliers.
pkg.universe.5.note: Nvidia's second supplier, with a $1.5B prepayment. But +336% in a year: almost all of it is priced in, and the Arizona plant will lower the margin at first.
pkg.universe.6.exposure: assembly and test are 63% of revenue
pkg.universe.6.note: The largest independent assembler, profit +90% in a year. But +150% year to date — expensive.
pkg.universe.7.note: The cheapest valuation in the link — the option for getting in at a sensible price.
pkg.universe.8.note: Badly left behind: −39% in a year, even though demand for inspection rises with complexity. The best «laggard» option.
pkg.universe.9.note: A pure bet on quality inspection, valued more soberly than most names in the link.
pkg.update.bottomLine: The bottom line: the constraint is genuine and prices are still rising, but this is not «shortage forever» — an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build, the shortfall has already halved, and Nvidia is paying for a second supplier itself. Meanwhile the link's shares are up 4–12x in a year. So the sensible bet here is not «buy the shortage» but buy the equipment and materials layer (Besi, ASMPT, Disco, Towa) plus TSMC — they earn regardless of who wins the fight for orders.
pkg.update.headline: The constraint is real — but it is clearing, and the shares have already played it
pkg.update.stories.0.detail: On 23 July 2026 Amkor announced a multi-year advanced-packaging agreement with Nvidia carrying $1.5B of prepayments against capacity expansion; Amkor's shares jumped about 17%. The meaning is twofold: Nvidia is directly paying for a second supplier to exist outside TSMC — so TSMC's monopoly is not permanent. Earlier, in June 2026, Amkor and TSMC signed a 10-year agreement to transfer TSMC's technology to the Arizona plant — TSMC deliberately routes its overflow to «neutral» contractors so the volume does not go to Samsung. But real volume out of Arizona only comes from 2028–2029.
pkg.update.stories.0.title: Nvidia put down $1.5B of prepayments with Amkor
pkg.update.stories.1.detail: The key disclosure on this theme: how much packaging brings the company, and what it says about assembly volumes. TSMC is nearly doubling output (to 120–140K wafers a month), with another 50–60K added by contractors. While volumes and margin keep rising, the shortage thesis holds.
pkg.update.stories.1.title: TSMC in Q2: 67.7% gross margin, packaging above 10% of revenue on the 2026 plan
pkg.update.stories.1.verdict: the most reliable leading signal on AI-chip demand stays strong
pkg.update.stories.2.detail: According to one industry source (SemiAnalysis, needs confirmation), Nvidia dropped the chip version with four dies and 16 memory modules: at that size the package warps and scrap becomes unacceptable. It was replaced by a design half the size. This is the first case of packaging constraining the architecture of the chip itself — a direct blow to the «packages will keep growing forever» thesis.
pkg.update.stories.2.title: The largest Rubin version was cancelled
pkg.update.stories.2.verdict: the physical limit has shown itself
pkg.update.stories.3.detail: On 1 July 2026 ASE raised advanced-packaging prices by more than 20%, and Powertech raised memory prices by up to 30%. The price of assembling a wafer holds around $10K. While the makers keep raising prices and customers keep paying, the thesis works.
pkg.update.stories.3.title: Prices are still being raised
pkg.update.stories.3.verdict: the pricing power is still theirs
pkg.update.stories.4.detail: On Epoch AI's data, memory's share of an AI chip's cost rose from 52% to 63% over two years, while packaging's fell from 19% to 15%. So the binding constraint is physically here while the profit accumulates in memory. Meanwhile the four largest designers took more than 90% of all assembly and memory by value but only ~12% of leading-edge silicon — which explains why the binding constraints in 2025 were packaging and memory rather than the processors themselves.
pkg.update.stories.4.title: The money goes to memory, not packaging
pkg.update.stories.4.verdict: the key nuance of the theme
pkg.update.stories.5.detail: TrendForce (15 June 2026), citing institutional investors: the supply–demand gap in assembly will narrow from roughly 20% to 10% by the end of 2026, with conditions improving further in 2027. The cause is TSMC nearly doubling output, plus orders flowing to the contractors. In memory the shortage holds through 2027; here it melts sooner.
pkg.update.stories.5.title: The shortage began to narrow: from ~20% to ~10%
pkg.update.summary: July 2026 brought several important pieces of packaging news at once: Nvidia paid a second supplier up front, the largest version of a future chip was cancelled on physics, and the shortage officially began to narrow. Here is what of that changes the picture for an investor.
pkg.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Next the constraint becomes memory (which has to be bought before assembly can start) and physics: at very large package sizes the package starts to warp and scrap rises. According to one industry source, that is exactly why Nvidia cancelled the largest version of a future chip.
pkg.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Right now the constraint is the assembly of large packages at TSMC itself: both the basic and the advanced versions are fully booked. The cause is the large silicon interposer, which is hard to make without defects.
pkg.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: TSMC directs 10–20% of all its investment to packaging and related work (on a total of $60–64B in 2026, that is ~$6–13B). One important advantage: packaging does not need $150M+ lithography tools, so it requires far less investment per unit of output than an ordinary chip fab.
pkg.valueCapture.takeaway: The margin sits in equipment (Besi at 62% gross) and at TSMC — not at the independent assembly houses, where it is 14–26%: their work is closer to contract labour. That says directly who to take the exposure through: Besi (AMS: BESI), ASMPT (HKG: 522), TSMC (NYSE: TSM).
pkg.verdict.bear.0: Oversupply by 2027–2028: the shortfall drops below 5%, the queue shortens, and plant utilisation falls below 85%.
pkg.verdict.bear.1: The money goes to memory, not packaging: packaging's share of chip cost falls further — below 15%.
pkg.verdict.bear.2: A pause in AI spending hits high-beta names: the giants cut spending guidance and Nvidia trims orders (historically assembly houses fell 30–50%).
pkg.verdict.bull.0: The shortage holds to 2027 and pricing power with it: the queue stays longer than 52 weeks, price increases from TSMC and ASE stick, and the shortfall does not fall below 10%.
pkg.verdict.bull.1: Each chip needs more packaging — revenue grows even without more chips: the package grows from 5.5 to 9.5 «reticle fields» (the area of a single lithography pass, ~858 mm²), and the number of memory chips per package reaches 12 and beyond.
pkg.verdict.bull.2: Equipment and materials earn however the shares split: orders accelerate at Besi and ASMPT, and solderless bonding (dies joined directly, with no solder ball) goes into volume.
pkg.verdict.horizon: 2–3 years — the window of advanced-assembly (CoWoS) shortage through 2027–2028; after that, the risk of the winners changing on the shift to panels and glass substrates.
pkg.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the advanced-packaging shortage hold through 2027 — or will TSMC's expansion and the arrival of Intel/Samsung level the market and strip away the pricing power?
pkg.verdict.sizing: Advanced packaging (CoWoS): 370K wafers/month (2024) → 670K (2025) → ~1M (2026). The high-end segment grows ~23%/yr to 2030.
pkg.verdict.summary: The constraint is real: without this assembly no accelerator can be produced, and effectively only TSMC (the world's largest contract chipmaker) does it. But two drawbacks pull the score down. First, the entry price: the sector has already been re-rated (individual names are up 5–12x in a year), so the easy money is made. Second, the shortage clears faster here than in memory: the supply–demand gap is already narrowing from ~20% to ~10%, and a new assembly plant takes only ~18 months to build. The protection from competitors is high at TSMC and at the assembly-equipment makers (Besi), but low at ordinary assembly houses, where the work is closer to contract labour. Hence a 6, not an 8.
pkg.whatIsIt: This is the final assembly of an AI accelerator: a large processor no longer fits on one piece of silicon, so it is cut into several smaller dies and assembled into a single package together with the memory stacks. All the dies sit on a shared silicon interposer carrying tens of thousands of ultra-fine wires that connect processor to memory, and the whole thing is encapsulated in a protective compound and ground flat. Without this assembly a modern accelerator physically does not exist.

rack.intro:
This node covers two things at once: the AI-scale rack itself (the physical machine) and the business that buys such racks on debt and rents out their compute time (a neocloud). A modern model cannot be trained on a single accelerator — it simply does not fit in its memory — so dozens of GPUs have to be joined so that they work as one machine. That is what an AI-scale rack is, and without it training frontier models is physically impossible.

How it works — the hardware. The current generation's flagship is the GB200 NVL72: 72 Blackwell accelerators and 36 Grace processors, joined by the ultra-fast NVLink bus into a single 13.8 TB memory domain. The model is spread across all 72 accelerators at once, and each reads its neighbour's memory at nearly the speed of its own — so the rack behaves like one giant accelerator rather than 72 separate servers. The price of that density is heat: a single rack draws more than 120 kW (an ordinary server draws single-digit kW), and air can no longer carry it away, so coolant runs directly over plates on the chips. An assembled rack costs $3–8M.

How it works — the rental economics. The operator borrows against its future GPUs, buys thousands of chips (access to them is the main growth limiter), installs them in data centres and sells capacity on 3–5 year take-or-pay contracts: the customer pays for reserved capacity even if it goes unused. That shifts idle risk onto the customer and gives the operator a predictable stream to service the debt.

The most critical property. A rack is valuable exactly as long as all 72 accelerators work as one: a single failed node or bus fault stops training across thousands of GPUs at once, so the reliability of the interconnect and the cooling matters more than any individual specification. In the rental economics, utilisation is critical: break-even sits at around 70% utilisation, with almost no margin of safety. Plus an unresolved question about useful life: in the accounts GPUs are depreciated over 4–6 years, while their real economic life may turn out to be 2–3 (an estimate) — in which case the paper profit disappears.

Who pays, and how much. Capital intensity is extreme: the market leader's capex is $31–35B for 2026, around five years of revenue, with roughly $28B raised in debt and equity over 12 months. More than 40% of every capex dollar goes to Nvidia as the GPU supplier; lenders charge anywhere from SOFR+2.25% (investment grade) to ~15% on early loans. The customers — AI labs and hyperscalers — pay almost any price, because access to scarce GPUs matters more to them than the cost, and building their own infrastructure takes longer than renting ready capacity.

Size and concentration. Neocloud revenue passed $25B (2025), growing more than 200% in a year; forecasts for 2030–2031 differ sixfold — from $65B to $400B. The leader (CoreWeave) has around 600K GPUs and a $99.4B order book, but also around $35B of debt and negative cash flow of $4.7B in a quarter. Hence the central question: are neoclouds durable infrastructure platforms, or temporary operators earning only on a GPU shortage?

rack.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: break-even is ~70% utilisation: at 85% a 1,024-GPU cluster earns +$340K/month, at 55% it loses $330K. While reserved pricing rises (+40%) and spot falls (−64–75%), the shortage still feeds it; when the spread compresses, the thesis breaks.
rack.mentalModel.framework: A neocloud buys GPUs on debt and rents out the compute time on 3–5 year contracts. The profit is the spread between the GPU-hour rental rate and the cost of servicing the debt. The risk is that the asset itself depreciates faster than the loan against it amortises: the H100 spot rate has fallen 64–75% while the debt remains. The position holds while a GPU shortage keeps reserved rates (+40%) above the cost of capital; once the shortage ends or the chip obsolesces, the spread compresses and the debt obligations stay.
rack.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = number of GPUs × utilisation (>70% is needed to break even) × GPU-hour rental rate (spot falling, reserved rising +40%)
rack.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: CoreWeave has ~600K GPUs, >1 GW of active capacity and a $99.4B order book (10 customers at ≥$1B). Scale unlocks investment-grade financing and hyperscaler-class contracts that smaller players cannot get. But the hyperscalers themselves are an order of magnitude larger.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: the main differentiator, but a weakening one: 300+ new players entered in 2025, Nvidia's Lepton marketplace is commoditising rental, and Nvidia is spreading its allocation ever wider. The advantage is real, but the pressure is rising.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: the new binding constraint and a growing protection: whoever has contracted gigawatts (CoreWeave 3.5 GW, Nebius 3.5 GW) holds a genuinely scarce resource. CoreWeave's failed bid for Core Scientific ($9B for 1.3 GW) showed how hard it is fought over.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: the first investment-grade GPU-backed financing ($8.5B, A3/A(low)) is a structural barrier to smaller players. But the leverage is fragile: the model requires permanent market access against collateral that obsolesces faster than the debt.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: the weak link: take-or-pay contracts lock in the payment but not the loyalty — the workloads themselves are portable, and a customer can move to another provider in days. The only real lock-in runs through GPU allocation, not through the product.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the weakest vector: AWS/Azure/GCP are 63% of cloud infrastructure and can take the niche back. Meta Compute (July 2026) is a customer turned competitor. A structural threat, not a hypothesis.
rack.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is thin (a composite score of 4/10) and shifting: the old support — scarce GPU access — is eroding, and the new one is contracted gigawatts of power plus investment-grade financing. The real advantage now belongs to whoever holds capacity and cheap capital, not to whoever holds the GPUs. Switching costs are close to zero, and the hyperscalers can take the market back.

rack.picksTakeaway: The main beneficiaries of GPU rental are Nvidia and the lenders, not the operator. Play the theme with less risk through a clean balance sheet (Nebius) and landlords with no GPU risk (Equinix, Digital Realty, Applied Digital). rack.problems.items.0.gap: A new player without secured power must join a 5–7 year grid connection queue (ERCOT, MISO, PJM) — a wait that money cannot shorten. That is precisely why only about 25% of contracted capacity across the industry has actually been brought online. The binding constraint is years of waiting for power, not capital: chips can be bought in weeks, a gigawatt connection cannot.
rack.problems.items.0.problem: Neocloud growth is no longer constrained by chips but by electricity. A single GB200 rack (the flagship 72-accelerator cabinet) draws more than 100 kW, and a large AI site needs hundreds of megawatts and whole gigawatts of capacity. In the US the queue to connect new generation to the grid is stretching to 5–7 years (ERCOT, MISO, PJM — the regional grid operators). Of the capacity already contracted, only about 25% has actually been brought online — the rest is stalled precisely for lack of power. Tellingly, CoreWeave lost a $9B auction for Core Scientific — an attempt to acquire 1.3 GW of ready capacity.
rack.problems.items.0.solution: Capacity is being sourced around the grid: on-site generation — gas turbines and small nuclear reactors — plus long-term power purchase contracts and buying plots that are already connected. A separate source is converting former crypto-mining sites: they already have a large grid connection and power contracts built for mining, and they are being switched to AI workloads. Liquid cooling (coolant running directly over the chips instead of air) packs more computation into each megawatt, reducing how much energy a unit of work requires.
rack.problems.items.0.winners: The winners are those who already hold capacity and connected sites: CoreWeave (3.5 GW contracted), Nebius (3.5 GW → more than 4 GW), IREN (a 4.5 GW pipeline). Former miners are especially well placed because their grid connection is already built: TeraWulf (a 12.8 GW pipeline, with Google holding 8% of the equity), Hut 8 (8.5 GW), Cipher (1.3 GW, with an AWS contract). The owners of connected land — Equinix (3 GW of ready land) and Digital Realty (5 GW) — lease it out with no GPU (accelerator chip) obsolescence risk.
rack.problems.takeaway: This barrier rewards those who already have the power — former miners with connected sites, neoclouds with gigawatt contracts and owners of ready land — and may let new players (the miners) in at the expense of pure GPU operators without secured capacity.
