rack.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: Bloomberg: Meta is building a cloud unit, «Meta Compute», led by Santosh Janardhan. Zuckerberg: «clearly on the table». Meta's stock rose 9% and the neoclouds fell. AWS/Azure/GCP are 63% of total cloud infrastructure. Simultaneously customers and competitors.
rack.roadmap.disruption.0.verdict: The core structural threat — Meta's Meta Compute cloud unit (July 2026), Alphabet's $205B capex
rack.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: DeepSeek (Jan 2025) knocked NVIDIA −17%. Kimi K3 (July 2026) triggered the worst week for chips in a year. But both reversed. Google's token throughput is +7x y/y to 3.2 quadrillion a month. Enterprise AI spend went $1.7B→$37B. H100 reserved pricing is rising despite efficiency gains.
rack.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: NVIDIA holds 7% of CoreWeave ($2B), invested $2B in Nebius, and is discussing a ~$250B OpenAI backstop. Bernstein's Rasgon flags parallels with dot-com and telecom vendor financing. Boston College: «demand is not as big as it appears — companies buying from each other».
rack.roadmap.disruption.2.verdict: Systemic risk — the NVIDIA→neocloud→AI lab chain. A ~$250B OpenAI backstop is under discussion
rack.roadmap.generations.1.note: ~$6.50/hr. Sold out through 2026. The primary volume platform. CoreWeave has $13B+ of orders
rack.roadmap.generations.5.note: Google is courting neoclouds for TPU adoption. But «customers currently only requesting NVIDIA» (CoreWeave, March 2026)
rack.roadmap.takeaway: NVIDIA's 18–24 month GPU cadence against 4–6 year depreciation is the core tension. Rubin (H2 2026) is the key fleet-obsolescence test. Hyperscaler capacity recapture and circular financing are the structural threats. Custom silicon is a substitution risk. GPU futures may financialise and compress spreads.
rack.scenarios.cases.0.name: Bear
rack.scenarios.cases.0.note: the GPU shortage ends, spot commoditises reserved pricing, hyperscalers take workloads back, and CoreWeave breaches a covenant or fails to refinance — for the leveraged names that is close to zero
rack.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
rack.scenarios.cases.1.note: the leaders become durable platforms, the order book converts, power is contracted, Nebius keeps a clean balance sheet and CoreWeave survives the refinancing shock — but the multiple compresses from hype levels
rack.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
rack.scenarios.cases.2.note: demand is insatiable (tokens +7x y/y), reserved pricing holds, investment-grade financing scales, and neoclouds establish themselves as AI's infrastructure layer
rack.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~+5…+10%/yr (probability-weighted, Nebius) — but with enormous dispersion in both directions for the leveraged names
rack.scenarios.takeaway: The asymmetry here is two-sided and extreme: CoreWeave's bear case is a genuine zero (refinancing against obsolescing collateral), its bull case a multiple. This is an option, not a compounder: hold Nebius as the core (clean balance sheet) and CoreWeave at a size that survives a refinancing shock, with the sector at ≤2–4% of the portfolio.
rack.supply.balance.0.detail: The reserved tier is tight (Blackwell sold out, reserved +40%). Spot/on-demand is oversupplied (H100 −64–75%, 300+ new entrants). CoreWeave has >1 GW active of 3.5 GW contracted. Capex $31–35B
rack.supply.balance.1.detail: Rubin R100 in volume. CoreWeave targets >1.7 GW → 8 GW by 2030. Nebius >4 GW. The Hopper fleet cascades to inference. A ~$50B miner funding gap (VanEck)
rack.supply.capacityAdds.0.name: CoreWeave: 43 data centres → targeting >8 GW by 2030. Capex $31–35B (2026, ~5x TTM revenue). ~$28B raised over 12 months
rack.supply.capacityAdds.1.name: Nebius: 3.5 GW contracted → >4 GW. Capex $20–25B (2026). >$6B raised in Q1 2026
rack.supply.capacityAdds.2.impact: A ~$50B near-term funding gap. Only ~25% of leased capacity delivered. Delivery is the key de-risking event
rack.supply.capacityAdds.3.impact: 63% of cloud infrastructure. Meta Compute. Alphabet's $205B capex. The long-term competitive threat
rack.supply.crowdingOut: 300+ new GPU cloud providers entered in 2025 (Value Add VC), fragmenting the on-demand/spot tier and driving the H100 price decline. The reserved tier remains differentiated.
rack.supply.leadTime: NVIDIA GPU allocation is the primary lead time. Blackwell is sold out through 2026. Power/data centres are the emerging constraint (CoreWeave's failed $9B Core Scientific bid for 1.3 GW). HBM memory runs 36–52 week lead times.
rack.supply.takeaway: Supply is bifurcated: reserved is tight (the primary moat), spot is oversupplied (300+ entrants). Both the shortage and the glut narratives are true. Capacity expansion is explosive ($31–35B at CoreWeave alone). GPU scarcity is the moat, but it is eroding. Power is increasingly the binding constraint.
rack.supply.utilization: Break-even is ~70% on debt-financed clusters. 55% utilisation = −$330K/month on a 1,024-GPU cluster; 85% = +$340K. «Almost no margin of safety.» CoreWeave reports a 95% re-booking rate on H100 batches.
rack.thesis.bigIdea: Neoclouds borrow to buy GPUs and rent them out. The equity market prices them as the power plants of the AI era; the credit market prices them as bankruptcy candidates: CoreWeave's 5-year CDS (default insurance, whose price is the market's view of the risk) embeds a ~50% chance of default. Both valuations describe the same company. The real margin is taken by Nvidia (which sells the GPUs, takes a stake in the buyer and gets its own money back) and by the lenders, leaving the shareholder only a thin residual — what is left after them — on a fast-depreciating asset. The bet belongs on the company without heavy debt (Nebius), not on the leveraged bet that can go to zero in a bad scenario (CoreWeave).
rack.thesis.stream.0.t: The business that borrows to buy GPUs and rents them out
rack.thesis.stream.1.t: A neocloud is a company that buys tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs (mostly with borrowed money), assembles them into clusters and rents out the computation by the hour. Everything converges here: chips from the [[asic|custom accelerators|earns on every chip]] and [[hbm|memory|decoupled from the cycle]] sections, plus the [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]] without which the cluster cannot be switched on. The market exploded and called these operators «the power plants of the AI era».

rack.thesis.stream.10.t: Who takes what in the GPU rental chain
rack.thesis.stream.11.t: So the «AI cloud growth story» mostly enriches Nvidia and the lenders. The shareholder owns a thin, leveraged slice — strong while GPUs hold their price, and dangerous when they stop.
rack.thesis.stream.12.t: The real constraint is not demand — it is capital and GPUs
rack.thesis.stream.13.t: There are three constraints. First, Nvidia's GPU allocation: this is both the main barrier and the main dependency, and you live or die by how many chips you are sold. Second, access to [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]] and sites: CoreWeave bid $9B for Core Scientific purely for 1.3 GW of capacity. Third, permanent access to capital markets: the model works only while the debt can be refinanced.
rack.thesis.stream.14.items.0.l: the main barrier and the main dependency
rack.thesis.stream.14.items.0.n: however many GPUs you are sold is how much business you have
rack.thesis.stream.14.items.1.n: for the sake of 1.3 GW of electrical capacity
rack.thesis.stream.14.items.2.n: which has to be refinanced continuously
rack.thesis.stream.15.t: The disputed detail: how fast a GPU loses value
rack.thesis.stream.16.t: And here is the number the whole model rests on — how fast a GPU actually loses value. The operators write GPUs off over 4–6 years (CoreWeave 6, Nebius 4). But Nvidia ships a new generation almost every year (Hopper → Blackwell → Rubin), and sceptics argue the real useful life is closer to 2–3 years. If so, the depreciation in the accounts is understated by tens of billions, and much of the reported profit is on paper. Spot rental prices already hint at this: H100 rates have fallen 64–75% from a peak above $8/hour as 300+ new entrants flooded the market.
rack.thesis.stream.17.items.0.l: the period GPUs are written off over in the accounts
rack.thesis.stream.17.items.0.n: CoreWeave 6, Nebius 4; the «profit» depends directly on this
rack.thesis.stream.17.items.1.n: Hopper → Blackwell → Rubin — the old kit devalues faster than it is written off
rack.thesis.stream.17.items.2.n: from a peak above $8/hour — 300+ players flooded the market
rack.thesis.stream.18.t: A business that rents out a fast-depreciating asset bought on debt is durable while the asset holds its price — and fragile the second it stops.
rack.thesis.stream.19.t: The equity market and the credit market disagree about one company
rack.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: a $99.4B order book; anchors are OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta
rack.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: one of the fastest-growing segments of AI infrastructure
rack.thesis.stream.20.t: Here is the key signal. The equity market and the credit market look at CoreWeave and see opposite things. Analysts rate it a buy with a target of ~$142. Its 5-year CDS — the cost of insuring its debt against default — embeds roughly a 50% chance of default. Equity is pricing a growth star; credit is pricing a bankruptcy candidate. About the same company.

rack.thesis.stream.21.items.0.n: the equity market is paying for growth
rack.thesis.stream.21.items.1.l: probability of default in the 5-year CDS
rack.thesis.stream.21.items.1.n: the credit market is paying for distress
rack.thesis.stream.21.items.2.l: will the take-or-pay book cover the debt repayment
rack.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: if GPU residual values collapse, nobody yet knows
rack.thesis.stream.22.t: When the equity market and the credit market disagree this sharply about one company, the credit market is usually the one to respect.
rack.thesis.stream.24.t: CoreWeave at ~6–9x revenue looks inexpensive — until you remember the ~$35B of debt and −$4.7B of quarterly cash flow that the multiple ignores. The market prices the $99.4B order book as if it were guaranteed to convert into revenue on a 6-year GPU life. Nebius at ~8–9x forward revenue treats a $7–9B ARR target almost as fact — but it has a clean balance sheet and conservative 4-year depreciation to back it.
rack.thesis.stream.25.t: Our read: Nebius (clean balance sheet, conservative depreciation) is the fair bet; CoreWeave is a leveraged bet that cannot be taken in size. Cheap on the multiple, expensive on the risk.
rack.thesis.stream.26.t: Where the sector is going — and where the money is going
rack.thesis.stream.27.t: Where the model is going: from renting bare GPUs to full managed AI platforms — the winners become sticky infrastructure rather than swappable rental. Spot rental is commoditising (H100 −64–75%, 300+ players), but reserved pricing is rising (+40% in six months) as large players sign multi-year contracts. The next differentiator is not the GPUs themselves but access to power and reliability.
rack.thesis.stream.28.t: The main shift ahead is from training to inference. Training a model is a one-off burst, while inference (answering queries) runs continuously and will become the bulk of computation. That changes the economics: in inference what matters is not peak capacity but utilisation and cost per token — the winner is whoever has cheaper energy and higher utilisation. In parallel «sovereign AI» is rising: countries are building their own national clusters so as not to depend on foreign clouds — funds in the UAE (MGX), Saudi Arabia (HUMAIN) and the EU are investing tens of billions.
rack.thesis.stream.29.t: Where the money is going: Nvidia seeds capital into its own customers (7% of CoreWeave, $2B in Nebius) to guarantee demand; investment-grade debt is scaling (the first rated GPU-backed financing, at $8.5B); the hyperscalers and labs sign anchor contracts (OpenAI, Microsoft and Meta at CoreWeave; Microsoft's $9.7B at IREN). And the picks and shovels are the site landlords (Equinix, Digital Realty, Applied Digital), who lease powered land and carry no GPU obsolescence risk at all.

rack.thesis.stream.30.items.1.n: credit is getting cheaper for the leaders — but not for everyone
rack.thesis.stream.30.items.2.n: anchor deals are the fuel of the whole model
rack.thesis.stream.31.t: The scale of capital is no longer venture but infrastructure. Direct-lending and infrastructure funds are moving into GPU data centres (Blackstone, Apollo, the $30B+ BlackRock–Microsoft–MGX–Nvidia partnership) — financing construction against long-term contracts, like roads or pipelines. Securitisation of GPU debt is appearing too: bonds backed by future rental. For leaders with anchor contracts this is cheap capital; for everyone else it is the absence of capital.
rack.thesis.stream.32.items.0.n: increasingly borrowed infrastructure capital rather than equity
rack.thesis.stream.32.items.1.n: only a few will survive — consolidation is inevitable
rack.thesis.stream.32.items.2.n: the UAE (MGX), Saudi Arabia (HUMAIN), the EU — tens of billions
rack.thesis.stream.33.t: Hence the coming consolidation. 300+ operators flooded the market, but only a few will survive: three things decide it — access to [[power|energy|not generation, but connection]], balance-sheet strength and Nvidia's allocation. Weak players on expensive debt and spot pricing break first when the cycle turns, and their capacity and contracts pass to the strong. So this theme is a bet not on «neocloud growth» in general but on specific survivors.
rack.thesis.stream.34.t: The specifics: the whole model rests on anchor contracts and staked-out power. Here is who has signed with whom, and who has the best capacity position.
rack.thesis.stream.35.note: Sources: deal press releases and filings, 2025–2026.
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.0.3: weak: the $9B bid for Core Scientific (1.3 GW) failed
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.1.3: its own data centres + a clean balance sheet — it builds to contract
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.2.3: the best: a 4.5 GW pipeline, its own fleet and power
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.3.3: a landlord: 15-year contracts on powered land
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.4.3: the price leader, but with no large power position
rack.thesis.stream.36.t: The next race is for power. Best positioned are those who have already staked out gigawatts: IREN (a 4.5 GW pipeline), Nebius (its own sites) and landlords like Applied Digital. CoreWeave, the no. 1 on contracts, is the weakest on owned power — its $9B bid for Core Scientific for 1.3 GW of [[power|capacity|not generation, but connection]] failed. Whoever locks up gigawatts under contract first takes the next wave of deals.
rack.thesis.stream.37.t: Who actually buys this computation? Three groups. First, the hyperscalers themselves, renting others' capacity to cover their own shortfall: Microsoft is the single largest buyer, renting from CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Lambda at once. Second, AI labs without their own data centres: OpenAI (the CoreWeave deal), plus Anthropic, Mistral and xAI. Third, and growing, corporations and states building «sovereign AI» (the same UAE and Saudi funds). Tellingly, even hyperscalers that could build their own choose to rent — because speed and access to power matter more than building from scratch.
rack.thesis.stream.38.t: What the players are betting on: Nvidia bets on many neoclouds at once (diluting demand, reducing dependence on the hyperscalers); the neoclouds bet on staking out power and anchor contracts before the GPU cycle turns; and an investor who wants the theme with less risk bets on the landlords (bond-like contracts, no GPU risk) and on a clean balance sheet (Nebius) rather than on a leveraged operator.

rack.thesis.stream.41.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
rack.thesis.stream.42.t: Neoclouds are real infrastructure, and the demand is real. But the model is renting a fast-depreciating asset on debt, and the value goes first to Nvidia and the lenders. The shareholder gets the residual: strong while GPUs hold their price, and brutal when they stop.
rack.thesis.stream.43.t: Compressed into one thought: play the theme through a clean balance sheet (Nebius) and the landlords (bond-like contracts, no GPU risk), not through the leveraged bet (CoreWeave). And the main beneficiary of all this renting is not the operator but Nvidia, which sells the hardware, takes a stake in the customer and gets its money back.
rack.thesis.stream.5.t: A single H100 GPU costs $25–40K, and fully deployed — with power, cooling and networking — around $45–50K. It rents for $1.80–3.50 an hour (the budget segment) and up to $8–11 at the hyperscalers. At first glance the economics look brilliant: CoreWeave has a 69% gross margin and 56% adjusted EBITDA. But that is BEFORE depreciation and interest on the debt.
rack.thesis.stream.6.t: After those, the picture changes. In one quarter CoreWeave posted a GAAP loss of −$740M: interest on the debt alone ate ~46% of EBITDA, and cash flow was minus $4.7B. The gross margin is real — but it is a mirage above two expenses that consume it: the asset depreciates fast, and the debt used to buy it demands interest.

rack.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: rental is $1.80–3.50/hour in the budget tier, $8–11 at the hyperscalers

rack.thesis.stream.8.t: Where the margin actually leaks to
rack.thesis.stream.9.t: Follow the money. Nvidia takes more than 40% of all capex, selling GPUs at a ~75% margin — and then takes a stake in its own customers (7% of CoreWeave, $2B in Nebius) and gets its own money back. The lenders earn a secured return (SOFR+2.25% for the best of them). And the neocloud's shareholder gets only the residual — what is left after Nvidia and the lenders.
rack.tldr.0: Neocloud revenue (companies renting out compute capacity with accelerator chips) passed $25B (2025, Synergy Research), growing >200% in a year. CoreWeave leads (~600K GPUs, 43 data centres, >1 GW of capacity). But analysts cannot agree on the market's size: forecasts run from $65B to $400B by 2030–2031 — a sixfold spread. The main source of that uncertainty: whether the hyperscalers take this niche back once their own GPU supply is sorted.
rack.tldr.1: CoreWeave is the most aggressive player: $5.1B of revenue (+170%), a $99.4B order book, adjusted EBITDA (profit before interest, tax and depreciation) of ~56%. But ~$35B of debt, negative cash flow of $4.7B in a quarter, interest expense at ~46% of EBITDA, and Microsoft at 67% of 2025 revenue. Nebius is the preferred pure play: $399M of revenue in a quarter (+684%), $9.3B of cash, GPUs depreciated over 4 years (more conservative). The former crypto miners (APLD, IREN, WULF) essentially lease space to hyperscalers on 15-year terms.
rack.tldr.2: A sensible strategy: cap neoclouds at 2–4% of the portfolio and prefer the infrastructure landlords — the data-centre owners who lease space (Digital Realty, Equinix) — plus Nvidia, which captures most of the value, over debt-funded GPU renters. Nebius is the best pure choice among the neoclouds. CoreWeave is a high-leverage option (heavily dependent on borrowed money), and the position size must survive a refinancing shock.
rack.unitEconomics.costCurve: A 100-H100 cluster (Mercatus): $4.5M capex; year-3 residual ~25% ($1.1M); operating cost $0.41/GPU-hr. At 75% utilisation the 3-year IRR is 7–33% (driven entirely by the alternative cloud cost). Against hyperscaler on-demand at $3.50/hr it is decisively positive; against reserved at $1.80/hr it is marginal.
rack.unitEconomics.grossMargin: CoreWeave: 69.4% GM (TTM), adj. EBITDA ~56%, GAAP net −$740M in Q1 (after depreciation + interest). Nebius AI cloud at 45% adj. EBITDA. Lambda ~50% GM (~61% ex-hardware). Operating cost ~$0.41/GPU-hr (power + colo + ops). Break-even ~70% utilisation.
rack.unitEconomics.takeaway: High headline returns (55–69% GM before depreciation), but radical asset-life uncertainty (4–6 years in the accounts against Burry's 2–3 year estimate). Break-even at ~70% utilisation leaves almost no margin of safety. IRR depends critically on residual values and on the alternative cloud cost. Not comparable to traditional colo (15–20 year assets, 7–9% cap rates).
rack.unitEconomics.yields.0.note: Down 64–75% from the 2023 peak above $8/hr. 300+ new entrants are driving spot down. Reserved is rising +40%
rack.unitEconomics.yields.3.note: Burry: a 2–3 year economic life against 6-year books = ~$176B of understated depreciation across 2026–2028. Intrator: 95% re-booking at original pricing
rack.update.bottomLine: Genuine hypergrowth ($25B+ of revenue, 58–165% a year) alongside an extreme set of risks: debt, fast GPU obsolescence, customer concentration and circular financing. The facts so far lean toward the leaders becoming durable platforms — but their valuations already embed that outcome as near-guaranteed. This is a high-volatility satellite position: Nebius is the cleanest option (no debt burden), Equinix/DLR the best protected (no chip obsolescence risk), and CoreWeave the bet with maximum leverage and maximum risk. One question decides it: will the contracted take-or-pay payments cover debt amortisation if GPU residual values collapse?
rack.update.headline: Neoclouds: $25B+ of hypergrowth — the durability bet is unresolved, and the CDS-versus-equity divergence is extreme

rack.update.summary: Neocloud revenue passed $25B (2025, +223% y/y in Q4). CoreWeave: a $99.4B order book, ~600K GPUs — but ~$35B of debt, with CDS pricing a ~50% chance of default. Nebius is the cleaner alternative ($9.3B of cash, 4-year depreciation). Reserved GPU prices are rising (+40%); spot has fallen 64–75%. Meta launched its own Meta Compute cloud (July 2026) — a customer turned competitor. The circular financing of Nvidia→neocloud→lab raises the question: is this real demand, or capital being recycled?

rack.valueCapture.margins.4.source: Private, valued at ~$5.9B. The price leader: H100 at ~$2.49/hr against CoreWeave's $4.25. An IPO is planned for H2 2026
rack.valueCapture.takeaway: NVIDIA captures the majority of capex. Debt providers earn secured returns. Neocloud equity holders earn the residual spread — which looks strong at adj. EBITDA (~56%) and collapses at GAAP net after depreciation and interest. Whether that is a durable margin or temporary arbitrage of GPU scarcity is unresolved.
rack.verdict.bear.0: Earning on a price spread with borrowed money, for as long as the shortage lasts: H100 spot prices (one-off rental at the current moment) have fallen 64–75%, 300+ new entrants fragment demand, and the main advantage (a shortage of GPUs — scarce accelerator chips) is eroding precisely in the segment where pricing is set.
rack.verdict.bear.1: A fragile capital structure: CoreWeave has ~$35B of debt, cash flow of minus $4.7B in a quarter, interest expense at ~46% of EBITDA (profit before interest, tax and depreciation), and CDS (default insurance) pricing in a ~50% chance of default over 5 years. The model depends on permanent access to capital markets, against collateral (GPUs) that obsolesces faster than the debt amortises.
rack.verdict.bear.2: Circular financing + customer concentration: Nvidia invests in neoclouds → the neoclouds buy GPUs → AI labs (funded by Nvidia) rent capacity from the neoclouds. Meta Compute (July 2026) is a customer that became a competitor. If one link breaks, the chain fails systemically.
rack.verdict.bull.0: Demand really is insatiable and confirmed by data: Google's token processing (units of text a model handles) grew 7x in a year to 3.2 quadrillion a month. Corporate AI spending grew 22x in two years ($1.7B→$37B). Reserved GPU prices (scarce accelerator chips) are up +40% — neoclouds (companies renting out compute capacity) serve the fastest-growing segment.
rack.verdict.bull.1: The financing model is maturing: GPU-backed debt has reached investment grade (A3/A(low), SOFR+2.25%), spreads over the base rate have compressed 175 basis points (1.75 percentage points) in a year, and take-or-pay contracts (the customer pays for reserved capacity even if unused) shift idle risk onto customers.
rack.verdict.bull.2: Order books give multi-year visibility: CoreWeave $99.4B (75% within 4 years), Nebius >$46B, TeraWulf >$12.8B, Applied Digital ~$16B — with customer diversification.
rack.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — enough for a full GPU generation turnover (Hopper → Blackwell → Rubin) and the first serious debt stress test; that is when it becomes clear whether the model is durable.
rack.verdict.keyQuestion: Are neoclouds long-term platforms, or temporary arbitrageurs of a GPU shortage who get squeezed by the hyperscalers once supply normalises?
rack.verdict.sizing: Neocloud revenue >$25B (2025). Forecasts $65–400B (2030–2031). A single-digit % of total cloud infrastructure ($25B against ~$107B/quarter for all cloud), but over-indexed to the fastest-growing GPU/AI slice
rack.verdict.summary: Genuine hypergrowth ($25B+, >200% a year) — but with an extreme spread of forecasts ($65–400B by 2030–2031). The competitive advantages are thin: GPU allocation (scarce accelerator chips) from Nvidia + a proprietary software platform + long-term contracts — against hyperscalers building their own capacity and 300+ new entrants turning one-off rental into a commodity with no mark-up. Leverage + accelerated write-down of chip value + customer concentration + circular financing (money going round in a loop between the chip supplier and its own customers) = very high risk. Reserved GPU prices are rising (+40%), but spot prices (one-off rental at the current moment) have fallen 64–75%. The reserved-versus-spot price dynamic is the key real-time indicator: if the gap between them narrows, the shortage is ending. The verdict: a high-beta satellite position, not a portfolio core.
rack.whatIsIt: A large cabinet packed with compute chips, wired together so that all of them work as one enormous machine. A modern AI model cannot be trained on a single chip — it does not fit — so dozens of chips have to be bound into a single whole. The node's second meaning is the companies that buy these cabinets on debt and rent out their compute time to those training models. In an AI data centre this is the basic working unit: without it, training a frontier model is physically impossible.
renewables.picks.0.group: Owners of the scarcity — scale, grid and differentiation
renewables.picks.0.note: The value is moving from the panel to the scarcity: interconnection, transmission, storage, firm capacity and differentiated equipment. These names are the ones that own it.

renewables.picks.0.rows.2.why: It takes the capital regardless of whether AI's electricity comes from renewables, from gas or from grid modernisation. Grid and gas offer better near-term economics than manufacturing wind turbines.
renewables.picks.0.rows.3.exposure: CdTe thin-film modules, manufactured in the US
renewables.picks.0.rows.3.priced: Profitability depends heavily on tax credits and tariffs; backlog concentration; risk of cancellations and policy change.
renewables.picks.0.rows.3.why: Differentiated technology independent of China's crystalline silicon, with US protection. A 45.1 GW backlog ($13.6B), Q2'26 revenue $1.06B, net income $423M — a rare margin for modules.

renewables.picks.0.rows.4.priced: Price competition, steel costs, customer concentration; cheap modules can push buyers towards simple fixed-tilt mounts.
renewables.picks.0.rows.4.why: A less commoditised layer of the chain than the panel: hardware plus software raises output, and switching supplier is harder than buying a module; outside cell and wafer economics.
renewables.picks.1.note: More directly tied to storage, or carrying more execution risk and leverage; not to be confused with a pure bet on the scarcity.
renewables.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Not a pure renewable bet — the valuation is set by all of Tesla; cell prices, Chinese competition, fire and warranty risk.
renewables.picks.1.rows.0.why: A more direct beneficiary than panel manufacturing: demand for grid storage is growing and manufacturing scale matters; a recognised integrated product and a creditworthy counterparty.
renewables.picks.1.rows.1.risk: A 13.7% hardware margin, project delays, working capital, competition from vertically integrated Chinese suppliers — high-beta execution, not a compounder.
renewables.picks.1.rows.1.why: Direct access to the grid battery market; a $5.3B backlog, ~85% of 2026 revenue covered, guidance of $3.2–3.6B.
renewables.picks.1.rows.2.risk: High leverage and project complexity; sensitivity to rates and regulation.
renewables.picks.1.rows.2.why: Development and asset ownership with hyperscaler contracts; exposure to the growth of contracted generation.
renewables.picks.1.rows.3.exposure: wind turbines + a large service base
renewables.picks.1.rows.3.risk: Aggressive competition for market share, and warranty, inflation and execution risk in turbine manufacturing.
renewables.picks.1.rows.3.why: Service means long contracts, recurring revenue and a better-protected margin than selling new turbines.
renewables.picks.1.rows.4.risk: Regulatory and regional complexity; the outcome depends on tariff decisions.
renewables.picks.1.rows.4.why: Grids plus generation — exposure to the transmission shortage, not only to panels.
renewables.thesis.bigIdea: The market argues in extremes: some say «AI needs power 24/7, and sun and wind are intermittent — a bad bet», others say «AI needs energy, buy any renewable». Both are wrong. Sun and wind have already won on the cheapest and fastest new megawatt-hour, and the hyperscalers have turned them into bankable 10–20 year contracts. But cheap does not mean round the clock, and generation is becoming abundant: the world added 692 GW during 2025. So the value is moving away from the panel itself (already a commodity) towards the scarcity: grid connection, transmission, storage, firm capacity and shovel-ready permitted projects. The winner is not whoever makes more panels, but whoever owns that constraint.
renewables.thesis.stream.0.t: What it is, and what AI needs it for
renewables.thesis.stream.1.t: Sun and wind are the cheapest and fastest new source of electricity: onshore wind ~$33 and solar ~$44 per MWh, with no fuel risk, and they can often be built faster than nuclear or large gas. Hyperscalers contract them 10–20 years ahead. But there is a limit to this: a [[rack|data centre|borrows to buy GPUs]] needs power every second, while the sun delivers current by day and the wind delivers by weather. So renewables can cheaply cover a large share of annual consumption, but on their own they do not provide 24/7 reliability without batteries, transmission, surplus capacity and firm generation.

renewables.thesis.stream.11.t: The grid is the real constraint
renewables.thesis.stream.12.t: The shortage is not of projects but of the ability to connect them and move the current. At the end of 2024 ~10,300 projects were sitting in US interconnection queues — some ~1,400 GW of generation and ~890 GW of storage; of these, ~408 GW already had an interconnection agreement but had not yet been built. The most valuable asset is not the technology but the right to inject electricity into the grid at a commercially usable point (which needs [[transformers|transformers and substations|the steel inside it]] and [[power|the connection itself|not generation, but connection]]). And as solar grows, so does curtailment: in H1 2026 California curtailed ~4.5M MWh of renewables — more than in the whole of 2025.

renewables.thesis.stream.14.t: Batteries are a more direct beneficiary than panels
renewables.thesis.stream.15.t: Storage is a more direct beneficiary of AI than most panel manufacturing. A battery shifts daytime solar into the evening, regulates frequency, provides fast reserve and participates in the capacity market — the revenue comes from several sources at once (arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity payments, tolling). Lithium is strong over a 1–4 hour horizon, but a four-hour system does not cover several days of poor weather. Long-duration technologies (iron-air, flow, pumped hydro) offer more upside, but carry far more commercial risk.

renewables.thesis.stream.17.t: Who is buying — the hyperscalers are changing the financing
renewables.thesis.stream.18.t: The main effect of AI is not a rise in the spot price of solar but the appearance of a creditworthy long-term buyer next to a large load. A 10–20 year power purchase agreement (PPA) turns an unfinanceable project into a bankable asset: it puts a floor under revenue, removes price risk, allows debt to be raised and the asset later sold to an infrastructure fund. Below are the disclosed deals; note also the shift from «annual coverage with certificates» towards firm, local, hourly clean energy.
renewables.thesis.stream.19.note: A PPA is a long-term power purchase agreement; it is what makes a project bankable.

renewables.thesis.stream.20.t: The players' financials — who is earning
renewables.thesis.stream.21.t: First Solar is a rare case of high margins in modules: a 45.1 GW backlog ($13.6B), Q2 2026 revenue of $1.06B and net income of $423M, with 2026 sales guidance of $4.9–5.2B. But that profitability is heavily tied to tax credits and tariff protection. Fluence is a direct bet on grid storage: a $5.3B backlog with ~85% of 2026 revenue covered, but a hardware margin of only 13.7% — this is high-beta execution, not a placid compounder. NextEra converts load growth into contracted construction: a ~33 GW backlog after Q1 2026, +4 GW in the quarter, and a ~110 GW battery pipeline.

renewables.thesis.stream.23.t: Where it is heading — money and technology
renewables.thesis.stream.24.t: The model that captures the value is not «hold the asset forever» but capital recycling: the developer builds or assembles a portfolio, contracts it, finances construction, sells a stake to institutional capital and reinvests while retaining management. KKR bought 50% of a 1.2 GW portfolio from TotalEnergies for €1.8B; Shell, by contrast, sold its European renewable assets (500 MW + a 3.5 GW pipeline) — capacity can keep growing even as some owners exit, because growth does not guarantee returns to everyone. And the best-protected layer is grid equipment (GE Vernova, Eaton, Schneider) and transmission contractors (Quanta): they take the capital regardless of what wins in generation.

renewables.thesis.stream.25.rows.1.1: a global platform + hydro for firmness + capital recycling (the Microsoft framework)

renewables.thesis.stream.26.t: What is already in the price — a value map
renewables.thesis.stream.27.t: On the sector's analytical scale, the most attractive economics are not in generation itself but one layer to the side: in grid equipment, transmission, secured interconnection and storage integration. Commodity modules and offshore wind rate low, and residential installers lowest of all, with almost no direct link to AI. Hence the reclassification: Sunrun is «distributed energy», not «generation for AI».
renewables.thesis.stream.3.t: Cheap does not mean round the clock

renewables.thesis.stream.30.rows.1.1: good for developers and owners, bad for undifferentiated manufacturers

renewables.thesis.stream.30.rows.5.1: if efficiency rises faster, part of the pipeline slips (but demand is diversified by electrification)
renewables.thesis.stream.31.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
renewables.thesis.stream.32.t: Renewable energy is the cheap foundation of the AI energy system and one of the largest physical recipients of the cycle's capital: a 1 GW campus consumes ~7.9 TWh a year, and covering that with solar means ~3.6 GW of capacity. But generation is becoming abundant (692 GW added during 2025), and on its own it does not deliver round-the-clock firm power. So renewables do not cancel gas and nuclear — they grow alongside them.
renewables.thesis.stream.33.t: The conclusion: not «AI needs energy, buy any renewable», but own the scarcity. The excess returns go to those who control grid connection, transmission, storage, differentiated equipment and firm capacity: NextEra and Brookfield Renewable (scale, hydro and capital recycling), GE Vernova (grid + gas + wind), First Solar (a protected niche), Nextracker (trackers and software). Commodity modules, residential installers and uncontracted offshore are weaker as a direct AI bet. The best position is one layer to the side of commoditised generation itself.
renewables.thesis.stream.34.head.1: What to cover the theme with
renewables.thesis.stream.34.note: Not a recommendation — a match of instrument to style; the decision is the investor's.
renewables.thesis.stream.34.rows.0.1: NextEra, Brookfield Renewable — developers with a backlog, interconnection and hyperscaler contracts

renewables.thesis.stream.34.rows.3.0: A direct bet on storage (higher risk)

renewables.thesis.stream.34.rows.4.1: commodity modules, residential solar (Sunrun), uncontracted offshore
renewables.thesis.stream.4.t: The key mistake is to treat annual coverage as hourly coverage. A 1 GW campus at 90% utilisation consumes ~7.9 TWh a year; to cover that across the year needs ~3.6 GW of solar (at a 25% capacity factor). But such a fleet delivers appreciably more than 1 GW at midday and almost nothing at night. To get close to a 24/7 regime, the system adds geographically dispersed wind and solar, batteries, demand management, transmission, hydro, geothermal, [[nuc|nuclear|already built, licensed and connected]] or [[gasturbines|gas|the fastest route]]. So nameplate renewable capacity cannot be compared directly with a data centre's load without adjusting for timing and reliability.

renewables.thesis.stream.6.t: The optimal system is not panels alone
renewables.thesis.stream.7.t: The economically optimal energy system for AI is not «more panels» but a combination: cheap renewable generation + short-duration batteries + expanded transmission + firm generation (gas, nuclear, hydro or geothermal) + energy management software + long-term contracts. Renewable energy here is a cheap foundation, not a complete replacement for gas and nuclear. That is precisely why renewables and gas complement rather than compete with each other over the coming build phase.
renewables.thesis.stream.8.t: Where the value sits — no longer in the panel
renewables.thesis.stream.9.t: The panel itself has fallen sharply in price thanks to enormous capacity, above all in China — it is already a commodity on thin margins. The value is moving up the chain: a secured grid connection, development rights, eligibility for local-content support, trackers, inverters and power electronics, EPC contracting, operations and maintenance, storage integration and power trading. The development premium can exceed the manufacturing premium: a panel can be shipped anywhere, but a grid-connected project in a good location cannot be reproduced.
silicon.picks.0.group: The core — platform, network and manufacturing
silicon.picks.0.note: They collect value under either outcome of the «GPU versus ASIC» argument — no need to guess which architecture wins.
silicon.picks.0.rows.0.priced: All the quality and growth is already in the price; the risk is the multiple and customer concentration, not obsolescence.
silicon.picks.0.rows.0.why: The default platform: the customer pays for time-to-model and the performance of a whole cluster, not for the price of a chip. The ~75% data-centre margin is payment for the platform, not for the silicon.
silicon.picks.0.rows.1.exposure: the giants' custom accelerators + networking (Ethernet, SerDes)
silicon.picks.0.rows.1.priced: High customer concentration; part of the growth is already in the quote.
silicon.picks.0.rows.1.why: It helps the cloud giants build their own chip and sells the network to go with it — taking value even while Nvidia keeps the lead. AI revenue +143% year on year, guidance of $16B/qtr.
silicon.picks.0.rows.2.exposure: manufacturing and packaging of almost every leading-edge AI chip
silicon.picks.0.rows.2.priced: The gentlest valuation among the leaders relative to quality; the main risk is geopolitics around Taiwan.
silicon.picks.0.rows.2.why: The toll collector: it prints Nvidia, AMD, Google TPU, Amazon Trainium and the custom ASICs. It wins regardless of whose architecture prevails.
silicon.picks.0.rows.3.priced: Behind on software, networking and system integration; judge it by production adoption, not by benchmarks.
silicon.picks.0.rows.3.why: The only real alternative to Nvidia on the open market; data-centre revenue +57%, targeting >60% annual growth. It sells CPUs and GPUs as a pair.
silicon.picks.1.note: They win only on a step change in efficiency; Nvidia answers with price, software and new inference-oriented chips.
silicon.picks.1.rows.0.exposure: custom AI silicon + optical interconnect + networking
silicon.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Competition with Broadcom, and dependence on execution across a few large orders.
silicon.picks.1.rows.0.why: The second exposure after Broadcom to custom chips and interconnect; the inflection in custom silicon is expected closer to 2028.
silicon.picks.1.rows.1.exposure: a deterministic chip for low-latency inference
silicon.picks.1.rows.1.risk: Less flexible than a GPU; expensive capacity build-out; needs a software ecosystem of its own.
silicon.picks.1.rows.1.why: Built for predictable fast inference — interactive agents and real-time applications.
silicon.picks.1.rows.2.exposure: a chip the size of a whole wafer, for large models
silicon.picks.1.rows.2.risk: Manufacturing concentration, a narrow software ecosystem, slow customer adoption.
silicon.picks.1.rows.2.why: It removes the losses from chip-to-chip communication by using one giant chip — large models and scientific workloads.
silicon.thesis.bigIdea: The market trades AI chips as an either/or bet: ordinary GPUs against the custom chips the cloud giants build for themselves — as though Nvidia were about to be replaced. But there will be no replacement, there will be heterogeneous growth: Nvidia is losing not its lead but only part of the increment, while the whole market grows faster than its share declines. The real barrier is not the chip itself but CUDA and the platform as a whole (chip + network + software + a finished system), which cannot be assembled in one cycle. So the winner is not whoever guesses GPU or ASIC correctly, but whoever takes value under either outcome: Nvidia owns the platform, Broadcom owns custom silicon and networking, and TSMC makes them all.
silicon.thesis.stream.0.t: The chip that does the neural network's arithmetic
silicon.thesis.stream.1.t: The AI chip is what physically performs the model's computation: multiplying billions of numbers while the neural network «thinks». Everything else is assembled around it — the [[server|server]], the [[rack|rack|borrows to buy GPUs]], the building, the electricity. It is the most valuable node in the whole build and the most competitive: only a handful of companies design such chips, but the whole market pays for them. And one player — Nvidia — collects a margin here that hardware almost never sees: around 75% on every dollar of data-centre revenue. That is payment for a platform, not for a chip.
silicon.thesis.stream.10.t: In the listed market, exposure to AI chips is covered first of all by three names, and they are not interchangeable. Nvidia is the default platform. AMD is the only real alternative on the open market. Broadcom is not a competitor to Nvidia but the company that helps the cloud giants build their own chips and sells them the networking to go with them. The difference shows in the margin: it goes to whoever owns the platform or an irreplaceable link, not to whoever merely «makes a fast chip».
silicon.thesis.stream.11.rows.0.1: The default platform: chip + CUDA + network
silicon.thesis.stream.11.rows.2.1: The alternative to Nvidia on the open market
silicon.thesis.stream.12.t: The giants are building their own chips — but they are not throwing Nvidia out
silicon.thesis.stream.13.t: Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta design their own accelerators for four reasons: to cut the cost of their own workload, to secure supply, to have leverage in negotiations with Nvidia, and to tune the chip to their own models. But «our own chip» does not mean «without Nvidia». GPUs are still needed where models change fast, where the cloud's external customers sit, and where the workload is too small to pay back designing a separate chip. The most mature example is Google: its TPU is now seven generations old, and Google still goes on buying GPUs by the billion.
silicon.thesis.stream.14.items.0.n: the most mature — and still not 100%
silicon.thesis.stream.14.items.1.n: for now the most dependent on Nvidia of all
silicon.thesis.stream.14.items.2.l: Trainium chips already in service at AWS
silicon.thesis.stream.14.items.2.n: custom silicon has left the experimental stage
silicon.thesis.stream.16.t: Not all of the $690–715B of annual capex goes on the chips themselves — most of it goes into buildings, electricity and cooling. But within «hardware» the split is telling: Nvidia GPUs are still the largest single line, custom chips are growing faster but are still several times smaller in absolute money, and memory and networking are taking a growing share of the system's value. The money is going not «away from GPUs» but around them — to lift the constraints that the sheer scale of GPU clusters creates.
silicon.thesis.stream.17.items.1.n: growing faster, but still several times smaller
silicon.thesis.stream.17.items.2.n: HBM is taking a growing share
silicon.thesis.stream.18.t: What the market thinks: «Nvidia is about to be replaced»
silicon.thesis.stream.19.t: The common fear runs like this: Nvidia's margin is indecently high, and its largest customers have both the money and the scale to build their own chips — so replacement cannot be far off. From there the market keeps pricing in a rapid collapse in Nvidia's share. The logic is right about one thing: a high margin really does give customers a motive to move to their own silicon. But it underestimates how hard it is to reproduce not the chip but everything around it.
silicon.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: one quarter — and that is after a year of records
silicon.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: the four cloud giants' capex for the year
silicon.thesis.stream.20.t: Why this is growth, not replacement
silicon.thesis.stream.21.t: Building a chip is only part of the task. Assembling the software, the network, the supply chain and reliable operations around it is far harder, and that is exactly where custom projects stall. So the likely outcome is not «the giants replace Nvidia» but «the giants run repetitive internal workloads on their own chips and go on buying Nvidia for the frontier and for customers». Custom silicon's share of accelerator spending grows from 15–25% today to 25–40% by 2030 — and even that does not take money away from Nvidia, so long as the whole market grows faster than its share falls.
silicon.thesis.stream.22.t: The market trades a binary choice, «GPU or ASIC». In reality this is heterogeneous growth: GPUs remain the default platform, and custom chips take only the workloads that are stable and large enough.
silicon.thesis.stream.23.t: Where it is heading — and where the money is going
silicon.thesis.stream.24.t: Technically the centre of gravity is shifting from «pure arithmetic» to memory and communication: the chip that wins is not the one with the most FLOPS (nominal operations per second) but the one that moves data most efficiently — hence the growth of [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]], [[pkg|advanced packaging|became the main event]] and [[netsilicon|networking chips]]. In inference, the binding constraint is increasingly memory rather than compute.
silicon.thesis.stream.25.t: Where the money is going: by 2030 the base case is Nvidia systems $300–420B, custom chips $120–190B, memory $140–210B, networking $120–180B. So GPUs remain the largest pool, but each additional dollar spreads further across custom silicon, memory, networking, optics and power. The best exposure is not a binary Nvidia-versus-ASIC bet but the companies that take value under either outcome.
silicon.thesis.stream.26.rows.0.1: the platform as a whole (chip + CUDA + network) — selling the entire compute domain, not a chip
silicon.thesis.stream.26.rows.1.1: the giants want their own chip but not all the surrounding work — it takes the design and the network
silicon.thesis.stream.26.rows.2.1: almost any winner is printed and packaged there
silicon.thesis.stream.26.rows.3.1: becoming the reliable «second source» wherever a non-Nvidia option is required
silicon.thesis.stream.26.rows.4.1: their own silicon on repetitive workloads, Nvidia on frontier ones
silicon.thesis.stream.27.t: What is already in the price
silicon.thesis.stream.28.t: The quality of these businesses is not in question — the price is. On the sector's analytical scale, valuation attractiveness is lowest precisely at Nvidia (the consensus bet, everyone is already in it): all the growth is in the quote, and the risk is customer concentration and the multiple, not technological obsolescence. Broadcom and AMD are valued a little more gently, and TSMC is the «cheapest» relative to quality. That does not mean «do not buy Nvidia» — it means its margin for error is the smallest of them all.
silicon.thesis.stream.29.items.0.n: all the growth is in the price, the risk is the multiple
silicon.thesis.stream.29.items.1.l: the useful life of a leading-edge chip
silicon.thesis.stream.29.items.1.n: it goes obsolete before it breaks — residual-value risk
silicon.thesis.stream.29.items.2.n: utilisation decides it: at 35% it is 2.8 years, at 85% it is 0.8
silicon.thesis.stream.3.t: Why it is a platform, not a chip
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.0.0: The giants fail to earn back on their AI services
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.0.1: a sharp fall in orders even with AI demand alive — the main underrated risk
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.1.0: Custom ASICs are adopted faster than expected
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.1.1: pressure on Nvidia's and AMD's share, but not on the whole market
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.2.0: A shortage of electricity slows the build-out
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.2.1: the chip exists, but there is [[power|nowhere to connect it|not generation, but connection]] — the whole industry hits this wall
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.3.0: Model efficiency grows faster than demand
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.3.1: fewer chips per workload — but cheaper means more applications
silicon.thesis.stream.31.rows.4.1: unlikely soon, but it would demolish Nvidia's main argument
silicon.thesis.stream.32.t: The first risk is the only genuinely systemic one: it hits the whole industry, and it is worth keeping in mind at every capex report. The others shift shares within the sector but do not zero out the growth. That is exactly why the way in is through those who collect value under either outcome.
silicon.thesis.stream.33.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
silicon.thesis.stream.34.t: AI chips are not a binary transition from «Nvidia» to «custom ASICs» but heterogeneous growth. Nvidia remains the default platform wherever flexibility and speed to a working model matter; custom chips take the stable, high-volume workloads; AMD is bidding for the role of second source; and memory, packaging and networking grow faster than the chips themselves, because computation is increasingly constrained by moving data rather than by arithmetic.
silicon.thesis.stream.35.t: The conclusion: do not choose «GPU or ASIC», hold the companies that take value under both outcomes. Nvidia is the purest and the most expensive way (the platform, but it is all in the price already); Broadcom is the best picks-and-shovels play on the shift to custom silicon and networking; TSMC is the neutral toll collector across every architecture; AMD is the only liquid bet on share gains. And the next winner is not whoever has the fastest processor, but whoever minimises total cost and time to deployment across the whole chain: chip, memory, network, software, power and utilisation.
silicon.thesis.stream.36.head.1: What to cover the theme with
silicon.thesis.stream.36.note: Not a recommendation — a match of instrument to style; the decision is the investor's.
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.0.0: Neutral — not guessing which architecture wins
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.0.1: TSMC: prints and packages almost any winner — GPU, ASIC or TPU
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.1.1: Nvidia: the strongest barrier (CUDA + the system), but the premium is in the price
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.2.0: A bet on the shift to custom silicon
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.2.1: Broadcom: takes the design and the network regardless of whose accelerator wins
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.3.0: A bet on share gains in the open market
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.3.1: AMD: the only liquid alternative to Nvidia — judge it by adoption, not by benchmarks
silicon.thesis.stream.36.rows.4.1: specialist inference: Groq, Cerebras — in small positions; they pay off only on a step change, not on a small edge
silicon.thesis.stream.4.t: What wins is not the fastest silicon but the silicon on which a model is got working fastest. Nvidia sells not an accelerator but everything at once: the chip, ultra-fast [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory, the network between thousands of chips, cooling and — above all — CUDA. CUDA is Nvidia's language, libraries and tools, on which almost all the world's AI software has been written over 15 years. A competitor can build a chip that is no worse in benchmarks and still lose: the customer will not be able to run its models on it reliably and quickly. Delaying a frontier product by a few months costs more than any saving on the price of the chip.
silicon.thesis.stream.5.items.0.n: that, not the chip, is the main barrier for competitors
silicon.thesis.stream.5.items.1.l: what a training chip is chosen on
silicon.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: being late with a model costs more than the hardware premium
silicon.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: the business is still in its fast-growth phase
silicon.thesis.stream.6.t: Not «GPU versus ASIC», but different tasks on different hardware
silicon.thesis.stream.7.t: The market is fragmenting because no single type of chip wins on every count at once — development speed, bandwidth, latency, energy, cost per answer. Training changes every few months and demands flexibility — that is GPU territory. Inference (running an already-trained model) becomes uniform and predictable over time — and then it pays to build [[asic|a separate chip for one task|earns on every chip]]. Hence a simple rule: the more stable the task and the more of it there is, the stronger the argument for custom silicon.
silicon.thesis.stream.8.rows.0.0: Frontier models that change every month
silicon.thesis.stream.8.rows.1.0: A stable model at cloud scale
silicon.thesis.stream.8.rows.1.1: a custom ASIC or Google's TPU
silicon.thesis.stream.8.rows.3.1: a GPU or a specialist chip (Groq)
silicon.thesis.stream.8.rows.5.0: An assistant running on the device itself
silicon.thesis.stream.8.rows.5.1: an NPU in the phone or laptop
silicon.thesis.stream.9.t: Who is at stake — three names, each in its own way
test.picks.0.note: Two companies split the tester market; chipmakers cannot replace them in-house. A bet on AI chips getting more complicated, without being tied to any particular chip.
test.picks.0.rows.0.exposure: testers for logic chips (66% of the market) and for memory (HBM, high-speed DRAM); a de facto monopoly in AI chip test
test.picks.0.rows.0.priced: The monopoly premium is largely in the price; the main risk is the cyclicality of equipment orders.
test.picks.0.rows.0.why: Share of logic testers rose from 56% to 66% in a year, and the operating margin from 29% to 44% on revenue of $7.5B (+47%). Testing AI chips and HBM is getting more expensive faster than chip output is growing.
test.picks.0.rows.1.exposure: the second player in test; a «wafer to data centre» strategy, strong in compute-chip and memory test
test.picks.0.rows.1.risk: After a record first half, Q3 2026 flattens out — the cyclicality of orders; part of the growth is already in the price.
test.picks.0.rows.1.why: Gross margin ~60%, Q2 2026 revenue +104%, on compute chips +~600%. A broader business than Advantest's.
test.picks.1.note: Not the testers themselves, but the mechanics and optical inspection needed around them. More cyclical and lower-margin, but growing on the same demand.
test.picks.1.rows.0.exposure: chip handlers, contact interfaces and consumables through which the chip connects to the tester
test.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Lower margin and scale than Advantest; pronounced cyclicality.
test.picks.1.rows.0.why: The consumable, recurring part of test: contact interfaces wear out and have to be replaced. Grows with the volume of test.
test.picks.1.rows.1.exposure: optical inspection for advanced [[pkg|packaging]] and HBM
test.picks.1.rows.1.risk: Inspection is not test; expensively valued, cyclical.
test.picks.1.rows.1.why: A direct beneficiary of the growth in chiplet packaging and HBM — more checkpoints on every chip.
test.picks.1.rows.2.exposure: measurement and inspection (metrology, inspection) for advanced packaging
test.picks.1.rows.2.risk: An adjacent link; depends on the packaging capex cycle.
test.picks.1.rows.2.why: Grows on the increasing complexity of packaging and HBM; a broad metrology portfolio.
test.picksTakeaway: The main way to play the theme is Advantest: 66% of the logic tester market at a 51.7% operating margin, a bet on AI chips getting more complicated without being tied to any particular chip. Teradyne is the second bet, with a broader business (gross margin ~60%). The adjacent names (Cohu — mechanics and consumables; Camtek and Onto — optical inspection of packaging) grow on the same demand, but at lower margins. The main long-term risk for the whole group is Chinese localisation of test: so far from below (memory, mechanics — Changchuan, Wuhan Jingce), but what to watch is high-speed test.
test.thesis.bigIdea: Every AI chip is checked on an expensive machine before it ships, and the number of those machines needed per chip keeps rising: chiplets and HBM add checkpoints, and some defects only show up under load in an assembled system. So demand for test is growing faster than chip output. The market for these machines is close to a monopoly: Advantest holds 66% of logic testers at a 51.7% operating margin, because neither Nvidia nor TSMC can replace it in-house. The conclusion: test is a way to earn on AI chips getting more complicated without betting on any particular chip; the main bet is Advantest, the main risk is Chinese localisation.
test.thesis.stream.0.t: What it is, and how big the market is
test.thesis.stream.1.t: Test is the mandatory check every chip goes through before it ships: the finished chip is placed on a tester, power and millions of signals are applied, and the response is watched across a range of temperatures. The market for these machines for logic chips is put at $8.7–9.5B for 2026, against $6.9B a year earlier, and the whole test-equipment market is heading for $12–14B. It grows faster than chip output for a simple reason: a complex AI chip occupies a tester for longer, and [[pkg|chiplets|became the main event]] and [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] add new checkpoints — the same output volume now needs more machines.
test.thesis.stream.10.items.0.n: up from 44% for the whole of last year
test.thesis.stream.12.t: Testers are bought by foundries (TSMC), packaging and assembly houses, memory makers and AI chip designers — Nvidia and the owners of [[asic|custom chips|earns on every chip]]. Demand is contracted well ahead: Advantest raised its full-year guidance several times in one year, because AI orders are arriving earlier than expected and are broadening from training into inference — across GPUs, custom ASICs, CPUs and DRAM. How close the tie to the key customer is also shows in TSMC naming Advantest a supplier award winner at the end of 2025 for its ability to ramp capacity quickly against urgent demand.
test.thesis.stream.13.t: Competitors — and what is happening in China
test.thesis.stream.14.t: Two players split the market: Advantest (66% of logic testers) and Teradyne; in memory test Advantest has also strengthened on HBM. The main long-term risk is China. Test belongs to the back end of manufacturing, which is easier to localise than lithography, and the Chinese are already moving: Changchuan (ticker 300604) and Wuhan Jingce are producing testers for memory above 256 Gbit and handlers in volume. But high-speed analogue and RF test, and the checking of advanced packaging, still belong to Advantest and Teradyne. China is biting from below, the top end belongs to the duopoly; the speed of that movement is the key question for the sector.
test.thesis.stream.15.items.1.l: memory already being tested in China
test.thesis.stream.15.items.1.n: Changchuan, Wuhan Jingce — localisation from below
test.thesis.stream.15.items.2.n: the high-value end is not localising yet
test.thesis.stream.15.items.2.v: the top end is the duopoly's
test.thesis.stream.16.t: Where the technology and the capital are going
test.thesis.stream.17.t: Every technological step reinforces the thesis. [[pkg|Chiplets|became the main event]] and 3D assembly multiply the number of checkpoints; HBM4 with hybrid bonding adds more checks; testing in the assembled system is growing ~12% a year. Money and development are concentrating in two players: Advantest is aiming at 70%+ share and pushing its test-development software platform (SiConic), while Teradyne is building a «wafer to data centre» line. Both are betting on the same thing: the complexity of AI chips will grow faster than their number — and with it the share of the value that goes into test.
test.thesis.stream.18.items.0.l: Advantest share of logic testers over the year
test.thesis.stream.18.items.1.n: a new segment for test vendors
test.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: plus recurring revenue on software and service
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.0.0: Chinese testers reach high-speed analogue/RF and advanced packaging
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.0.1: the barrier has been breached from below — the main risk to the duopoly is materialising
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.1.1: pricing power and margin are holding (bullish)
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.2.0: The number of checkpoints per chip keeps rising (chiplets, HBM4, system-level test)
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.2.1: test is outrunning chip output — the thesis holds
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.3.0: A pause in purchases after a new platform is introduced
test.thesis.stream.20.rows.3.1: a cyclical dip in orders, not a structural break
test.thesis.stream.22.t: Test is a near-monopoly part of the chain that cannot be taken in-house, with a margin above 50% and demand growing faster than chip output. Advantest holds 66% of the logic tester market and is heading for 70%.
test.thesis.stream.23.t: The bet is Advantest: AI chips getting more complicated, without being tied to any particular chip, with twofold economics (machines plus software and service). Teradyne is the second bet, with a gross margin of ~60%. The main risk is not the order cycle but Chinese localisation: so far it is coming from below (memory, mechanics), but what to watch is high-speed test and advanced packaging.
test.thesis.stream.3.t: How it works: hardware and software
test.thesis.stream.4.t: Hardware. The chip is connected to the tester through a board and a contact interface. The tester supplies power and sends millions of signals at full speed, measuring the response — voltage, current, delays. A handler holds the temperature: chips are checked both cold and hot, because a defect is often visible only at the edges of the range. Advantest's flagship is the V93000 tester, used to check AI chips in advanced packaging; [[hbm|HBM memory|decoupled from the cycle]] is checked cell by cell through the full height of the stack.
test.thesis.stream.5.t: Software. The test program defines which signals to apply and what counts as normal; adaptive test and data analysis across millions of chips carry more and more of the weight. A separate trend is testing in the already-assembled system (system-level test): some defects only appear under real load, and that segment is growing ~12% a year. Advantest is pushing its test-development software platform (SiConic) into this space too — that is, taking not only the hardware but the creation of the tests. The accumulated database and the software are half the barrier: hardware can be bought, thirty years of data cannot.
test.thesis.stream.6.t: Why Nvidia or TSMC do not do this themselves
test.thesis.stream.7.t: Chipmakers buy testers from Advantest rather than building their own, for several reasons at once: Advantest has 30+ years of failure data across thousands of different products, which no one can assemble alone; designing a chip and building the equipment that checks it are different competencies; and the tester itself has become extraordinarily complex (parallel checking of hundreds of chips, thermal control), so only a specialist serving the whole market can economically hold the leading edge. The proof of the barrier is in the numbers themselves: 66% of the market and a margin above 50%. If test were easy to take in-house, an equipment supplier would have neither that share nor that margin.
test.thesis.stream.8.t: Financials: one of the most profitable parts of the chain
test.thesis.stream.9.t: Test earns better than almost all the rest of the chain. In the April–June 2026 quarter Advantest posted revenue of ¥367.5B (~$2.5B, +39% year on year) and a 51.7% operating margin — against 44% for the whole of last year; the full-year revenue guidance was raised to roughly $9.5B (+26%). Teradyne runs a gross margin of about 60%, its second-quarter revenue doubled, and revenue on compute chips grew almost 600%. The economics are twofold: the one-off sale of a tester ($1–5M) plus recurring revenue on programs, upgrades and servicing of the installed base.
transceivers.competition.concentration: The top four (Huawei, Ciena, Nokia, ZTE) = >80% of optical transport. In the Western market: a Ciena–Nokia (+Infinera) duopoly or oligopoly (Huawei/ZTE banned). DCI top three: Ciena, Nokia, Cisco.
transceivers.competition.entryBarrier: Extreme: a DSP tape-out at 3 nm, InP fabs, electro-optic integration, decades of intellectual property in coherent algorithms. That is exactly why Nokia bought Infinera — R&D scale against Huawei and Ciena.
transceivers.competition.players.0.edge: WaveLogic DSP IP + RLS HyperRail + Nubis linear drive; an 18-month lead in 1.6T
transceivers.competition.shareTrajectory: >$1B of optical orders per quarter; Acacia +200% FY26; 450+ customers; DSP leadership
transceivers.competition.switchingCost: High: an optical module has to be tested and qualified at each customer — a matter of months. The key intellectual property sits in the signal-processing DSP chip (which costs hundreds of millions to develop). But the risk is rising: hyperscalers are starting to buy modules directly, bypassing the systems vendors.
transceivers.demand.backlog: Ciena: $7.7B (+$600M sequentially). Cisco Acacia: >$1B of orders per quarter. Coherent: record bookings. Nokia: €1B of AI & Cloud orders in Q1.
transceivers.demand.takeaway: Demand is outstripping supply across the chain. Backlogs are at records. Cloud is the fastest-growing segment (Ciena +70%). Scale-across is a structural driver (5–20×). But concentration is high (two of Ciena's customers = 34%), and hyperscaler capex is cyclical.
transceivers.dependencies.correlation: Highly correlated with the AI data-centre campus build-out, distributed training (scale-across) and hyperscaler capex (~$650B in 2026). DCI physically connects multi-GW campuses. Links to networking chips (IPoDWDM), the network fabric, and photonics (a shared InP/laser supply).
transceivers.dependencies.takeaway: Optical transport depends upstream on InP lasers (the constraint), DSP IP (3 nm) and ROADM components (Lumentum). Downstream it depends on hyperscaler capex and scale-across adoption. DCI is the physical layer connecting AI campuses.
transceivers.dependencies.upstream.1.sup: Coherent, Lumentum, Nokia/Infinera (→ the Photonics section)
transceivers.expectations.impliedGrowth: Ciena at a P/E of ~120–170× prices in near-flawless execution on 1.6T and holding cloud share while margins expand — zero margin for error. Coherent at a forward P/E of ~35× prices in ~20% D&C growth and a stable ~40% margin — far more reasonable. Fabrinet at a forward ~13× prices in almost nothing: the market values it as a contract assembler rather than as a key constraint in AI optics.
transceivers.expectations.marketBelieves: AI-DCI is a structural multi-year driver (transport +16%, the best growth since 2000), InP supply is the constraint, and the incumbents are capturing all of the increment. So quality (Ciena, Coherent) deservedly trades expensively.
transceivers.expectations.metrics.0.note: the best growth/valuation balance; D&C +41%, a 39.6% margin and expanding, Nvidia's $2B — the premium is justified by the InP content
transceivers.expectations.metrics.1.note: the purest bet on DCI, but the stock is +400% year on year — the multiple leaves no right to disappoint
transceivers.expectations.metrics.2.note: the cheapest key constraint: DCI modules +42%, ~$941M net cash, agnostic to the winner (all of them are customers)
transceivers.expectations.metrics.3.note: the «arms dealer» of line systems (>200k EDFAs), Nvidia's $2B; high beta (~89% annualised volatility)
transceivers.expectations.metrics.4.labe: Gross margin · layers of the chain
transceivers.expectations.metrics.4.note: Ciena's margin is expanding even as the cloud share grows — so far demand outweighs the disruption pressure
transceivers.expectations.takeaway: Ciena's extreme valuation is the price of the purest access to the theme, but at a P/E of ~120–170× all the good news is already in the price. The anomaly in the other direction is Fabrinet: a key constraint in AI optics with a clean balance sheet, priced like an ordinary contract assembler. Coherent is the middle ground between InP quality and a reasonable price.
transceivers.expectations.verdict: Coherent — fair · Ciena — expensive · Fabrinet — cheap
transceivers.expectations.weThink: The demand is real, but the market is underrating the split in margins: the coherent side is protected by the InP shortage, while datacom modules are already in a price war with the Chinese. Ciena at a triple-digit P/E leaves no right to be wrong — any capex pause or acceleration in merchant DSPs hits hard. The divergence from the market is over where the protection actually sits: not in the whole module, but in InP and the DSP.
transceivers.intro:
An optical transceiver is a replaceable module that plugs into a switch port and converts an electrical signal into light and back again. Inside a compute cluster it connects servers, switches and GPU racks; between sites it connects data centres tens and hundreds of kilometres apart. An electrical signal decays quickly in copper, so anything beyond a couple of metres travels as light — and each end of the link needs a transceiver.

How it works. On the transmit side a control chip produces a stream of bits, and a driver makes the light source blink in time with them. The source is a laser; to switch fast enough, the steady beam is passed through a separate modulator that blocks or passes it billions of times a second. Such a laser with an integrated modulator (an EML) is made from indium phosphide (InP) — a material that can both emit and modulate light; the alternative is silicon photonics, where the modulators are made directly on silicon. On the receive side a photodetector turns the light back into a weak current, and on fast links a digital signal processor (DSP) cleans up the distorted signal and recovers the bits; at medium speeds a simpler retimer takes its place, merely re-squaring the pulse edges.

Speed is raised generation by generation: 400G → 800G → 1.6T, and each step roughly doubles the throughput of a single port. But the higher the speed, the more individual lasers a module needs and the faster they must switch, while the DSP has to move to an ever finer node (3 nm for the 1.6T generation) to deliver the speed at an acceptable power draw. For long links between data centres, coherent modules (400ZR/800ZR) are used: their DSP encodes not only the brightness but the phase of the light, packing far more data into the same beam, and it plugs straight into the switch, displacing separate transport systems.

The critical point is the lasers. The industry's binding constraint is not module assembly but the supply of the indium phosphide lasers themselves: there are only a handful of InP fabs in the world, and every generation needs more of them, faster. Dell'Oro states outright that supply is probably the main factor holding growth back. The relief comes from moving InP production from 3-inch to 6-inch wafers: one wafer yields more than 4× as many devices at half the cost per device (estimate). But an InP fab, decades of accumulated work in electro-optic integration and qualification at every customer are things only a few companies have — which is why the component shortage keeps prices up.

Who is investing, and how much. Demand is pulled by the hyperscalers: their infrastructure capex is put at ~$650B in 2026 (about 75% of it AI-related), and they finance connectivity at almost any price — without it, expensive GPUs sit idle. Nvidia has invested ~$2B in optical component makers to secure supply. Module prices: 400ZR ~$1,500–3,000, 800ZR ~$3,000–6,000; the move to 800G cuts energy per bit transmitted by almost 99% against older systems (Cignal AI), and energy in a data centre has long cost more than the hardware itself.

The market. Dell'Oro forecasts optical transport above $18B in 2026 (+16% — the best growth since 2000); standalone coherent modules ~$2B (+37%), with 800ZR shipments above 200k ports. Manufacturing is concentrated: datacom modules by volume are held by several Chinese assemblers, while the components and the coherent side are held by a few Western owners of InP fabs and DSP designers.

A term that will come up later: the «node» (process technology), for example 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip-manufacturing technology. The figure in nanometres nominally denotes transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors, and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and more expensive that node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel are capable of the leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); the «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are a high-volume, cheap technology available to many.
transceivers.marketSizing.bomShare.note: optical transport/DCI is a smaller share of AI cluster capex than the switch fabric, but it gates inter-datacentre connectivity. Scale-across is a structural multiplier.

transceivers.mentalModel.drivers.1.note: 400ZR ~$1,500–3,000, 800ZR ~$3,000–6,000, 1.6T dearer still. Price per port rises automatically with each generation — without a single new customer. Ciena's WaveLogic 6 (1.6T) holds a lead of >18 months.
transceivers.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: margins diverge: the coherent side (Coherent at ~40% gross margin, Ciena's DSP) is protected by the InP shortage; datacom modules (InnoLight, Eoptolink) are commoditising under Chinese pressure. The mix decides whether this is a premium business or a race to the bottom on price.
transceivers.mentalModel.framework: The money in optical modules is made because every connection — inside a data centre and between data centres — requires its own transceiver, and every new generation (400G → 800G → 1.6T) sells more bits per dollar at a higher price per port. The position rests on two scarce things: indium phosphide (InP) lasers and coherent DSP chips on a leading-edge node — only a handful of companies produce them, and without them speed cannot be raised. Margins diverge by the type of content: the coherent side (Ciena, Coherent) is protected by the InP shortage and years of customer qualification, while simple datacom modules are commoditising under price pressure from Chinese manufacturers.
transceivers.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = ports shipped × ASP per port (which rises with each generation) × the share of high-margin content (InP lasers + coherent DSP versus a cheap datacom module)
developing a single DSP costs hundreds of millions and requires a tape-out at TSMC 3 nm. Ciena WaveLogic 6, Acacia Kibo, Marvell 1.6T — entry is closed to all but four or five players. This is where the core intellectual property sits.
InP lasers are the binding constraint of the whole chain (Dell'Oro: «supply is probably the main factor holding growth back»). Coherent is ramping 6-inch InP wafers: >4× the devices at less than half the cost. Fab scale is pricing power in a shortage.
Qualification and certification at the customer

every module goes through months of testing at the customer — which locks them in. But the protection is weakening: hyperscalers are buying ZR modules directly from the manufacturers, bypassing the systems vendors (cloud is 46% of Ciena's revenue).
Nvidia has put $2B into Coherent and ~$2B into Lumentum, plus multi-year purchase commitments. That is both validation and a tie to Nvidia's roadmap (Spectrum-X, CPO) — an ecosystem advantage newcomers do not have.
pluggable coherent economics beat everything: 800G cuts energy per bit by up to ~99% against older transponders. But that same cheapening commoditises the low end — a cost advantage is not uniquely defensible for long.
the weakest vector: 800G/1.6T datacom transceivers (non-coherent) are a price-war battlefield. InnoLight and Eoptolink are adding volume and pressing ASPs down. There is almost no protection here — only scale and generation speed.
transceivers.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is uneven: strong on the coherent side (a 3 nm DSP + the InP shortage + Nvidia alliances) and weak in datacom modules, where Chinese manufacturers are running a price race. The real competitive advantage is not in the module itself but in the two key constraints beneath it: InP lasers and DSP chips. While InP supply is limited the pricing power holds; when 6-inch InP and merchant DSPs expand supply (2027), the pressure will grow.
