transceivers.picksTakeaway: Coherent is the best growth/valuation blend (forward P/E ~35×, NVIDIA's $2B, InP breadth). Ciena is the highest-conviction pure play, but at a P/E of ~120–170× it is a starter position, to be added to on drawdowns. Fabrinet is the cheapest chokepoint ($941M net cash, DCI +42%, a contract-manufacturing multiple). Marvell offers merchant-DSP leverage. Nokia is the value turnaround. NEC is the subsea scarcity play. Enter in stages: current valuations argue against full positions in July 2026.
transceivers.problems.items.0.gap: To enter, a competitor needs an InP fab of its own (indium phosphide; the move to 6 inches and reaching a working yield took Coherent from 2025 to 2027) plus a DSP on a 3 nm process, and TSMC's 3 nm capacity is already allocated. Qualifying each new module at a customer means months of testing. The entry barrier is extreme: a first DSP tape-out at 3 nm (a tape-out being the release of a chip into production), an InP fab, and decades of proprietary work in coherent algorithms, all at once.
transceivers.problems.items.0.problem: Growth in optics is bottlenecked on indium phosphide lasers (InP — the material that can both emit and modulate light). Every transceiver needs a light source, and on high-speed links that means an InP laser with an integrated modulator (an EML — a laser that blinks in time with the bits); in the move 400G → 800G → 1.6T (each step doubling the port's speed) a module needs more lasers, and faster ones. There are few InP fabs in the world, and they are the scarcest link of all: Dell'Oro states outright that «supply is probably the main factor holding growth back». Lead times are stretched across the whole chain, Ciena has an order queue several quarters long, and demand is outrunning supply at every level.
transceivers.problems.items.0.solution: Coherent is moving InP (indium phosphide) production from 3-inch to 6-inch wafers: yields are higher, and one wafer produces more than 4× as many devices at half the cost per device. In parallel the DSP chip market (the chips that process and recover the signal) is widening: Marvell is producing a merchant DSP for third-party assemblers (COLORZ 1600), and 1.6T chips are already entering production (Ciena WaveLogic 6 on a 3 nm process, Cisco Kibo). Module assembly capacity is being added by Fabrinet, InnoLight and Eoptolink. The shortage should ease by 2027.
transceivers.problems.items.0.winners: Coherent — the largest InP (indium phosphide) scale and the move to 6-inch wafers, plus a $2B partnership with NVIDIA; Lumentum — lasers and line systems, with a ~$2B NVIDIA partnership; Fabrinet — contract assembly, the cheapest of the scarce links, working for every vendor at once. They win precisely because an InP fab of one's own, decades of accumulated work in electro-optic integration and qualification at every customer are things only they have — and none of it can be reproduced quickly.
transceivers.problems.takeaway: Relieving the scarcest link, InP (indium phosphide), reinforces the incumbent leaders: both the capacity and the accumulated know-how belong to Coherent and Lumentum. Marvell's merchant DSP opens a narrow new lane, but the component shortage itself stays with the same fab owners.

transceivers.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: The risk: cloud is higher-volume and potentially lower-margin. Against it: Ciena's operating margin +1,130 bps y/y. Watch the cloud margin mix closely.
transceivers.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Hyperscalers buy ZR directly from module makers and ride over the incumbents' line systems. Cloud has grown to 46% of Ciena's revenue. Ciena's margins EXPANDED despite the cloud mix — so far demand outweighs the pressure.
transceivers.roadmap.generations.2.note: Ciena WL6 = 1.6T single carrier (a >18-month lead); Acacia Kibo and Marvell COLORZ 1600 sampling
transceivers.roadmap.takeaway: 400ZR → 800ZR → 1.6T ZR: each generation raises both bandwidth and the addressable market. Pluggable ZR is real disruption but additive to the total coherent value chain. The 1.6T leadership race: Ciena has a >18-month lead. Coherent-Lite and inside-the-data-centre optics are the next frontier (10× the volumes). The subsea supercycle is strategically scarce.

transceivers.tldr.0: Optical transport: ~$16B (2025) → >$18B (2026, +16%; Dell'Oro — the best growth since 2000). Direct DCI purchases (data centre to data centre links) +40% over the year. Scale-across (training one model spread over several sites) = 5–20× more bandwidth between data centres. Coherent pluggable modules (replaceable long-reach modules) ~$1.8–2.0B (2025) → >$5B by 2029 (~30% a year); >50% of WDM bandwidth (transmission by light on many wavelengths in one fibre) already runs on pluggable modules.
transceivers.tldr.1: Ciena is the purest bet: FY26 guidance $6.3B (+32%); cloud +70% year on year; backlog $7.7B; WaveLogic 6 = 1.6T (1.6 terabits per second on a single optical carrier) with a lead of >18 months. Cisco/Acacia: >$1B of optical orders per quarter, +200% in FY26. Nokia+Infinera: a combined share of ~20%, second place.
transceivers.tldr.2: The central tension: pluggable modules (ZR — replaceable modules in place of separate transport boxes) pull value away from transport boxes towards DSPs, modules and line systems. The hyperscalers (the largest cloud operators) buy ZR directly. But Ciena's margin is expanding (operating margin +1,130 bps y/y) — so far AI demand outweighs the displacement pressure. The best balance: Coherent (growth versus valuation) + Fabrinet (the cheapest of the scarce links).
transceivers.unitEconomics.takeaway: Pluggable ZR has dramatically better economics (cost per bit, power per bit). But revenue per port is lower than for proprietary transponders. Ciena is expanding margins despite the cloud mix (+1,130 bps operating margin y/y) — so far demand outweighs disruption. Fabrinet is the cheapest exposure (12–13% gross margin, high ROIC, net cash).

transceivers.verdict.keyQuestion: Is AI-DCI demand growing faster than pluggable ZR and direct hyperscaler purchasing are diluting the systems vendors' margins?
transceivers.verdict.sizing: Optical transport: $16B → >$18B. Pluggables: ~$2B → >$5B by 2029. IPoDWDM: $4.4B by 2030. DCI doubles by ~2030 at a low-to-mid-teens CAGR.
transceivers.verdict.summary: AI-DCI (connecting data centres to one another) and scale-across (training one model spread over several sites) are a genuine multi-year structural driver; the transport market is growing 16%, its best showing since 2000. The competitive advantages are strong: coherent DSP chips (which process and recover the signal) on a 3 nm process, InP fabs (indium phosphide — the laser material), an installed base of long-haul optical equipment (ROADM) and qualification at the largest operators. But pluggable ZR (replaceable long-reach modules plugged straight into the switch) is squeezing the content of separate transport boxes, and the multiples are extreme (Ciena P/E ~120–170). The answer: Coherent (the best balance of growth and valuation, a $2B partnership with Nvidia) + Fabrinet (the cheapest of the scarce links), with Ciena on drawdowns.
transceivers.whatIsIt: This is a replaceable module about the size of a memory stick that plugs into a socket on a network switch and turns an electrical signal into light — and, at the other end of the link, light back into electricity. Inside and between data centres data travels as light down a strand of glass, because in a copper wire the signal decays badly after only a couple of metres. Each end of every such optical link carries one of these modules, and a large AI cluster needs hundreds of thousands of them — otherwise the expensive accelerators cannot be connected to one another.
